title: Claude Architect: 453 questions and answers
coverage: 453 original cards across 30 curriculum lessons and five domains, authored to cover every testable point in each lesson text (rules, distinctions, commands, exam traps, practice-scenario concepts, build-exercise outcomes). Not official exam questions.
source_status: Independent community guide; these cards are original and are not official exam questions.

cards.prompt: A Messages API response requests a client-side tool. After the application runs it, what lets Claude use the result?

options.text: Send the result linked to its tool-use ID with the conversation history.
options.rationale: Claude needs the observation and its association with the requested tool call.

options.text: Start a new conversation containing only the result.
options.rationale: This discards the task and the call that the observation answers.

options.text: Ask the same question again without adding the result.
options.rationale: Repeating the prompt does not tell the model what the tool returned.

options.text: Treat a successful tool execution as completion of the user's task.
options.rationale: A tool result may require further reasoning or additional actions.

cards.explanation: Claude needs the observation and its association with the requested tool call.

cards.prompt: An answer stops with max_tokens while its JSON is unfinished. How should the application classify it?

options.text: A completed tool call awaiting execution.
options.rationale: Truncation is not a valid tool-call completion signal.

options.text: A definitive refusal to answer.
options.rationale: A token limit and a refusal have different meanings.

options.text: Incomplete output requiring recovery.
options.rationale: The token limit ended generation before a usable result was established.

options.text: Successful output because HTTP returned 200.
options.rationale: Transport success does not imply complete generated content.

cards.explanation: The token limit ended generation before a usable result was established.

cards.prompt: An agent reaches its execution budget with required work unfinished. What should the result state?

options.text: Success because the configured loop has ended.
options.rationale: Finishing the loop is different from finishing the task.

options.text: Success if the final sentence sounds confident.
options.rationale: Wording cannot establish that requirements were satisfied.

options.text: No result until another unlimited loop finishes.
options.rationale: Removing limits defeats the configured resource boundary.

options.text: Partial completion with the unmet work and stop reason.
options.rationale: Budget exhaustion is an operational stop, not evidence of task success.

cards.explanation: Budget exhaustion is an operational stop, not evidence of task success.

cards.prompt: The response text says it is finished, but stop_reason is tool_use. What drives the next step?

options.text: Inspect and handle the requested tool calls under policy.
options.rationale: Structured API signals determine control flow; execution still needs validation.

options.text: Ignore the calls because the text says finished.
options.rationale: Natural-language phrasing is not the protocol signal.

options.text: Execute a tool inferred only from the final sentence.
options.rationale: Use the actual tool request and arguments, not an inferred action.

options.text: Treat the response as a final verified answer.
options.rationale: A requested operation has not yet supplied its result.

cards.explanation: Structured API signals determine control flow; execution still needs validation.

cards.prompt: A loop iteration returns a response whose stop_reason is end_turn. What should the controlling code do next?

options.text: Exit the loop and return the final response to the user.
options.rationale: end_turn is the model's signal that the work is finished, so the loop terminates and the answer is delivered.

options.text: Run the most recent tool once more to confirm its result.
options.rationale: No tool was requested; re-running one adds work the model never asked for.

options.text: Append an empty tool result and send the conversation again.
options.rationale: There is no pending tool call to answer, so another round trip produces nothing.

options.text: Keep iterating until the configured maximum count is reached.
options.rationale: Caps are a safety bound, not a reason to keep calling after the model has finished.

cards.explanation: end_turn means Claude has completed its work, so the loop terminates and the final response goes to the user.

cards.prompt: An engineer proposes ending the loop when Claude's reply contains a phrase such as "task complete". Why does the lesson reject that?

options.text: Claude never produces such phrases, so a loop checking for them would never end.
options.rationale: Claude can and does produce completion-sounding phrases; the problem is that they are ambiguous.

options.text: Natural language is ambiguous: a finishing phrase may describe one step, not the task.
options.rationale: Phrases like this are ambiguous; stop_reason exists precisely to remove that ambiguity.

options.text: Text blocks are stripped from the response before the application can read them.
options.rationale: Text blocks are returned normally; they simply are not a reliable completion signal.

options.text: Those phrases appear only when a response was truncated by the max_tokens limit.
options.rationale: Completion phrases are unrelated to truncation and can appear in any response.

cards.explanation: Natural language is ambiguous: Claude might announce finishing one file while intending to continue, so stop_reason is the authoritative signal.

cards.prompt: Where does a maximum iteration count belong in a well-built agentic loop?

options.text: As the primary termination check, replacing inspection of stop_reason entirely.
options.rationale: Caps as the primary mechanism either cut off useful work or run iterations that are not needed.

options.text: As the remedy for an agent that keeps exiting before its work is finished.
options.rationale: Caps address runaway loops; premature exit is fixed by checking stop_reason correctly.

options.text: As a safety bound that logs a warning, with stop_reason still driving termination.
options.rationale: A cap is acceptable as a backstop against runaway loops while stop_reason remains the control signal.

options.text: As a per-tool limit that cancels any tool invoked more than once in a run.
options.rationale: Repeated calls to the same tool are often legitimate, and this is not what a cap does.

cards.explanation: Iteration caps are acceptable only as a safety net against runaway agents; stop_reason remains the primary loop control.

cards.prompt: To stop an agent from returning plain text, a developer sets tool_choice to "any" on every request. What goes wrong?

options.text: The model can no longer read tool results from earlier iterations of the loop.
options.rationale: Forcing tool choice does not affect the model's access to prior tool results.

options.text: The API stops returning a stop_reason field, so the loop loses its signal.
options.rationale: stop_reason is still returned; the damage is that the model is never allowed to finish.

options.text: Tool results are no longer appended automatically to the conversation history.
options.rationale: Appending results is the application's job either way and is unaffected by tool_choice.

options.text: The model must call a tool even when the task is done, so the loop never terminates.
options.rationale: Forcing tool use removes the model's ability to signal completion, producing an infinite loop.

cards.explanation: Forcing tool_choice to "any" means Claude cannot end its turn naturally, so the agent keeps calling tools after the work is complete.

cards.prompt: A loop branches only on tool_use and end_turn, but the live API also returns values such as pause_turn and stop_sequence. Which rule keeps it safe?

options.text: Treat any value other than end_turn as unfinished work and inspect why before continuing.
options.rationale: Only end_turn means completion, so every other value is handled as not finished rather than assumed to be tool_use.

options.text: Treat any value other than tool_use as a completed turn and return the text.
options.rationale: This reports truncated, paused, or refused turns to the user as finished answers.

options.text: Map every unrecognised value onto end_turn so the loop always terminates cleanly.
options.rationale: Terminating on unknown values hides truncation and refusals behind an apparently normal answer.

options.text: Resend the identical request until one of the two familiar values comes back.
options.rationale: Blind retries burn tokens and never address the reason the turn stopped.

cards.explanation: Only end_turn means finished, so a production loop treats every other stop_reason as "not finished, check why" instead of assuming tool_use.

cards.prompt: An agent chooses its tools from the current context rather than following a developer-defined order. Which statement matches the lesson's position?

options.text: Fixed tool sequences are preferred because a predetermined order is easier to audit and log.
options.rationale: The lesson favours model-driven selection; auditability does not outweigh its flexibility.

options.text: Model-driven selection is favoured for its adaptability, but deterministic compliance needs override it.
options.rationale: The model adapts to unplanned situations, except where financial, security, or regulatory rules demand programmatic enforcement.

options.text: Model-driven selection removes any need for programmatic enforcement in financial workflows.
options.rationale: High-stakes workflows still require code-level enforcement regardless of how the model selects tools.

options.text: Model-driven selection applies only to the first call; later calls follow a fixed chain.
options.rationale: There is no such restriction; the model keeps choosing tools throughout the loop.

cards.explanation: Model-driven decision-making is preferred because it handles cases the developer never mapped, with programmatic enforcement taking over when compliance must be deterministic.

cards.prompt: Each iteration of the loop sends a request to the Messages API. What must that request carry?

options.text: Only the newest tool result, since the service retains the earlier turns for you.
options.rationale: The API is stateless for this purpose; omitting history strips the task and prior reasoning.

options.text: The tool definitions alone, because the model re-derives the task from the schemas.
options.rationale: Schemas describe capabilities, not the user's request or what has happened so far.

options.text: The conversation history: system prompt, prior messages, and the previous iteration's tool results.
options.rationale: The full accumulated history is what lets Claude reason about the new observation in context.

options.text: Only the original question, with the tool results condensed into a single sentence.
options.rationale: Condensing away the actual results loses the detail the next decision depends on.

cards.explanation: Every iteration sends the accumulated conversation history, including the system prompt, prior messages, and the tool results from the previous turn.

cards.prompt: A request returns HTTP 200 with stop_reason set to refusal. How should the loop classify it?

options.text: As a transport failure to retry with the identical payload.
options.rationale: Nothing failed in transport; resending the same request invites the same outcome.

options.text: As a normal completion, because the HTTP status code was 200.
options.rationale: A 200 status says the call succeeded, not that the model produced the requested work.

options.text: As a tool_use turn whose tool block was omitted from the response body.
options.rationale: No tool was requested; treating it as a tool turn leaves the loop waiting for a call that does not exist.

options.text: As a turn that ended without doing the work, handled separately from end_turn.
options.rationale: Current models can decline on an otherwise-normal 200 response, so refusal is a distinct outcome the loop must handle.

cards.explanation: Refusal is its own stop_reason on a successful HTTP response: the turn ended without completing the task and needs handling separate from end_turn.

cards.prompt: Which description matches an agentic loop as the lesson defines it?

options.text: Deterministic control flow in application code that drives repeated Messages API calls.
options.rationale: The loop is code-level control flow whose branching is decided by the stop_reason field.

options.text: A prompt pattern that asks Claude to keep working until it declares itself finished.
options.rationale: Relying on the model to announce completion in prose is the natural-language anti-pattern.

options.text: A retry wrapper that resends failed requests using increasing backoff intervals.
options.rationale: Retrying failures is error handling, not the execution cycle behind an agent.

options.text: A chat feature that holds a single conversation turn open for a longer period.
options.rationale: The loop spans many request and response cycles rather than extending one turn.

cards.explanation: An agentic loop is deterministic control flow defined in code, not a prompt trick, a retry wrapper, or a chatbot turn.

cards.prompt: After executing a tool Claude requested, how does the application add the outcome to the conversation?

options.text: Replace the assistant's tool_use block with the raw output before resending the history.
options.rationale: Overwriting the request loses the call the result answers and corrupts the history.

options.text: Append the assistant's response, then a user message carrying the tool_result for that call.
options.rationale: The assistant turn and the tool_result message together give Claude both the request and its observation.

options.text: Append the output as a system message placed ahead of the original instructions.
options.rationale: Tool results are not system instructions and do not belong at the front of the conversation.

options.text: Store the output in the tool definition so the model reads it on the next call.
options.rationale: Tool definitions describe inputs and behaviour; they are not a channel for results.

cards.explanation: The assistant response is appended, followed by a user message containing the tool_result, so Claude sees both the call and its outcome.

cards.prompt: Three independent analyses must feed a single report. Which design permits parallel work while keeping ownership of the final result clear?

options.text: Let workers continually delegate the complete task among themselves.
options.rationale: Unbounded delegation obscures ownership and creates unnecessary coordination.

options.text: Run specialist workers concurrently and have a coordinator reconcile their findings.
options.rationale: The coordinator owns synthesis while independent work can overlap.

options.text: Run the analyses sequentially because there is one final report.
options.rationale: A shared output does not make the analyses depend on each other.

options.text: Let each worker publish its own final report as the combined answer.
options.rationale: Separate reports do not resolve inconsistent findings or missing coverage.

cards.explanation: The coordinator owns synthesis while independent work can overlap.

cards.prompt: An analyst needs the researcher's evidence before drawing conclusions. What should the coordinator do?

options.text: Remove the researcher and keep the dependency unchanged.
options.rationale: Deleting a worker does not supply the missing facts.

options.text: Obtain the evidence, then pass it into the analysis task.
options.rationale: A data dependency must be satisfied even when other work can run concurrently.

options.text: Start both with no evidence exchange.
options.rationale: The analyst would lack its required input.

options.text: Ask the analyst to invent likely research findings.
options.rationale: Guessed evidence cannot replace the upstream result.

cards.explanation: A data dependency must be satisfied even when other work can run concurrently.

cards.prompt: A user asks a simple question already supported by available context. Must every specialist run?

options.text: Yes; the agent with the longest prompt must run first.
options.rationale: Prompt length does not determine task relevance.

options.text: No; multi-agent systems cannot answer simple questions.
options.rationale: The architecture can still handle simple requests directly.

options.text: No; invoke only the work needed for this request.
options.rationale: Unnecessary delegation adds cost and failure paths without supplying missing evidence.

options.text: Yes; every request must use the complete agent roster.
options.rationale: A fixed roster can waste work on irrelevant stages.

cards.explanation: Unnecessary delegation adds cost and failure paths without supplying missing evidence.

cards.prompt: Two workers give incompatible recommendations. What is the coordinator's strongest next action?

options.text: Choose whichever worker answered first.
options.rationale: Response speed is not a correctness criterion.

options.text: Combine both recommendations without mentioning the conflict.
options.rationale: That conceals a decision the evidence has not resolved.

options.text: Ask each worker to repeat its conclusion unchanged.
options.rationale: Repetition supplies no new basis for resolution.

options.text: Compare assumptions and supporting evidence before resolving or reporting disagreement.
options.rationale: Different premises or evidence quality can explain the conflict.

cards.explanation: Different premises or evidence quality can explain the conflict.

cards.prompt: A team proposes letting the search subagent hand its output straight to the synthesis subagent to save a coordinator round trip. What does hub-and-spoke require?

options.text: Allow it whenever both subagents were given the same tool restrictions.
options.rationale: Matching tool access does not change the routing rule; the coordinator still owns every exchange.

options.text: Allow it while the coordinator is busy aggregating other subagents' results.
options.rationale: Convenience is exactly the justification the pattern rejects for bypassing the hub.

options.text: Reject it; every message moving between subagents passes through the coordinator.
options.rationale: Centralised routing is the foundational constraint, and perceived efficiency does not justify breaking it.

options.text: Reject it only when the two subagents run with different system prompts.
options.rationale: The rule is unconditional rather than dependent on how the subagents are configured.

cards.explanation: All inter-subagent communication flows through the coordinator; direct subagent-to-subagent messaging is never the right answer here.

cards.prompt: Why does hub-and-spoke orchestration insist that every message pass through the coordinator?

options.text: It concentrates observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow in one place.
options.rationale: Centralising the traffic is what makes logging, uniform recovery, and deliberate context control possible.

options.text: It lets subagents share a memory store that survives between their invocations.
options.rationale: No shared store exists; subagent invocations are independent of one another.

options.text: It removes the need for decomposition because subagents negotiate scope among themselves.
options.rationale: Decomposition is the coordinator's job, and subagents negotiating scope would mean direct communication.

options.text: It guarantees every subagent inherits the coordinator's system prompt automatically.
options.rationale: Nothing is inherited automatically; context must be written into each subagent's prompt.

cards.explanation: Routing everything through the coordinator gives one point for observability, one error-handling policy, and deliberate control over what each subagent sees.

cards.prompt: A coordinator spawns a synthesis subagent after two research subagents finish. What context does the synthesis subagent begin with?

options.text: The coordinator's full conversation history, including both research subagents' outputs.
options.rationale: Subagents inherit no conversation history from the coordinator.

options.text: The coordinator's system prompt plus every tool result produced earlier in the run.
options.rationale: The coordinator's system prompt is not inherited, and prior tool results are not visible.

options.text: A shared workspace holding whatever findings the other subagents have written so far.
options.rationale: There is no shared memory or global state between agents in this architecture.

options.text: Only the information the coordinator explicitly wrote into its prompt for this invocation.
options.rationale: Subagent context is isolated, so the prompt is the only channel for anything it needs.

cards.explanation: Subagent context is isolated: the synthesis agent sees only what the coordinator deliberately placed in its prompt.

cards.prompt: A coordinator invokes the same web search subagent twice during one workflow. What does the second invocation know about the first?

options.text: Everything, because each subagent role keeps a memory that persists across invocations.
options.rationale: Subagents do not share memory between invocations; every call starts clean.

options.text: Nothing, unless the coordinator restates the earlier results inside the second prompt.
options.rationale: Each invocation is independent, so prior output has to be passed in again explicitly.

options.text: Its earlier queries only, which the runtime caches to prevent duplicate searches.
options.rationale: No query cache carries forward between invocations.

options.text: Its earlier results only, which are appended automatically to the new context.
options.rationale: Nothing is appended automatically; the coordinator must supply it.

cards.explanation: Every subagent invocation is independent, so the second call knows nothing of the first unless the coordinator repeats that information in the prompt.

cards.prompt: A multi-agent system delivers a market report covering two of the company's six product lines. Every subagent handled its assignment thoroughly. Where is the defect?

options.text: In the coordinator's decomposition, which never assigned the other four product lines.
options.rationale: A gap in scope rather than depth traces back to what the coordinator assigned in the first place.

options.text: In the search subagent's queries, which were worded too narrowly to surface the rest.
options.rationale: The search agent covered what it was given; it was never asked about the missing lines.

options.text: In the synthesis subagent, which dropped sections it could not attribute to a source.
options.rationale: Synthesis combined everything it received; the missing material never reached it.

options.text: In the document analysis subagent, which had no access to the missing material.
options.rationale: Access was not the constraint; no agent was assigned those product lines at all.

cards.explanation: Output that is incomplete in scope traces to the coordinator's task decomposition, not to the subagents that executed their assignments.

cards.prompt: A coordinator consistently splits topics too narrowly. Does adding more subagents close the coverage gap?

options.text: Yes, because extra capacity lets the system reach subtopics nobody assigned.
options.rationale: Unassigned subtopics stay unassigned no matter how many agents are available.

options.text: Yes, because each additional subagent widens its own scope when it finds a gap.
options.rationale: Subagents work within the assignment they are given; they do not expand it.

options.text: No, because additional subagents simply receive equally narrow assignments.
options.rationale: The constraint is the decomposition itself, so more workers inherit the same limitation.

options.text: No, because the correct fix is to let the subagents compare coverage with each other.
options.rationale: Subagents comparing notes would be direct communication, which the pattern forbids.

cards.explanation: More subagents receive equally narrow assignments; the fix is improving the coordinator's decomposition logic.

cards.prompt: A coordinator delegates one broad research question to four subagents. How should it assign the work?

options.text: Send all four the same question and keep whichever answer arrives first.
options.rationale: Four identical searches duplicate effort and still leave the topic partly uncovered.

options.text: Send all four the same question and merge the four answers into the report.
options.rationale: Merging duplicate coverage wastes capacity that distinct subtopics would have used.

options.text: Send each a different phrasing of the same question to improve overall recall.
options.rationale: Rewording the same question still points every agent at the same ground.

options.text: Give each a distinct subtopic or source type so their searches do not overlap.
options.rationale: Partitioning the research scope minimises duplication and widens the coverage the report gets.

cards.explanation: The coordinator partitions research scope, assigning distinct subtopics or source types so subagents do not cover the same ground.

cards.prompt: Reviewing a synthesis draft, the coordinator finds two subtopics thinly covered. What does the lesson expect next?

options.text: Re-delegate targeted queries for the thin subtopics, then re-invoke synthesis.
options.rationale: Iterative refinement means evaluating output for gaps and re-delegating until coverage is sufficient.

options.text: Publish the draft and record the thin coverage in a caveat at the end.
options.rationale: Documenting a gap is not the same as closing it, and the coordinator can still act.

options.text: Ask the synthesis subagent to expand those sections from what it already holds.
options.rationale: Synthesis cannot add coverage it was never given; new research has to be delegated.

options.text: Spawn a second synthesis subagent to rewrite the draft more thoroughly.
options.rationale: A second writer faces the same missing input as the first.

cards.explanation: Coordination is iterative: the coordinator detects gaps, re-delegates targeted research, and re-runs synthesis until coverage is adequate.

cards.prompt: A combined report treats each topic it covers in depth but omits whole categories. Which diagnostic does the lesson prescribe?

options.text: Missing scope usually means the subagents exhausted their token budgets early.
options.rationale: Budget exhaustion would shorten depth within assigned topics, not remove categories entirely.

options.text: Missing scope points at the coordinator's decomposition rather than at any subagent.
options.rationale: Gaps in breadth almost always mean the coordinator never assigned those categories.

options.text: Missing scope points at the synthesis step that assembled the finished sections.
options.rationale: Synthesis works from what it receives, so absent categories were absent upstream.

options.text: Missing scope means the subagents' tool restrictions were configured too tightly.
options.rationale: Tool restrictions would limit how an assigned topic is researched, not which topics exist.

cards.explanation: When output is incomplete in scope rather than depth, the coordinator's decomposition is almost always the root cause.

cards.prompt: Which responsibility belongs to the coordinator rather than to a subagent?

options.text: Performing the specialised retrieval or analysis for one assigned subtopic.
options.rationale: That is precisely the spoke's job, not the hub's.

options.text: Choosing the exact query wording for its own assigned source type.
options.rationale: A subagent works out its own method within the goal it was handed.

options.text: Deciding which specialists to invoke and aggregating what they return.
options.rationale: Selection, context passing, aggregation, and error handling are the coordinator's responsibilities.

options.text: Returning finished results to whichever agent most recently requested them.
options.rationale: Results always go back to the coordinator, and subagents do not request work from each other.

cards.explanation: The coordinator decomposes the task, selects and invokes subagents, passes context, and aggregates results; subagents execute their assigned specialty.

cards.prompt: A fresh subagent must investigate one failing test. Which handoff is most useful?

options.text: Send the full repository as text before stating the task.
options.rationale: An indiscriminate dump adds noise without defining the investigation.

options.text: Pass the parent's conclusion and require the worker to confirm it.
options.rationale: This encourages confirmation rather than independent examination.

options.text: Provide the failure, relevant files, constraints and expected result format.
options.rationale: A focused handoff supplies the information needed to perform and report the task.

options.text: Pass only the worker's role name and assume it knows the failure.
options.rationale: A role label does not communicate the current task evidence.

cards.explanation: A focused handoff supplies the information needed to perform and report the task.

cards.prompt: In the current Agent SDK, what does allowedTools primarily configure?

options.text: Tools that can run without individual approval prompts.
options.rationale: Auto-approval is distinct from defining the complete available tool set.

options.text: The only tool names that can exist in the session.
options.rationale: Availability and approval are separate configuration concerns.

options.text: The text of the subagent's system instructions.
options.rationale: Tool approval does not define the agent's role prompt.

options.text: A guarantee that the model will invoke each listed tool.
options.rationale: Permission to call a tool does not require a call.

cards.explanation: Auto-approval is distinct from defining the complete available tool set.

cards.prompt: A researcher sends facts to a synthesis worker. Which handoff preserves traceability?

options.text: A count of sources with no content.
options.rationale: A source count supplies neither findings nor evidence.

options.text: Claims paired with source identifiers and supporting excerpts.
options.rationale: Attribution requires evidence associations to survive the handoff.

options.text: Claims stripped of metadata to save a few tokens.
options.rationale: The synthesizer would lose the ability to attribute them.

options.text: Source titles with no associated findings.
options.rationale: Titles alone do not identify which claims are supported.

cards.explanation: Attribution requires evidence associations to survive the handoff.

cards.prompt: Which instruction gives a specialist a useful bounded assignment?

options.text: Require agreement with the coordinator's unverified guess.
options.rationale: That turns investigation into confirmation.

options.text: Ask it to improve everything it can find.
options.rationale: Unbounded scope obscures completion and ownership.

options.text: State the outcome, scope, constraints and required evidence.
options.rationale: A task contract defines success without assuming undisclosed context.

options.text: Provide a role name with no current objective.
options.rationale: A role is not a concrete task.

cards.explanation: A task contract defines success without assuming undisclosed context.

cards.prompt: Which name does the exam guide give the subagent-spawning mechanism, and what does current Claude Code call it?

options.text: The Spawn tool; current Claude Code renamed it Task and retired the original name.
options.rationale: There is no Spawn tool; the guide's name is Task.

options.text: The Agent tool; the exam guide itself offers no separate name for the mechanism.
options.rationale: The guide names it the Task tool; Agent is the newer product name.

options.text: The Task tool; current Claude Code removed it in favour of MCP subagent servers.
options.rationale: The mechanism was renamed, not removed, and MCP servers are a separate concern.

options.text: The Task tool; current Claude Code renamed it Agent and still accepts Task as an alias.
options.rationale: Answer Task on the exam, and expect Agent in current tool-use blocks, with Task working as an alias.

cards.explanation: The exam guide calls it the Task tool; current Claude Code renamed it Agent while keeping Task as a working alias.

cards.prompt: A coordinator with file and search tools configured never manages to start a single subagent. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Task, or Agent under its current name, is missing from the coordinator's allowedTools.
options.rationale: Spawning is gated on that tool being present, so without it the coordinator cannot invoke subagents at all.

options.text: The subagent definitions omit the description field the coordinator reads.
options.rationale: A missing description weakens selection but does not make spawning impossible.

options.text: The coordinator's system prompt never mentions delegation as part of its role.
options.rationale: Prompt wording influences behaviour but is not the gate on the spawning mechanism.

options.text: The subagents' tool restrictions exclude the tools the coordinator itself holds.
options.rationale: Subagent tool scoping affects what they can do once running, not whether they start.

cards.explanation: The coordinator's allowedTools must include Task, or Agent under its current name, or it has no mechanism to invoke subagents.

cards.prompt: What does an AgentDefinition specify for a subagent?

options.text: A description, a token budget, and the model version the subagent must run on.
options.rationale: Budget and model pinning are not the three fields the definition covers.

options.text: A description, a system prompt, and the tools the subagent is allowed to use.
options.rationale: Those three fields say when to invoke it, how it should behave, and what it may touch.

options.text: A system prompt, a retry policy, and the coordinator that the subagent reports to.
options.rationale: Retry policy and reporting target are not part of the definition.

options.text: A name, a session identifier, and the conversation history the subagent inherits.
options.rationale: Subagents inherit no conversation history, so no such field exists.

cards.explanation: An AgentDefinition carries a description used for selection, a system prompt, and the tool restrictions scoped to the subagent's role.

cards.prompt: A synthesis subagent returns a polished report with no citations, although both research subagents returned properly sourced output. What is the root cause?

options.text: The synthesis subagent needs direct search-tool access so it can verify sources itself.
options.rationale: Giving it tools works around the real problem instead of fixing the handoff.

options.text: The synthesis subagent's system prompt omits an instruction to cite its sources.
options.rationale: No instruction can make it cite sources it was never given.

options.text: The coordinator forwarded the claim text without the accompanying source metadata.
options.rationale: Stripping source URLs, document names, and page numbers leaves the synthesis agent nothing to attribute claims to.

options.text: The research subagents used an output format the synthesis agent cannot parse.
options.rationale: Both upstream agents are verified as returning correct, well-formed results.

cards.explanation: The synthesis agent can only cite what it receives; passing content without structured metadata is what removes the attribution.

cards.prompt: Which record shape lets a downstream agent attribute every claim it receives?

options.text: The claim paired with a running count of how many documents were searched.
options.rationale: A count says nothing about where any individual claim came from.

options.text: A list of source URLs kept separate from the claims to keep payloads small.
options.rationale: Separating them breaks the link between each claim and its origin.

options.text: The claim rewritten to mention its origin in prose, with metadata fields removed.
options.rationale: Prose mentions are not structured metadata and are easily lost in summarisation.

options.text: The claim together with source URL, document name, page number, and confidence.
options.rationale: Structured findings that carry content and metadata together give the downstream agent everything it needs to cite.

cards.explanation: Inter-agent findings should separate content from metadata while passing both, so each claim arrives with its source URL, document name, page number, and confidence.

cards.prompt: A coordinator needs a web search and an unrelated document analysis, neither depending on the other. How should it invoke them?

options.text: Emit both Task tool calls in a single response so the two run at the same time.
options.rationale: Independent subagents should be spawned in parallel from one coordinator turn to avoid needless latency.

options.text: Invoke the search first and feed its output into the document analysis call.
options.rationale: Manufacturing a dependency that does not exist serialises work for no benefit.

options.text: Invoke them in separate turns so each result is logged before the next starts.
options.rationale: Sequential turns add latency, and logging happens at the coordinator either way.

options.text: Invoke the search twice and let the second call cover the documents as well.
options.rationale: A search agent is not scoped to document analysis, and the duplicate call wastes a turn.

cards.explanation: Independent subagents should be spawned in parallel by emitting multiple Task tool calls in one coordinator response, which removes the latency of sequential turns.

cards.prompt: How should a coordinator word a subagent's assignment?

options.text: Spell out each step in order so the subagent cannot improvise its own approach.
options.rationale: Procedural instructions constrain the subagent and stop it adapting to what it finds.

options.text: State the outcome and the quality criteria, leaving the method to the subagent.
options.rationale: Goal-oriented prompts let the subagent adapt its approach while still meeting the bar that was set.

options.text: State only the role name and let the subagent infer the goal from its description.
options.rationale: A role without a current objective gives the subagent nothing concrete to deliver.

options.text: State the conclusion the coordinator expects so the subagent can confirm it.
options.rationale: Handing over a conclusion invites confirmation rather than investigation.

cards.explanation: Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria rather than procedures, which keeps subagents able to adapt their approach.

cards.prompt: After an initial codebase analysis, you want to compare two refactoring strategies from that same starting point. Which session control fits?

options.text: Resume the session twice so both strategies append to the same conversation.
options.rationale: Appending both strategies to one history mixes them instead of isolating each line of work.

options.text: Resume the session and explore both strategies inside one continuing thread.
options.rationale: Continuation is what resume is for; this scenario calls for independent branches.

options.text: Fork the session once per strategy so each explores from a copy of the analysis.
options.rationale: Forking creates independent branches from a shared baseline, which is exactly the divergent-exploration case.

options.text: Start two fresh sessions and re-read the whole codebase separately in each one.
options.rationale: Discarding the completed analysis repeats work the fork would have preserved.

cards.explanation: Fork creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline, which is the right control when comparing divergent approaches.

cards.prompt: In the current Agent SDK, how is fork_session actually used?

options.text: Instead of resume: fork_session itself names the session to branch from.
options.rationale: fork_session is a modifier and carries no session identifier of its own.

options.text: Only when a session is first created, marking it as branchable later on.
options.rationale: It is not a creation-time flag; it applies when starting from an existing session.

options.text: Only on the command line, since the SDK exposes no equivalent behaviour.
options.rationale: The SDK exposes it as an option, and the CLI has a matching flag.

options.text: Alongside resume: resume names the session and fork_session branches from it.
options.rationale: Resume selects the session and fork_session decides branch rather than append, so the two are set together.

cards.explanation: Fork is a modifier on resume: resume names the session to start from, and fork_session makes the run branch off instead of appending.

cards.prompt: A synthesis subagent must work from the output of two earlier agents. What does the coordinator pass into its prompt?

options.text: Both agents' findings in full, written into the synthesis subagent's prompt.
options.rationale: Complete prior findings must be included explicitly, because the subagent cannot look anything up.

options.text: A pointer to where both agents' findings were stored during this run.
options.rationale: There is no shared store the subagent can follow a pointer into.

options.text: The shorter output in full, with the longer one reduced to a single line.
options.rationale: Compressing one agent's work discards the detail synthesis depends on.

options.text: Neither, since the synthesis subagent can request them from the other agents.
options.rationale: Subagents never communicate directly, so it cannot request anything from its peers.

cards.explanation: Prior agents' findings must be passed in full inside the synthesis subagent's prompt, because it has no way to retrieve them itself.

cards.prompt: A deployment tool must reject requests unless required checks have passed. Where should that prerequisite be enforced?

options.text: Only in the assistant's instruction to remember the checks.
options.rationale: Prompt guidance does not establish an execution gate.

options.text: In a review message produced after the deployment finishes.
options.rationale: Post-action feedback cannot prevent the deployment.

options.text: By asking the model for a confidence score before deployment.
options.rationale: Confidence is not evidence that required checks passed.

options.text: In application logic that validates the prerequisite before executing deployment.
options.rationale: The executable boundary must check the state that authorizes the action.

cards.explanation: The executable boundary must check the state that authorizes the action.

cards.prompt: A sensitive tool receives no trustworthy proof that its prerequisite passed. What should the execution gate do?

options.text: Accept the model's statement that it probably passed.
options.rationale: A generated assertion is not verified state.

options.text: Execute first and collect the proof afterward.
options.rationale: That reverses the required dependency.

options.text: Treat missing state as an earlier successful check.
options.rationale: Missing data does not establish a successful check.

options.text: Decline execution until the prerequisite is established.
options.rationale: Absence of evidence must not silently become authorization.

cards.explanation: Absence of evidence must not silently become authorization.

cards.prompt: A human approved one operation, but its target changes before execution. What is required?

options.text: Validate the new proposal and obtain any required approval for it.
options.rationale: Approval is tied to the reviewed action, not arbitrary future variants.

options.text: Reuse approval because the tool name is unchanged.
options.rationale: The target is part of the operation's meaning.

options.text: Execute both targets to preserve the original intent.
options.rationale: That introduces an extra unapproved effect.

options.text: Record the change only after the operation succeeds.
options.rationale: An audit record cannot replace a required precondition.

cards.explanation: Approval is tied to the reviewed action, not arbitrary future variants.

cards.prompt: A workflow says it transferred a case, but the handoff API failed. What should it report?

options.text: Transfer completed after writing a local summary.
options.rationale: Preparing context is not delivering the handoff.

options.text: The handoff failed, with a supported recovery path.
options.rationale: User-visible status must match the actual operation outcome.

options.text: Transfer completed because the assistant announced it.
options.rationale: An announcement is not a successful API result.

options.text: Case resolved because the automated portion ended.
options.rationale: Ending automation does not resolve the user's case.

cards.explanation: User-visible status must match the actual operation outcome.

cards.prompt: An agent issues account credits without confirming ownership in about 7% of cases, although the system prompt requires the check. Which fix does the lesson call correct?

options.text: Rewrite the system prompt so the verification requirement is stated more forcefully.
options.rationale: A stronger prompt lowers the failure rate but never reaches zero, which a financial operation needs.

options.text: Add a code-level gate that blocks the credit tool until verification has returned a result.
options.rationale: Programmatic enforcement is deterministic, so the wrong execution order becomes impossible rather than unlikely.

options.text: Supply few-shot examples that show verification performed before every credit issued.
options.rationale: Examples shift probabilities; they cannot guarantee the ordering a money movement requires.

options.text: Add a routing classifier that sends credit requests into a verification-first pipeline.
options.rationale: Classifiers decide which agent handles a request, not the tool order inside that agent's run.

cards.explanation: Money movement needs deterministic guarantees, so a prerequisite gate in code is the fix rather than any prompt-side improvement.

cards.prompt: Which requirement is the lesson willing to leave to prompt-based guidance?

options.text: Cross-border transfers must pass an anti-money-laundering check before executing.
options.rationale: A single missed compliance check can bring legal penalties, so this needs enforcement in code.

options.text: Refunds must be preceded by a verified customer identity within the session.
options.rationale: A refund on the wrong account is a financial loss, which prompts cannot reliably prevent.

options.text: Responses should follow the team's preferred formatting and section ordering.
options.rationale: A formatting slip carries no business risk, so probabilistic guidance is acceptable here.

options.text: Administrative endpoints must be reached only after an authorisation check.
options.rationale: Bypassing authorisation is a security breach and belongs behind a programmatic gate.

cards.explanation: Formatting and style preferences are low-stakes, so prompt guidance is acceptable; money, security, and compliance require programmatic enforcement.

cards.prompt: Why does the lesson reject a routing classifier as the fix for a per-agent compliance failure?

options.text: Classifiers cannot be trained on enough labelled compliance examples to be accurate.
options.rationale: Accuracy of the classifier is not the issue; it operates at the wrong layer entirely.

options.text: Classifiers add latency that pushes long compliance workflows past their timeouts.
options.rationale: Latency is not the objection raised against this distractor.

options.text: Classifiers run after the tool call, so the non-compliant action has already happened.
options.rationale: Classifiers run before routing, not after tool execution; that timing argument belongs to post-execution hooks.

options.text: Classifiers pick which agent handles a request; the failure sits inside that agent's run.
options.rationale: Routing and workflow ordering are different layers, so a classifier cannot enforce a step order within an agent's run.

cards.explanation: A routing classifier only picks which agent handles a request; the compliance failure happens within the agent's execution sequence.

cards.prompt: Which set of fields does the lesson require in a structured escalation summary?

options.text: Customer ID, conversation summary, root cause, refund amount, and recommended action.
options.rationale: These five fields make the summary self-contained for a human who cannot see the conversation.

options.text: Customer ID, transcript link, agent name, session duration, and sentiment score.
options.rationale: A transcript link is no help when the human agent has no transcript access, and the operational metrics do not resolve the case.

options.text: Conversation summary, tool call log, model version, latency, and retry count.
options.rationale: Engineering telemetry does not tell the human who the customer is or what to do next.

options.text: Customer ID, recommended action, and a pointer to the conversation for the details.
options.rationale: Omitting the summary, root cause, and amount forces the customer to repeat everything.

cards.explanation: A handoff summary must carry customer ID, conversation summary, root cause analysis, refund amount where applicable, and recommended action.

cards.prompt: Why must an escalation summary be self-contained?

options.text: The transcript is deleted as soon as the escalation ticket is opened.
options.rationale: Deletion is not the reason; the human agent simply never has transcript access.

options.text: The receiving human agent cannot read the conversation transcript at all.
options.rationale: The summary is the only information the human receives, so anything missing has to be asked of the customer again.

options.text: The summary replaces the customer's record in the support system entirely.
options.rationale: A handoff note does not overwrite account records.

options.text: The receiving agent reads only the first line of any escalation note.
options.rationale: No such limit exists; the issue is access to the conversation, not attention.

cards.explanation: Human agents receive only the handoff summary, so an incomplete one forces the customer to repeat everything.

cards.prompt: A customer's single message raises a return, an address change, and a loyalty points question. What does the lesson prescribe?

options.text: Handle the first item now and ask the customer to raise the others separately.
options.rationale: Addressing only the first item and dropping the rest is the failure mode the lesson names.

options.text: Open three separate conversations so each item gets its own isolated context.
options.rationale: Sequential separate conversations discard the shared account context and burden the customer.

options.text: Split the message into three items, investigate them together on shared context, and answer once.
options.rationale: Decomposition, parallel investigation on shared account context, and a unified resolution is the prescribed handling.

options.text: Escalate the entire message to a human because compound requests exceed agent scope.
options.rationale: Compound requests are within scope; they simply need decomposing.

cards.explanation: Compound requests are decomposed into distinct items, investigated in parallel using shared context, and answered in one unified resolution.

cards.prompt: What can a SubagentStart hook do when a subagent is spawned?

options.text: Block the spawn whenever the coordinator omitted context the subagent needs.
options.rationale: Its documented output fields cannot deny the invocation.

options.text: Rewrite the subagent's prompt before the subagent begins running.
options.rationale: It cannot inject context into the subagent's run.

options.text: Attach additional tools to the subagent for the duration of that run.
options.rationale: The event is observational and does not reconfigure the subagent.

options.text: Observe and log the spawn, including the subagent's type and id.
options.rationale: SubagentStart is observational: it receives type and id and emits systemMessage or terminalSequence, without blocking or injecting.

cards.explanation: SubagentStart is observational, receiving the subagent's type and id; it cannot block the spawn or inject context into the run.

cards.prompt: You need to deny subagent spawns that arrive without required context. Which mechanism does that?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool, which can deny or rewrite the invocation.
options.rationale: Intercepting the outgoing spawn before it runs is the only place the invocation can be refused or corrected.

options.text: A SubagentStart hook, which inspects the spawn just before the subagent runs.
options.rationale: SubagentStart cannot block the invocation; its output fields do not include a decision.

options.text: A SubagentStop hook, which validates the invocation once results come back.
options.rationale: By then the subagent has already done the work with the wrong context.

options.text: A PostToolUse hook on the Agent tool, which screens the spawn afterwards.
options.rationale: Post-execution screening cannot prevent a spawn that has already happened.

cards.explanation: Enforcing rules on spawning itself requires a PreToolUse hook attached to the Agent tool, which can deny or rewrite the invocation before the subagent starts.

cards.prompt: A SubagentStop hook finds that the subagent's output does not match the expected schema. What does exiting with code 2 achieve?

options.text: It discards the output and returns an empty result to the coordinator.
options.rationale: Nothing is discarded; the subagent is sent back to continue.

options.text: It prevents the subagent from stopping and sends it back to keep working.
options.rationale: Exit code 2 is the documented blocking mechanism for this event, since it has no decision field.

options.text: It rewrites the output into the expected schema before the coordinator sees it.
options.rationale: SubagentStop does not transform the returned output.

options.text: It ends the whole session so the coordinator can restart the workflow cleanly.
options.rationale: The block is scoped to the subagent's completion, not the session.

cards.explanation: SubagentStop blocks completion by exiting with code 2, which returns the subagent to work rather than letting it finish.

cards.prompt: A subagent's frontmatter defines a Stop hook. What happens to it?

options.text: It is ignored, because Stop is valid only in the coordinator's configuration.
options.rationale: Subagents may define hooks in their own frontmatter, including Stop.

options.text: It fires when the coordinator's own turn ends rather than the subagent's.
options.rationale: Subagent-scoped hooks are bound to that subagent's lifetime.

options.text: It is converted automatically into a SubagentStop event for that subagent.
options.rationale: SubagentStop is the event that fires on subagent completion, so frontmatter Stop hooks auto-convert to it.

options.text: It is rejected when the definition loads and the subagent fails to start.
options.rationale: Nothing is rejected; the event is simply mapped to the subagent equivalent.

cards.explanation: Stop hooks declared in a subagent's frontmatter are automatically converted to SubagentStop, the event that fires when that subagent completes.

cards.prompt: A billing subagent declares a PreToolUse hook in its own frontmatter. Which tool calls does that hook intercept?

options.text: Every tool call in the session, including calls the coordinator makes itself.
options.rationale: Component-scoped hooks do not reach the coordinator's own calls.

options.text: Tool calls made by any subagent the coordinator spawns after that point.
options.rationale: Other subagents run under their own configuration, not the billing agent's.

options.text: Only calls the coordinator makes on the billing subagent's behalf.
options.rationale: The coordinator's calls are outside the subagent's scope entirely.

options.text: Only the tool calls made by that billing subagent during its own run.
options.rationale: Subagent-scoped hooks are limited to the component's lifetime, which is what allows per-subagent policy.

cards.explanation: Hooks declared in a subagent's frontmatter are scoped to that component's lifetime and intercept only its own tool calls.

cards.prompt: Which question does the lesson use to choose between prompt guidance and programmatic enforcement?

options.text: Would one failure cause financial loss, a security breach, or a compliance violation?
options.rationale: That consequence test is the decision rule: high-stakes single failures demand deterministic enforcement.

options.text: Does the workflow involve more than one tool call in a predetermined order?
options.rationale: Step count does not decide the mechanism; consequence of failure does.

options.text: Is the operation frequent enough to justify the engineering effort of a gate?
options.rationale: Frequency is not the criterion the lesson applies.

options.text: Can the model describe the required workflow correctly when it is asked to?
options.rationale: Describing a workflow correctly says nothing about executing it every time.

cards.explanation: The decision rule turns on consequence: if a single failure means financial loss, a security breach, or a compliance violation, enforcement must be programmatic.

cards.prompt: A hook must stop an impermissible file write before the filesystem changes. Which lifecycle point fits?

options.text: PreToolUse.
options.rationale: A pre-execution check can deny the proposed call before its side effect.

options.text: PostToolUse.
options.rationale: The tool has already executed at this point.

options.text: A hook that runs when the session ends.
options.rationale: Ending the session is too late to prevent an earlier write.

options.text: A summary generated after the tool result.
options.rationale: A summary describes the action rather than intercepting it.

cards.explanation: A pre-execution check can deny the proposed call before its side effect.

cards.prompt: A post-tool check detects that an external write violated policy. What can you conclude?

options.text: The original tool never ran.
options.rationale: A post-execution event follows execution.

options.text: The violation is harmless if hidden from the model.
options.rationale: Hiding a result does not remove its effect.

options.text: The write may already have happened; recovery is a separate operation.
options.rationale: An after-execution hook does not rewind external side effects.

options.text: The hook automatically undid the external write.
options.rationale: Detection does not imply rollback support.

cards.explanation: An after-execution hook does not rewind external side effects.

cards.prompt: Two backends return dates in different formats. Where can a consistent output contract be applied?

options.text: Only in the model's guess about each date.
options.rationale: Repeated inference is less explicit than a defined conversion.

options.text: By discarding dates from every result.
options.rationale: That can remove task-relevant information.

options.text: By changing all dates to today's date.
options.rationale: That destroys the underlying facts.

options.text: In deterministic adapter or supported result-processing logic.
options.rationale: Normalization should preserve meaning, including time zone and units.

cards.explanation: Normalization should preserve meaning, including time zone and units.

cards.prompt: A write is available through two tools, but a policy hook covers only one. What is missing?

options.text: Equivalent enforcement on every path that can perform the write.
options.rationale: A bypassable gate does not establish the intended boundary.

options.text: A longer description of the protected tool.
options.rationale: Description text does not cover the other execution path.

options.text: A lower temperature for the unprotected path.
options.rationale: Sampling settings are not access controls.

options.text: An additional post-run success message.
options.rationale: A message cannot prevent the unguarded action.

cards.explanation: A bypassable gate does not establish the intended boundary.

cards.prompt: What does a PreToolUse hook return in the current Agent SDK?

options.text: A boolean approved flag together with a message shown to the user.
options.rationale: The hook answers with a structured permission decision, not a bare boolean.

options.text: An exit code of 0 or 2, because the event exposes no structured decision.
options.rationale: Exit-code blocking is how SubagentStop works; PreToolUse has a decision field.

options.text: A permissionDecision naming allow, deny, ask or defer, optionally with updatedInput.
options.rationale: Those four decisions, with an optional argument rewrite, are what the hook returns before the tool runs.

options.text: A permissionDecision of allow or deny only, applied once the tool has run.
options.rationale: Two values is incomplete, and PreToolUse is evaluated before execution, not after.

cards.explanation: A PreToolUse hook returns a permissionDecision of allow, deny, ask, or defer, and may supply updatedInput to rewrite the tool's arguments.

cards.prompt: A hook must cap an oversized page-size argument before a search tool runs. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: PreToolUse returning updatedInput with the corrected arguments.
options.rationale: PreToolUse can rewrite a tool's arguments before execution, which is exactly an argument fix.

options.text: PostToolUse returning updatedToolOutput with the oversized result trimmed.
options.rationale: That repairs the output after the expensive call has already run.

options.text: SubagentStop returning the corrected arguments back to the coordinator.
options.rationale: SubagentStop fires on subagent completion and does not touch tool arguments.

options.text: A system prompt rule stating the maximum page size the tool will accept.
options.rationale: Prompt guidance is probabilistic and cannot guarantee the argument is capped.

cards.explanation: PreToolUse runs before execution and can supply updatedInput, which rewrites the tool's arguments before the call goes out.

cards.prompt: Which field lets a PostToolUse hook change what the model sees, for built-in and MCP tools alike?

options.text: updatedInput
options.rationale: updatedInput belongs to PreToolUse and rewrites arguments, not results.

options.text: updatedToolOutput
options.rationale: This is the current field for replacing a tool result before the model processes it, covering built-in and MCP tools.

options.text: updatedMCPToolOutput
options.rationale: This older field covered MCP tools only and is deprecated.

options.text: permissionDecision
options.rationale: permissionDecision governs whether a call proceeds; it does not alter results.

cards.explanation: PostToolUse sets updatedToolOutput to replace the result the model sees; the older updatedMCPToolOutput was MCP-only and is deprecated.

cards.prompt: When exactly does a PostToolUse hook run?

options.text: After the model has processed the result and before the next request is sent.
options.rationale: The hook fires earlier than that, while the result is still on its way to the model.

options.text: Before the tool executes, as soon as the model has emitted the tool call.
options.rationale: That is PreToolUse; confusing the direction is a documented exam trap.

options.text: After the whole turn ends, once the assistant's final message is complete.
options.rationale: It runs per tool result rather than once per turn.

options.text: After the tool executes and before the model processes its result.
options.rationale: That window is what lets the hook normalise or replace the result the model will reason about.

cards.explanation: PostToolUse runs after the tool has executed but before the model processes the result, which is why it can transform what the model sees.

cards.prompt: Refunds above $500 must always go to a human. Where does that rule belong?

options.text: In a PreToolUse hook that denies the refund call and routes it to escalation.
options.rationale: Blocking before execution is the only way the oversized refund is prevented rather than merely recorded.

options.text: In a PostToolUse hook that flags oversized refunds for review after the fact.
options.rationale: By then the refund has been processed; flagging does not undo it.

options.text: In the system prompt, which already describes the escalation threshold clearly.
options.rationale: Prompt instructions are probabilistic and a single miss is a large unapproved refund.

options.text: In the refund tool's description, so the model avoids requesting large amounts.
options.rationale: A description guides the model but enforces nothing.

cards.explanation: A threshold that must hold every time is enforced by a PreToolUse hook, which blocks the call before the refund can execute.

cards.prompt: Responses should normally use markdown headings and bullet points. What does the lesson recommend?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that blocks any reply lacking markdown structure.
options.rationale: Blocking machinery is unnecessary overhead for a presentation preference.

options.text: A PostToolUse hook that rewrites every tool result into markdown first.
options.rationale: Normalising tool results does not control how the assistant formats its reply, and the requirement does not warrant a hook.

options.text: Prompt guidance, because an occasional plain-text reply is not a business risk.
options.rationale: Formatting is a preference rather than a requirement, so probabilistic guidance is appropriate.

options.text: A prerequisite gate that checks formatting before the turn is allowed to end.
options.rationale: Gates exist for financial, security, and compliance prerequisites, not style.

cards.explanation: Formatting preferences carry no business risk from a single deviation, so prompt-based guidance is the right mechanism and a hook is unnecessary overhead.

cards.prompt: Three tools return dates in three different formats. Why not simply instruct the model to convert them?

options.text: The model cannot read date fields that arrive as Unix timestamps at all.
options.rationale: It can read them; the problem is that it does so inconsistently.

options.text: Model-side conversion is probabilistic, so parsing stays inconsistent across iterations.
options.rationale: Relying on the model to normalise introduces exactly the interpretation errors a hook removes.

options.text: Format instructions are stripped from the system prompt before each request.
options.rationale: Nothing strips those instructions; their weakness is reliability, not delivery.

options.text: Converting inside the prompt roughly doubles the token cost of each tool result.
options.rationale: Token cost is not the objection the lesson raises.

cards.explanation: Leaving normalisation to the model reintroduces inconsistency, such as misreading day and month order, which a PostToolUse hook eliminates.

cards.prompt: Which transformation is a PostToolUse normalisation hook responsible for?

options.text: Deciding whether a tool should have been called with the arguments it received.
options.rationale: That judgement happens before execution, in a PreToolUse hook.

options.text: Converting Unix timestamps and DD/MM/YYYY dates into one ISO 8601 format.
options.rationale: Reconciling heterogeneous date and status formats before the model sees them is the normalisation case.

options.text: Blocking a status update that would violate the refund approval policy.
options.rationale: Blocking is policy enforcement and must happen before the tool runs.

options.text: Choosing which of three backend systems the next tool call should target.
options.rationale: Routing decisions are not part of result normalisation.

cards.explanation: PostToolUse normalisation rewrites heterogeneous results into one schema, such as every date as ISO 8601 and every status as a readable string.

cards.prompt: Cross-border payments must always pass a sanctions screen, but prompt instructions let a few through. Which design meets the requirement?

options.text: A PostToolUse hook that queues any unscreened payment for manual review.
options.rationale: The payment has already executed by the time this fires, so the requirement is still violated.

options.text: A stronger system prompt that spells out the penalties for skipping the screen.
options.rationale: Stronger wording reduces the failure rate without eliminating it.

options.text: Few-shot examples showing the screen performed before each payment executes.
options.rationale: Examples improve behaviour probabilistically and cannot guarantee compliance.

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that denies the payment tool until the screen records a pass.
options.rationale: Pre-execution blocking is deterministic, so no payment can run without the screen.

cards.explanation: A regulatory requirement needs deterministic enforcement, so a PreToolUse hook blocks the payment tool until the screening result is recorded.

cards.prompt: Which mapping matches the lesson's decision framework?

options.text: Requirements that must hold every time use hooks; preferences use prompts.
options.rationale: Deterministic mechanisms serve absolute requirements and probabilistic ones serve preferences.

options.text: Requirements that must hold every time use prompts; preferences use hooks.
options.rationale: This inverts the framework and leaves absolute requirements unenforced.

options.text: Both requirements and preferences use hooks, since hooks are deterministic.
options.rationale: Hooks for style preferences are unnecessary overhead.

options.text: Both use prompts, with hooks reserved solely for normalising tool output.
options.rationale: Normalisation is one hook use, but policy enforcement is the other.

cards.explanation: Anything that must be followed 100% of the time is enforced with hooks; preferences where occasional deviation is tolerable are handled with prompts.

cards.prompt: Discounts above 20% require manager sign-off before they take effect. How is that implemented?

options.text: A PostToolUse hook records each applied discount and notifies the manager.
options.rationale: The discount is already applied when this fires, so approval is not a precondition.

options.text: The discount tool applies the change and emails the manager for confirmation.
options.rationale: Applying first and confirming later defeats the purpose of an approval requirement.

options.text: A PreToolUse hook intercepts the call and routes it to a manager approval queue.
options.rationale: Intercepting before execution means the discount applies only after approval comes back.

options.text: The system prompt instructs the agent to seek approval before large discounts.
options.rationale: Prompt guidance cannot guarantee that approval precedes every large discount.

cards.explanation: A PreToolUse hook intercepts the discount call above the threshold and pauses it for manager approval, so the tool executes only once approval is granted.

cards.prompt: A review needs both local file checks and checks of contracts between files. Which decomposition covers both?

options.text: Repeat the same local check several times without inspecting interfaces.
options.rationale: Repetition does not add the missing integration analysis.

options.text: Analyze files, then run an integration pass over their interfaces and findings.
options.rationale: Local review and cross-file review answer different questions.

options.text: Analyze files independently and assume their contracts are compatible.
options.rationale: Correct files can still disagree at their boundaries.

options.text: Inspect only the largest file and infer how the rest behaves.
options.rationale: File size does not establish dependency or coverage.

cards.explanation: Local review and cross-file review answer different questions.

cards.prompt: The next investigation depends on what an initial search discovers. Which plan fits?

options.text: Skip follow-ups because they were not known initially.
options.rationale: Unknown initial details do not eliminate required investigation.

options.text: Use findings to choose bounded follow-up tasks.
options.rationale: Discovery-driven work needs a way to adapt after new evidence.

options.text: Commit to every possible follow-up before reading results.
options.rationale: That can waste work on irrelevant branches.

options.text: Run synthesis before retrieving any evidence.
options.rationale: The dependency is not satisfied.

cards.explanation: Discovery-driven work needs a way to adapt after new evidence.

cards.prompt: A large review is detailed on two files and superficial on the rest. What should decomposition make explicit?

options.text: Only the average number of comments per file.
options.rationale: Comment quantity is not evidence of adequate review.

options.text: A rule to ignore files without immediate findings.
options.rationale: No quick finding does not mean the file was reviewed.

options.text: Bounded review units and a record of which units were examined.
options.rationale: Explicit coverage reduces the chance that fluent output conceals omissions.

options.text: Only a larger final response length.
options.rationale: Longer output does not demonstrate broader inspection.

cards.explanation: Explicit coverage reduces the chance that fluent output conceals omissions.

cards.prompt: Two tasks edit the same shared artifact and assume incompatible states. What must be resolved before parallel execution?

options.text: Only the order in which their names appear.
options.rationale: Display order does not coordinate writes.

options.text: Only the total model token budget.
options.rationale: A budget does not define shared-state semantics.

options.text: Nothing; concurrency automatically merges intent.
options.rationale: Independent writers can overwrite or contradict each other.

options.text: Their write ownership and dependency or merge contract.
options.rationale: Parallelism needs an explicit way to prevent or reconcile conflicting updates.

cards.explanation: Parallelism needs an explicit way to prevent or reconcile conflicting updates.

cards.prompt: What characterises a fixed sequential pipeline?

options.text: Steps are chosen at run time from whatever the previous step happened to discover.
options.rationale: That describes dynamic adaptive decomposition, not a fixed pipeline.

options.text: Steps run concurrently and a final step merges whichever results arrive first.
options.rationale: Concurrency and racing are not what defines prompt chaining.

options.text: Steps are defined in advance and run in the same order whatever they find.
options.rationale: The sequence is predetermined and does not change based on intermediate results.

options.text: Steps repeat until an evaluator judges the accumulated output complete enough.
options.rationale: Looping on an evaluator is a refinement pattern rather than a fixed chain.

cards.explanation: A fixed sequential pipeline runs predetermined steps in order, each feeding the next, and the sequence does not change based on intermediate results.

cards.prompt: What does a fixed sequential pipeline give up?

options.text: The ability to change later steps when an earlier step finds something unexpected.
options.rationale: Fixed pipelines cannot adjust, which is the trade-off for their predictability.

options.text: The ability to log the output of every step for later debugging and monitoring.
options.rationale: Per-step logging is one of the pattern's advantages, not a cost.

options.text: The ability to feed one step's output into the next step's input.
options.rationale: Chaining outputs into inputs is the definition of the pattern.

options.text: The ability to produce the same result for the same input on a repeat run.
options.rationale: Consistency is precisely what fixed pipelines provide.

cards.explanation: Fixed pipelines trade adaptability for consistency: if a step discovers something that should change the approach, the sequence cannot adjust.

cards.prompt: While adding tests to a legacy system, the agent finds that the module it planned to test depends on an untested one. Which approach handles this?

options.text: A fixed pipeline, which keeps the planned order and records the dependency.
options.rationale: A fixed pipeline cannot reorder itself around a finding made mid-run.

options.text: A fixed pipeline with extra steps inserted before execution begins.
options.rationale: Steps added in advance still cannot respond to a dependency nobody knew about.

options.text: One large pass across every module so no dependency can come as a surprise.
options.rationale: A single pass over many modules invites attention dilution and still needs a plan.

options.text: Dynamic adaptive decomposition, which reorders the plan around the new dependency.
options.rationale: Open-ended work generates subtasks from what it discovers, so the plan reprioritises to test the dependency first.

cards.explanation: Dynamic adaptive decomposition generates and reorders subtasks from what it discovers, which is what lets it test the depended-on module first.

cards.prompt: What is the cost of dynamic adaptive decomposition?

options.text: It cannot respond to new findings that appear midway through the work.
options.rationale: Responding to findings is its defining strength.

options.text: Execution time and resource use are less predictable, and debugging is harder.
options.rationale: The plan varies with what is found, so completion time and debugging both become harder.

options.text: It always requires more subagents than an equivalent fixed pipeline.
options.rationale: Agent count is not what distinguishes the patterns.

options.text: It produces shallower results on the open-ended tasks it targets.
options.rationale: It produces more thorough results on exactly those tasks.

cards.explanation: Because the plan evolves with what is discovered, execution time and resource use are hard to estimate and failures are harder to trace.

cards.prompt: A workflow extracts the same eight fields from thousands of invoices. Which pattern fits?

options.text: A fixed sequential pipeline, because the fields and format are known in advance.
options.rationale: Predictable, structured input with predetermined outputs is the fixed-pipeline case.

options.text: Dynamic decomposition, so the agent can decide which fields matter per invoice.
options.rationale: The fields are already determined, so adaptability buys nothing and costs predictability.

options.text: Dynamic decomposition, because the volume of documents makes the scope open-ended.
