options.rationale: Volume is not the same as unknown scope; the task itself is fully specified.

options.text: A single combined pass over batches of invoices with no separate integration step.
options.rationale: Processing many items in one pass is how attention dilution appears.

cards.explanation: Document extraction has predetermined fields and formats, which is the structured, predictable case that fixed pipelines serve best.

cards.prompt: A review shows thorough comments on the first files, thin comments on later ones, and the same pattern flagged in one file but ignored in another. What is this?

options.text: A context window overflow that silently dropped the later files from the prompt.
options.rationale: The later files were reviewed, just shallowly, so nothing was dropped.

options.text: A tool restriction that hid part of the codebase from the reviewing agent.
options.rationale: Restricted access would remove files entirely rather than degrade depth gradually.

options.text: Attention dilution caused by processing too many items in a single pass.
options.rationale: Degrading depth across items plus contradictory verdicts on identical code is the signature of this failure mode.

options.text: A sampling setting that made later judgements inconsistent with earlier ones.
options.rationale: Inconsistency here comes from how attention is spread, not from sampling parameters.

cards.explanation: Degrading depth across items, plus identical code judged differently in different files, are the telltale symptoms of attention dilution.

cards.prompt: What does the lesson say about fixing attention dilution with a larger context window or a stronger model?

options.text: It works, because all the items then fit comfortably inside one prompt.
options.rationale: Fitting the items was never the constraint; attention allocation is.

options.text: It works when combined with a prompt demanding equal thoroughness for every item.
options.rationale: Better prompts raise average quality without guaranteeing per-item attention.

options.text: It fixes the depth drop-off but still leaves cross-item issues undetected.
options.rationale: It does not fix the depth drop-off at all.

options.text: It does not work, because the problem is architectural and needs multiple passes.
options.rationale: Attention dilution is a structural issue that per-item passes plus an integration pass resolve.

cards.explanation: Attention dilution is an architectural problem, so a bigger model or wider context does not solve it; multi-pass decomposition does.

cards.prompt: A team splits fourteen files into three batches and reviews each batch separately. What still goes wrong?

options.text: Issues spanning batches, such as data flow and inconsistent patterns, go unnoticed.
options.rationale: Batching narrows each pass but leaves nothing looking across the batches for cross-cutting concerns.

options.text: Each batch loses depth toward its end in the same way a single pass would.
options.rationale: Smaller batches largely restore per-item depth; the gap is between batches.

options.text: The batches cannot be reviewed using the same agent configuration.
options.rationale: Reusing one configuration across batches is perfectly possible.

options.text: The review becomes non-deterministic because the batch ordering varies.
options.rationale: Ordering is not the weakness the lesson identifies in batching.

cards.explanation: Batching reduces dilution inside each batch but misses cross-batch data flow and pattern inconsistencies without a dedicated integration pass.

cards.prompt: Why does analysis depth fall off across items in a single large pass?

options.text: Later items are truncated out of the prompt once the token limit is reached.
options.rationale: The items are still present; they simply receive less attention.

options.text: Attention is spread across all items, so each additional item receives less of it.
options.rationale: Per-item attention decreases as item count rises, which is why early items get disproportionate depth.

options.text: The model forgets its instructions after a fixed number of files are processed.
options.rationale: There is no fixed forgetting threshold; the effect is gradual attention spreading.

options.text: Tool results from the earlier items overwrite the later items in the context.
options.rationale: Nothing overwrites anything; all items remain in context.

cards.explanation: The model allocates attention across every item in context, so more items means less attention each, and later items get skimmed.

cards.prompt: An agent must find the root cause of an intermittent failure in a system nobody on the team knows. Which decomposition fits?

options.text: A fixed pipeline running the team's standard debugging steps in their usual order.
options.rationale: A predetermined order cannot follow evidence that only appears mid-investigation.

options.text: A fixed pipeline that runs every available diagnostic once and reports the output.
options.rationale: Running everything blindly is still a predetermined sequence that ignores what it learns.

options.text: Dynamic adaptive decomposition, because the investigation must follow what it finds.
options.rationale: The root cause is unknown at the start, so subsequent steps have to be generated from discoveries.

options.text: A single combined pass over all logs and source files at the same time.
options.rationale: One large pass over many items dilutes attention and produces uneven analysis.

cards.explanation: Debugging an unfamiliar system has unknown scope, so the investigation has to generate its next steps from what it discovers.

cards.prompt: You resume a debugging session after another developer changed the implicated files. What is the most reliable way to continue without reasoning from stale tool results?

options.text: Ask the model to remember the old files more precisely.
options.rationale: Better recall cannot verify newly changed code.

options.text: Resume the session and ask the agent to re-read the changed files.
options.rationale: The old tool results stay in the conversation history and can still influence reasoning, so this is only a partial fix.

options.text: Start a fresh session with a structured summary of prior findings and re-analyse only the changed files.
options.rationale: A resumed session keeps the old tool results in history, so they can still steer reasoning; a fresh session seeded with a structured summary and the list of changed files keeps the knowledge without the stale evidence.

options.text: Trust all earlier tool results because the session was restored.
options.rationale: Restoring a record does not make its contents current.

cards.explanation: A resumed session keeps the old tool results in history, so they can still steer reasoning; a fresh session seeded with a structured summary and the list of changed files keeps the knowledge without the stale evidence.

cards.prompt: You want to compare a new approach while preserving an existing conversation path. Which session operation fits?

options.text: Fork the conversation, then verify how workspace changes are isolated.
options.rationale: Conversation branching does not by itself guarantee filesystem isolation.

options.text: Overwrite the old session's messages.
options.rationale: That destroys the branch you wanted to preserve.

options.text: Reuse the same conversation and hide previous decisions.
options.rationale: That does not create an independent comparison path.

options.text: Assume a new conversation always clones the filesystem.
options.rationale: Conversation state and workspace state are different resources.

cards.explanation: Conversation branching does not by itself guarantee filesystem isolation.

cards.prompt: A saved session shows a tool request immediately before a crash. What must recovery establish?

options.text: That a new operation ID is always safe.
options.rationale: A new ID may defeat deduplication and repeat the effect.

options.text: Whether the external operation already completed before retrying it.
options.rationale: Conversation history alone may not resolve the side effect's actual state.

options.text: That every unrecorded result means the operation never happened.
options.rationale: A crash can occur after execution but before persistence.

options.text: That resuming the session reverses the tool automatically.
options.rationale: Resumption does not undo external actions.

cards.explanation: Conversation history alone may not resolve the side effect's actual state.

cards.prompt: Why retain the identifier of a resumable agent session?

options.text: It replaces every tool's authorization checks.
options.rationale: Resuming context does not grant new permissions.

options.text: It proves the task was successfully completed.
options.rationale: A session can be saved while work remains unfinished.

options.text: It selects the saved conversation to continue.
options.rationale: The identifier locates historical session state; it does not verify external facts.

options.text: It makes all future sessions share one filesystem snapshot.
options.rationale: Session identity does not supply that isolation guarantee.

cards.explanation: The identifier locates historical session state; it does not verify external facts.

cards.prompt: What is the stale context problem?

options.text: A resumed session loses its tool results, so the agent must re-read every file again.
options.rationale: Resume restores the results; the difficulty is that it restores outdated ones.

options.text: A long session exceeds the context window and silently drops its earliest messages.
options.rationale: Dropping old messages is a different issue from reasoning on outdated file contents.

options.text: A forked branch cannot observe the changes made in the session it came from.
options.rationale: Branch isolation is expected behaviour, not the stale context problem.

options.text: Restored history holds file reads from before the edits, so the agent uses old contents.
options.rationale: Resuming replays outdated file reads alongside current information, which produces contradictory advice.

cards.explanation: Resuming restores the whole history, including file reads taken before the edits, so the agent reasons from contents that no longer exist.

cards.prompt: After editing four files in a sixty-file project, a resumed agent recommends changes that are already in place. What does the lesson advise?

options.text: Start fresh with an injected summary of prior findings and target the four changed files.
options.rationale: A clean session carries no stale tool results, while the summary preserves what was learned and scopes re-analysis.

options.text: Resume the existing session and ask the agent to re-read the four changed files first.
options.rationale: The outdated tool results stay in history and can still influence tangential reasoning.

options.text: Start fresh with no carried context and re-analyse all sixty files before continuing.
options.rationale: Full re-exploration discards knowledge that a summary would have preserved.

options.text: Fork the existing session so the four edited files are examined on a separate branch.
options.rationale: A fork copies the same stale history into the new branch.

cards.explanation: A fresh session with a structured summary removes the stale tool results while preserving prior knowledge and scoping re-analysis to the changed files.

cards.prompt: Why is forking a poor answer to stale context after file edits?

options.text: The fork discards the analysis baseline the original session produced.
options.rationale: A fork preserves the baseline; that is its purpose.

options.text: The fork copies the existing history, so the outdated tool results come with it.
options.rationale: Branching from a session that already holds stale reads carries that staleness into the branch.

options.text: The fork cannot read files that were changed after the original session ended.
options.rationale: A forked session reads current files normally.

options.text: The fork merges back into the original session and overwrites its history.
options.rationale: Branches stay independent and do not merge back.

cards.explanation: Fork branches from the existing session, so the stale tool results are inherited along with everything else.

cards.prompt: Three of fifty files changed since the last session. What does targeted re-analysis mean here?

options.text: Re-read all fifty files so the analysis is uniformly current across the project.
options.rationale: Re-reading forty-seven unchanged files is the wasteful full re-exploration the lesson rejects.

options.text: Re-read the three changed files plus the ten modules that import from them.
options.rationale: Expanding the set beyond what changed reintroduces the cost the approach avoids.

options.text: Re-read only the three changed files and rely on the summary for the rest.
options.rationale: The summary covers everything unchanged, so fresh reading is needed only where the code moved.

options.text: Skip re-reading entirely and let the agent infer the edits from the summary alone.
options.rationale: The summary describes prior findings, not the new contents of the edited files.

cards.explanation: Targeted re-analysis re-reads only the files that changed, with the prior summary covering everything that did not.

cards.prompt: The project's dependencies were upgraded between sessions. Which strategy does the decision matrix give?

options.text: A fresh start with a summary, because many files may have changed indirectly.
options.rationale: Dependency updates ripple through the project, so the safest baseline is one with no cached reads.

options.text: Resume, because the team did not hand-edit any of its own source files.
options.rationale: Indirect changes still invalidate cached results, so resuming carries stale context.

options.text: Fork, because the upgrade is one alternative worth comparing against the old state.
options.rationale: Forking is for divergent exploration and would inherit the outdated reads anyway.

options.text: Resume with a longer history limit so more prior tool results stay available.
options.rationale: Keeping more outdated results makes the problem worse rather than better.

cards.explanation: Dependency updates can change many files indirectly, so the matrix calls for a fresh start with an injected summary.

cards.prompt: A session has run long and its history is crowded with irrelevant tool results. What does the lesson advise?

options.text: Resume and instruct the agent to ignore the results that are no longer relevant.
options.rationale: Instructing the model to disregard context is unreliable and leaves the clutter in place.

options.text: Fork the session so the accumulated clutter stays behind on the original branch.
options.rationale: A fork copies the history, clutter included.

options.text: Resume and ask the agent to summarise and compress its own history in place.
options.rationale: The original results remain in the conversation regardless of any summary written into it.

options.text: Start fresh and inject a curated summary of what the session established.
options.rationale: Degraded context benefits from a clean baseline that keeps the knowledge and drops the noise.

cards.explanation: When context has degraded over a long session, a fresh start with an injected summary gives a clean baseline while preserving the findings.

cards.prompt: Which statement about --resume in the current Claude Code CLI is accurate?

options.text: It creates a session under the given name when no such session exists yet.
options.rationale: Resume never creates a session; it only continues one that already exists.

options.text: It continues an existing session by id or name, or opens an interactive picker.
options.rationale: Sessions are named when started with --name, or renamed mid-session, and resume selects among those that exist.

options.text: It always branches from the named session instead of appending to it.
options.rationale: Appending is the default; branching requires the fork flag alongside it.

options.text: It requires the fork flag to be set before it will restore any history at all.
options.rationale: Resume restores history on its own; the fork flag only changes append into branch.

cards.explanation: --resume only continues sessions that already exist, taking a session id or name or offering a picker; sessions are named at start with --name or renamed later.

cards.prompt: How do you continue the most recent conversation in the current directory without naming it?

options.text: Pass --resume with no argument, which silently selects the newest session.
options.rationale: Resume without an argument opens a picker rather than auto-selecting.

options.text: Pass --name with the directory path so the session is located by folder.
options.rationale: --name assigns a session name when starting; it does not look sessions up by path.

options.text: Pass -c, the continue flag, which resumes the most recent conversation there.
options.rationale: The continue flag picks up the latest conversation in the working directory with no name needed.

options.text: Pass --fork-session, which reopens the newest session as an independent branch.
options.rationale: The fork flag only has an effect alongside resume or continue and creates a branch.

cards.explanation: The -c or --continue flag resumes the most recent conversation in the current directory without requiring a session name.

cards.prompt: You want to compare a testing-focused plan against a documentation-focused plan, both built on one completed analysis. Which option fits?

options.text: Fork the session once per plan so each branch builds on the same baseline.
options.rationale: Two independent approaches from a shared starting point is exactly the divergent-exploration case.

options.text: Resume the session twice so both plans append to the same conversation history.
options.rationale: Appending both plans to one history mixes them instead of keeping them independent.

options.text: Start two fresh sessions with summaries so the two plans stay entirely separate.
options.rationale: Summaries would be needed only if the baseline were stale, and this discards a valid analysis.

options.text: Run both plans inside one resumed session and compare them at the very end.
options.rationale: Each plan then reasons about the other's output rather than exploring independently.

cards.explanation: Comparing two independent approaches from a shared analysis baseline is the case fork_session exists for.

cards.prompt: What does resuming a session restore?

options.text: A condensed summary of the prior session, with raw tool results discarded.
options.rationale: Summarising is what a fresh start with summary injection does instead.

options.text: Only the messages recorded since the last successful tool call in the session.
options.rationale: Resume does not truncate the history in that way.

options.text: The prior session's file reads, automatically refreshed against current contents.
options.rationale: Nothing is refreshed automatically, which is why stale reads persist.

options.text: The entire conversation history, including every tool result from that session.
options.rationale: Full restoration is what makes resume efficient and also what makes it stale after edits.

cards.explanation: Resume restores the whole conversation history, including all tool results, analyses, and reasoning from the prior session.

cards.prompt: What belongs in the structured summary injected into a fresh session?

options.text: The complete text of every file the prior session read during its analysis.
options.rationale: Carrying raw file contents forward recreates the stale data the fresh start removes.

options.text: Prior findings, the files they concern, and recommendations, without raw tool output.
options.rationale: A good summary preserves conclusions concisely and leaves the outdated raw results behind.

options.text: The prior session identifier so the agent can retrieve the old history itself.
options.rationale: An identifier pulls back the stale history rather than replacing it.

options.text: The prompts used previously, so the agent can repeat the same analysis steps.
options.rationale: Repeating the analysis wastes the knowledge the summary was meant to carry.

cards.explanation: The injected summary captures findings, affected files, and recommendations, preserving knowledge without carrying raw or outdated tool output.

cards.prompt: An assistant repeatedly confuses two similar lookup tools. What should you improve first?

options.text: Rename both tools to shorter but less descriptive names.
options.rationale: Shorter ambiguous names do not clarify the boundary.

options.text: Increase the response token budget for every call.
options.rationale: More output tokens do not fix an unclear tool contract.

options.text: Tell the model to choose randomly when descriptions overlap.
options.rationale: Random choice makes errors less predictable, not less likely.

options.text: Clarify each tool's purpose, input constraints and selection boundaries.
options.rationale: Descriptions should distinguish when each operation is appropriate.

cards.explanation: Descriptions should distinguish when each operation is appropriate.

cards.prompt: A tool needs a project ID and a bounded result count. What makes its interface safer to use?

options.text: A prose example with no validation.
options.rationale: Examples do not enforce input boundaries.

options.text: A single unparsed string containing any command.
options.rationale: That obscures the permitted argument structure.

options.text: Defaulting every missing project ID to an unrelated project.
options.rationale: A convenient default can change the operation's target.

options.text: Explicit argument types and constraints, validated by application code.
options.rationale: A model-facing schema and runtime checks serve complementary roles.

cards.explanation: A model-facing schema and runtime checks serve complementary roles.

cards.prompt: When should two similar tools remain distinct rather than be merged?

options.text: When their authorization or effects require separate contracts.
options.rationale: Similar inputs do not make operations equivalent in risk or semantics.

options.text: Whenever their names have different lengths.
options.rationale: Name length is not a meaningful design boundary.

options.text: Never; all tools should become one unrestricted executor.
options.rationale: An unrestricted interface can erase useful capability limits.

options.text: Only when one tool returns more characters.
options.rationale: Output size alone does not determine the contract.

cards.explanation: Similar inputs do not make operations equivalent in risk or semantics.

cards.prompt: A lookup returns a monetary value. Which output best preserves its meaning?

options.text: A sentence saying the amount looks reasonable.
options.rationale: A judgment is not the requested factual result.

options.text: Amount with currency, units and the relevant source identity.
options.rationale: A number alone may be ambiguous to downstream reasoning.

options.text: A bare number with currency inferred later.
options.rationale: Inference can attach the wrong interpretation.

options.text: A rounded value that discards required precision.
options.rationale: Rounding can change a decision-relevant quantity.

cards.explanation: A number alone may be ambiguous to downstream reasoning.

cards.prompt: A reviewer checks a tool description that already states the tool's purpose, the input formats it accepts, and a few example queries. Which two elements are still missing from a production-grade description?

options.text: The edge cases it does not handle, and boundaries naming which sibling tool to use instead.
options.rationale: A production-grade description carries five elements, and these are the two that are absent here.

options.text: A schema version number, and the average latency of the backend call it performs.
options.rationale: Neither is part of the five elements; latency and versioning do not help the model choose between tools.

options.text: The endpoint it calls internally, and the authorisation scope the caller has to hold.
options.rationale: Implementation and auth details are not among the five elements and do not disambiguate overlapping tools.

options.text: An estimate of token cost, and the name of the team that maintains the integration.
options.rationale: Ownership and token accounting are operational metadata, not selection signal for the model.

cards.explanation: The five elements are purpose, expected inputs, example queries, edge cases and limitations, and explicit boundaries against similar tools.

cards.prompt: Traffic logs show a support agent answering 'where is my order #44120?' by calling get_customer rather than lookup_order. Each tool carries a single short sentence of description and both accept similar identifiers. What is the most effective first step?

options.text: Add six worked examples to the system prompt showing which tool each phrasing should reach.
options.rationale: Few-shot examples add token overhead while leaving the descriptions that confuse the model untouched.

options.text: Rewrite both descriptions with accepted identifier formats, example queries, limits, and when to use the other tool.
options.rationale: Descriptions are the primary selection mechanism, so expanding them is the low-effort fix that addresses the root cause.

options.text: Merge the pair into one lookup_entity tool that inspects the identifier and picks the backend itself.
options.rationale: Consolidation is a defensible long-term choice but costs far more effort than rewriting two descriptions.

options.text: Put a keyword classifier in front of the model that selects the tool before the turn begins.
options.rationale: A routing classifier is over-engineered as a first response and bypasses the model's own language understanding.

cards.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for selection, so expanding them is the lowest-effort fix that removes the ambiguity causing the misroute.

cards.prompt: Why do few-shot tool-selection examples fail to cure misrouting that comes from one-sentence tool descriptions?

options.text: Few-shot examples are ignored whenever a request also carries tool definitions.
options.rationale: Models do read few-shot examples alongside tools; the objection is effectiveness, not whether they are read.

options.text: Examples can only travel in the tool schema itself, never in a system prompt.
options.rationale: Examples can be placed in a system prompt; the lesson's objection is that they do not fix the cause.

options.text: They add token overhead on every turn while the descriptions that confuse the model stay the same.
options.rationale: This treats the symptom rather than the disease, which is why the lesson rejects it as a first step.

options.text: They force a tool call on every turn, so the model can no longer answer in plain text.
options.rationale: That is what forcing tool choice does; few-shot examples impose no such constraint.

cards.explanation: Few-shot examples pay a recurring token cost without changing the descriptions that caused the confusion.

cards.prompt: A team proposes a keyword routing layer that picks the tool before each model turn, to settle selection errors between two vaguely described tools. Why does the lesson treat this as the wrong first response?

options.text: Routing layers cannot be built without first extending the tool-use protocol they sit in front of.
options.rationale: Nothing prevents a team from building one; the objection is proportionality, not feasibility.

options.text: Classifiers only become the right answer once an agent is carrying more than twenty tools.
options.rationale: The lesson never endorses classifiers at any toolkit size; large toolkits are handled by consolidation or scoping.

options.text: A classifier removes the need for tool descriptions, so the remaining schemas decay over time.
options.rationale: The problem is not schema decay; the descriptions are simply never repaired.

options.text: It adds infrastructure and sidesteps the language understanding a rewrite would have fixed.
options.rationale: The exam favours low-effort, high-leverage fixes, and a classifier is disproportionate to the problem.

cards.explanation: A routing classifier is over-engineered as a first step: it adds infrastructure and bypasses the natural language understanding that would work once descriptions are clear.

cards.prompt: Which ordering reflects the preference the lesson says the exam applies?

options.text: Improve descriptions before adding a classifier, scope access before granting it, evaluate community servers before custom builds.
options.rationale: The exam consistently favours the low-effort, high-leverage option at each of these decision points.

options.text: Build a custom server before surveying the community ones, and grant broad access first so that a later audit can narrow it.
options.rationale: Both halves invert the guidance: community servers come first and access starts scoped.

options.text: Consolidate the toolkit before reading the descriptions, and force a specific tool before ever allowing a free choice.
options.rationale: Consolidation and forced tool choice are targeted remedies, not the default opening move.

options.text: Add few-shot examples first, then a routing classifier, and rewrite the descriptions only once neither has helped.
options.rationale: This is the exact ordering the lesson rejects; descriptions come first, not last.

cards.explanation: The exam consistently rewards the cheapest fix that addresses the cause: better descriptions, scoped access, and existing servers before custom work.

cards.prompt: A single analyze_document tool is described as 'Analyses a document and returns results', and the agent invokes it for jobs it cannot actually perform. What does the lesson recommend?

options.text: Keep the single tool and add a free-text instruction argument that says which analysis it should run this time.
options.rationale: A free-text argument leaves the contract undefined and the ambiguity the model faces unchanged.

options.text: Split it into purpose-specific tools for extraction, summarisation and claim verification, each with its own contract.
options.rationale: Splitting a generic tool into narrow jobs with defined input and output contracts removes the ambiguity.

options.text: Leave the tool exactly as it stands and describe each supported analysis in the system prompt instead.
options.rationale: The system prompt cannot supply the per-tool contracts the model needs at selection time.

options.text: Register it on a second MCP server so the client presents it to the model under a clearer namespace.
options.rationale: Server placement is invisible to the model and changes nothing about the tool's contract.

cards.explanation: A broad tool with one vague description should be split into purpose-specific tools, each doing one narrow job with a defined input and output contract.

cards.prompt: Two tools carry confusingly similar names though their implementations are sound and distinct. What does renaming one of them accomplish?

options.text: It alters the tool's behaviour so ambiguous calls start failing loudly instead of succeeding.
options.rationale: Renaming is an interface change; the behaviour behind the name is untouched.

options.text: It makes the client reload the toolkit, which clears the model's earlier selection habits.
options.rationale: There is no selection habit to clear; the model reads the tool definitions afresh each request.

options.text: It resolves the overlap at the interface level without any change to the implementation behind it.
options.rationale: A clearer, more specific name disambiguates the tool for selection while the code stays as it is.

options.text: It lets both tools keep the same description, because the names now carry the distinction.
options.rationale: The lesson pairs the rename with a specific description; names alone are not the selection mechanism.

cards.explanation: Renaming a confusingly similar tool fixes the overlap at the interface level, and the implementation behind it does not need to change.

cards.prompt: You rewrite two tool descriptions to production grade, yet customer-related phrasings keep reaching the wrong tool. Which cause does the lesson point to?

options.text: Tool descriptions are cached by the client, so the text from before the rewrite is still being sent.
options.rationale: The lesson describes no such caching; it points at a conflict inside the prompt.

options.text: The model weighs tool names more heavily than descriptions whenever a request carries both of them.
options.rationale: Descriptions are the primary selection mechanism, not a tiebreaker behind names.

options.text: Descriptions running beyond three sentences are truncated before the model ever gets to see them.
options.rationale: No such truncation exists; production-grade descriptions are expected to run several sentences.

options.text: A keyword-sensitive system prompt instruction is creating a tool association that overrides them.
options.rationale: Instructions such as 'always check customer details first' bind a keyword to a tool regardless of the descriptions.

cards.explanation: Keyword-sensitive system prompt instructions can silently override well-written descriptions, so the prompt has to be reread after any description rewrite.

cards.prompt: An agent holds twenty-two tools and picks the wrong one frequently. Why is rewriting all twenty-two descriptions the wrong remedy?

options.text: Past roughly four or five tools the failure is decision complexity, which better wording does not reduce.
options.rationale: This is an overload problem rather than an ambiguity problem, so the toolkit has to shrink.

options.text: Descriptions stop influencing selection once a request carries more than ten tool definitions.
options.rationale: There is no such cutoff; descriptions still matter, they simply cannot carry a toolkit this large.

options.text: Requests are rejected when every tool description runs to several sentences.
options.rationale: No length limit forces this; the objection is that rewriting leaves the decision complexity intact.

options.text: Rewritten descriptions only take effect after the agent's session restarts from scratch.
options.rationale: Definitions are sent with each request, so a rewrite applies immediately; that is not the issue.

cards.explanation: Descriptions fix misrouting when a small toolkit contains two lookalike tools; with twenty-two tools the problem is decision complexity, which rewriting does not touch.

cards.prompt: You want evidence that weak descriptions, rather than the model, caused the misrouting. What does the lesson's exercise have you do?

options.text: Run the same toolkit against a second model and keep whichever one routes more accurately.
options.rationale: Swapping models tests the model, not the hypothesis that the descriptions were at fault.

options.text: Run a fixed set of queries before and after the rewrite and compare which tool was chosen each time.
options.rationale: A before-and-after selection log on an unchanged query set isolates description quality as the variable.

options.text: Count the tokens each description contributes and keep the rewrite only if the total falls.
options.rationale: Production-grade descriptions are longer; token count is not the measure of success here.

options.text: Ask the model to justify each choice afterwards and treat the justification as ground truth.
options.rationale: A self-reported rationale is not evidence of selection accuracy against known-correct answers.

cards.explanation: Logging which tool is selected for a fixed query set before and after the rewrite gives concrete evidence that description quality drove the change.

cards.prompt: What role does a tool's description play when a model decides which tool to call?

options.text: It is metadata for human reviewers, while selection is driven by the input schema's field names.
options.rationale: Descriptions are not supplementary documentation; they are what the model reads to choose.

options.text: It is consulted only to break ties when two tools accept identical argument types.
options.rationale: The description is the main input to every selection decision, not a tiebreaker.

options.text: It is the primary signal the model reads when choosing among the tools it has been given.
options.rationale: The lesson opens on exactly this point: descriptions are the mechanism, not an afterthought.

options.text: It is attached to the result so the model can verify afterwards that its choice was right.
options.rationale: Descriptions are presented before the call, as part of the tool definition, not with the result.

cards.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism a model uses for tool selection, which is why weak ones produce misrouting.

cards.prompt: An MCP tool reaches its backend, but the requested operation is denied. How should the result support recovery?

options.text: Return a tool error with a clear permission-failure category in application metadata.
options.rationale: The caller needs to distinguish an operation failure from a successful result.

options.text: Return an empty success result to avoid interrupting the model.
options.rationale: Empty success hides the access failure.

options.text: Return a success message and place the failure only in a private log.
options.rationale: The orchestrator cannot act on evidence it does not receive.

options.text: Repeat the same denied operation until the tool returns data.
options.rationale: An unchanged request does not repair missing permission.

cards.explanation: The caller needs to distinguish an operation failure from a successful result.

cards.prompt: A tool rejects an invalid date argument. What is the appropriate recovery?

options.text: Treat the response as an empty valid search.
options.rationale: The search did not successfully execute.

options.text: Raise the maximum output tokens.
options.rationale: Output capacity does not correct input syntax.

options.text: Correct the argument using the tool's validation details.
options.rationale: Repeating an unchanged invalid request is not a transient-failure strategy.

options.text: Retry the identical input indefinitely.
options.rationale: Time does not fix the invalid format.

cards.explanation: Repeating an unchanged invalid request is not a transient-failure strategy.

cards.prompt: A backend temporarily times out. Which retry policy is defensible?

options.text: Retry immediately without a limit.
options.rationale: That can amplify the failure and exhaust resources.

options.text: Retry every error, including denied access.
options.rationale: Different failure classes need different recovery.

options.text: Hide the failure and return fabricated data.
options.rationale: That produces false success instead of recovery.

options.text: Bound attempts and elapsed time, with delay and safe repeat semantics.
options.rationale: A transient fault may recover, but retries still need limits and side-effect awareness.

cards.explanation: A transient fault may recover, but retries still need limits and side-effect awareness.

cards.prompt: Which distinction matters when reporting an MCP tool failure?

options.text: Protocol failures differ from failures inside a successfully invoked tool.
options.rationale: Tool execution errors can be represented with isError; malformed protocol requests are a different layer.

options.text: Every backend rejection must be reported as successful text.
options.rationale: That hides the failure signal.

options.text: Custom retry categories are mandatory MCP envelope fields.
options.rationale: Application metadata must not be mistaken for protocol-required fields.

options.text: A tool error necessarily means the MCP server is unreachable.
options.rationale: The server can be reachable while the operation fails.

cards.explanation: Tool execution errors can be represented with isError; malformed protocol requests are a different layer.

cards.prompt: Which set names the four tool-failure categories the exam guide uses?

options.text: Transient, syntax, network, and fatal.
options.rationale: Syntax, network and fatal are not the guide's categories; they cut across the four it defines.

options.text: Retryable, non-retryable, partial, and unknown.
options.rationale: Retryability is a boolean attached to a category, not a category in its own right.

options.text: Client, server, protocol, and application.
options.rationale: This is a layer taxonomy, not the recovery-oriented categories the guide names.

options.text: Transient, validation, business, and permission.
options.rationale: These are the four categories, each mapping to a distinct recovery strategy.

cards.explanation: The guide names transient, validation, business and permission, because each one demands a different recovery action.

cards.prompt: A refund tool rejects a request for 750 because automatic refunds stop at 500. How should the calling agent respond?

options.text: Treat it as a business error, skip the retry entirely, and escalate with the refund details.
options.rationale: A policy limit applies identically on every attempt, so the agent needs an alternative path such as escalation.

options.text: Retry twice after a short delay, since the limit may be recalculated between attempts.
options.rationale: Business errors never resolve through retrying; the same violation recurs each time.

options.text: Resend the same amount under a different customer identifier to clear the check.
options.rationale: Changing the identifier does not change the policy and misrepresents the request.

options.text: Report it as a validation error and ask the user to reformat the refund request.
options.rationale: The request is well formed; it violates a business rule rather than an input contract.

cards.explanation: Refund limits are business errors: the request is technically valid but breaks a policy, so the agent escalates rather than retries.

cards.prompt: What question does the isRetryable flag answer?

options.text: Whether the caller rather than the service was responsible for the failure.
options.rationale: Fault attribution is implied by the category, not by this boolean.

options.text: Whether resending this exact request, unchanged, could succeed.
options.rationale: That is the narrow question the flag answers, which is why only transient failures get true.

options.text: Whether the agent should continue working on the task at all.
options.rationale: A false value never means abandon the task; validation errors are recovered by the agent unaided.

options.text: Whether the tool has side effects that make a second call unsafe.
options.rationale: Side-effect safety is a separate retry concern and is not what the flag encodes.

cards.explanation: isRetryable answers only whether resending the identical call can work, so transient failures are true and every other category is false.

cards.prompt: A tool rejects the value 'order-abc' because order IDs must take the form #NNNNN. Which combination is correct?

options.text: isRetryable true, because the agent is able to recover from the failure on its own.
options.rationale: Agent recoverability is not what the flag measures; resending this exact call still fails.

options.text: isRetryable true, because the format check may pass on a subsequent attempt.
options.rationale: The same string fails the same check every time, so nothing changes on a retry.

options.text: isRetryable false, though the agent still recovers by correcting the ID and issuing a new call.
options.rationale: Resending as-is is pointless, yet the category and description tell the agent how to fix the input.

options.text: isRetryable false, which means the task should be handed to a human reviewer.
options.rationale: That reading confuses validation with business and permission errors, the two that need another party.

cards.explanation: Validation errors are isRetryable false because the same call fails identically, but errorCategory and the description let the agent fix the input itself.

cards.prompt: A customer lookup runs successfully against the database and matches nobody. What should the tool return?

options.text: isError true with errorCategory validation, echoing the search terms that were supplied.
options.rationale: Nothing about the input was malformed; the query was valid and simply matched no rows.

options.text: isError true with errorCategory transient, so the agent can attempt the query again later.
options.rationale: Marking a successful query as transient is exactly what triggers the wasted retry loop.

options.text: isError true with an empty content array, leaving the agent to infer that nothing matched.
options.rationale: Any isError true response tells the agent execution failed, which is not what happened.

options.text: isError false, text stating the query ran and found no matches, and a result count of zero.
options.rationale: A successful query with no rows is a valid result and must look nothing like a failure.

cards.explanation: A successful query that matches nothing is a valid empty result: isError false, an explicit statement that the query ran, and a zero result count.

cards.prompt: An agent retries a contact lookup three times and then escalates to a human, and investigation shows the contact was never in the database. What is the root cause?

options.text: The tool's empty response is shaped like a failure, so the agent reads no matches as retriable.
options.rationale: Without a structural difference between access failure and empty result, the agent cannot tell them apart.

options.text: The retry ceiling is too low, so the lookup never gets enough attempts to surface the record.
options.rationale: More attempts return the same empty result; the record does not exist.

options.text: The escalation threshold fires too early and should wait for further retry attempts first.
options.rationale: Escalation timing is not the issue; the escalation should never have been reached.

options.text: The agent should never retry a lookup at all, so every miss ought to reach a human at once.
options.rationale: Blanket escalation would send genuine no-match answers to humans and drop legitimate transient retries.

cards.explanation: Confusing a valid empty result with an access failure is the canonical anti-pattern: the tool has to make the two responses structurally different.

cards.prompt: Where do errorCategory, isRetryable and description belong in an MCP tool result?

options.text: In dedicated envelope fields that CallToolResult defines alongside isError.
options.rationale: The protocol result defines only content, structuredContent and isError; these three are not envelope fields.

options.text: In structuredContent, as an application-level convention layered on top of the protocol.
options.rationale: structuredContent is where structured data belongs, and this metadata is a convention rather than protocol.

options.text: In the JSON-RPC error object that replaces the tool result when a call fails.
options.rationale: That object is for protocol-level failures, not for a tool that ran and reported a failure.

options.text: In the tool's input schema, so the model can read them before deciding to call.
options.rationale: The input schema describes arguments; error metadata is produced by the call, not declared ahead of it.

cards.explanation: CallToolResult defines only content, structuredContent and isError, so the error metadata rides in structuredContent as an application-level convention.

cards.prompt: A tool fails and returns the text 'Operation failed' with no other detail. What does the calling agent lose?

options.text: Any way to see which tool produced the failure in the first place.
options.rationale: The tool-use identity is preserved regardless of how uninformative the message is.

options.text: Any way to present the failure to the user in readable language.
options.rationale: The agent can relay the message; what it cannot do is choose a recovery.

options.text: Any basis for deciding whether to retry, correct the input, or take an entirely different path.
options.rationale: Without category, retryability and a description, every failure looks the same and recovery is guesswork.

options.text: Any record that the call happened, since untyped errors are dropped from the history.
options.rationale: The call and its result stay in the conversation; only the diagnostic detail is missing.

cards.explanation: Generic messages strip out the metadata that lets an agent distinguish a transient timeout from a policy violation and choose the right recovery.

cards.prompt: A research subagent queried five sources, and two of them still timed out after its own retries. What should it report upward?

options.text: A success carrying the three results, since the coordinator consumes only finished findings.
options.rationale: Reporting partial work as complete success hides the failure and misleads the coordinator.

options.text: A single failure for the whole step, so the coordinator can restart it from the beginning.
options.rationale: Discarding three successful results terminates a workflow over a partial failure.

options.text: An empty result, leaving the coordinator to decide whether the step should run again.
options.rationale: Silently suppressing the error as an empty result is the anti-pattern the lesson warns against.

options.text: The three results it did obtain, together with which sources failed and what it had already attempted.
options.rationale: Selective propagation includes partial results and the attempts made, so the coordinator can decide with context.

cards.explanation: Local recovery first, then selective propagation: report what succeeded, what failed and what was already tried, so the coordinator is not deciding blind.

cards.prompt: In a multi-agent system, which failures should a subagent resolve itself before involving the coordinator?

options.text: Transient failures such as a timed-out search, which it retries locally before escalating.
options.rationale: Local recovery for transient faults keeps the coordinator out of routine retry loops.

options.text: Permission failures, by retrying under whichever credentials it happens to be able to reach.
options.rationale: Permission errors need a different principal, which is a decision above the subagent.

options.text: Business-rule failures, by relaxing the rule far enough that the call is accepted.
options.rationale: A subagent must not weaken a policy constraint; those failures escalate.

options.text: Every failure it encounters, so the coordinator never has to reason about tool errors.
options.rationale: Suppressing unresolvable failures leaves the coordinator making decisions without the facts.

cards.explanation: Subagents recover locally from transient faults and propagate only what they cannot resolve themselves.

cards.prompt: A tool returns access denied because the service account cannot read financial records. What recovery does the lesson prescribe?

options.text: Retry after a short delay, since credential checks often clear on a second attempt.
options.rationale: Permission errors are not retryable; the same account is refused every time.

options.text: Escalate, or reissue the call as a principal that holds the required access.
options.rationale: The caller, not the call, has to change, so the agent escalates or uses different credentials.

options.text: Reformat the request arguments and resend the same call under the same account.
options.rationale: The arguments were fine; the account lacked authorisation.

options.text: Return an empty result so the surrounding workflow can carry on without the data.
options.rationale: That disguises a failure as a valid empty result, the exact confusion the lesson warns about.

cards.explanation: Permission errors are resolved by a different principal: escalate, or retry with credentials that carry the required access.

cards.prompt: A read-only summarizer has been given search, write, billing and reporting tools. What is the best first change?

options.text: Select a fixed tool count without considering the task.
options.rationale: A count is not a substitute for relevant capability design.

options.text: Expose the tools required by its task and enforce read-only permissions.
options.rationale: Role-appropriate capability limits reduce unnecessary choices and side effects.

options.text: Keep all tools and mention read-only behavior only in its prompt.
options.rationale: Guidance alone does not remove executable write capabilities.

options.text: Add a second copy of each read tool to make reads more prominent.
options.rationale: Duplicating choices increases ambiguity.

cards.explanation: Role-appropriate capability limits reduce unnecessary choices and side effects.

cards.prompt: After a required first tool call, the next turn should allow normal decisions. What should change?

options.text: Treat the forced call as proof that its result was valid.
options.rationale: Selection does not validate execution or content.

options.text: Use an appropriate flexible tool_choice on the next request.
options.rationale: Tool choice applies to requests; repeatedly forcing the same operation can create a loop.

options.text: Force the same tool on every later request.
options.rationale: That conflicts with the requested flexible continuation.

options.text: Delete the first tool result from history.
options.rationale: The model still needs that observation.

cards.explanation: Tool choice applies to requests; repeatedly forcing the same operation can create a loop.

cards.prompt: Moving an unchanged collection of tools to another server does not improve selection. Why?

options.text: Every server can expose only one tool.
options.rationale: MCP does not impose that general restriction.

options.text: The model automatically forgets tools on older servers.
options.rationale: That behavior cannot be assumed.

options.text: The model may still receive the same ambiguous tool interfaces.
options.rationale: Server placement alone does not clarify names, contracts or relevance.

options.text: Server names always override all tool descriptions.
options.rationale: Selection depends on the exposed interfaces and context.

cards.explanation: Server placement alone does not clarify names, contracts or relevance.

cards.prompt: A worker needs approved-document lookup but not arbitrary network access. Which tool fits?

options.text: A universal URL fetcher with a polite warning.
options.rationale: A warning does not enforce collection restrictions.

options.text: An unrestricted shell with a document-search example.
options.rationale: That exposes much more capability than the task requires.

options.text: A tool that copies all documents into every response.
options.rationale: That creates unnecessary disclosure and context volume.

options.text: A document lookup restricted to the authorized collection.
options.rationale: A narrow capability encodes the intended access boundary.

cards.explanation: A narrow capability encodes the intended access boundary.

cards.prompt: What tool count per agent does the lesson give as the target?

options.text: One tool per agent, with a coordinator assembling every multi-step task from them.
options.rationale: Splitting to a single tool each multiplies coordination overhead well beyond what the lesson advises.

options.text: Ten to twelve tools, which keeps most workflows inside one agent.
options.rationale: Selection reliability is already degrading well before this range.

options.text: Four to five tools, each scoped to that agent's defined role.
options.rationale: This is the optimal range the lesson states, with relevance to the role mattering as much as the count.

options.text: As many as the context window allows, since unused tools only cost tokens.
options.rationale: Every extra tool adds decision complexity, so the cost is selection accuracy, not just tokens.

cards.explanation: The lesson puts the optimal range at four to five tools per agent, scoped to that agent's role.

cards.prompt: Why should a synthesis agent be denied a web search tool, even when its toolkit is well under the limit?

options.text: Search tools cannot function for an agent that has not also been given a fetch tool.
options.rationale: Nothing technically prevents it; the objection is behavioural.

options.text: Two agents in one system are not permitted to expose the same tool name.
options.rationale: Tool names may repeat across agents; scoped cross-role tools rely on exactly that.

options.text: Search results are too large to hand between agents without truncating them.
options.rationale: Payload size is not the reason; the lesson is about misuse of out-of-role capability.

options.text: It will tend to run its own searches instead of using the results it was handed, duplicating work.
options.rationale: Tools outside an agent's specialisation get misused, wasting context and repeating work already done.

cards.explanation: Relevance matters as much as count: an agent handed a capability outside its role tends to use it, duplicating work and burning context.

cards.prompt: A data platform server exposes three query tools plus nineteen transformation tools that all take a dataset, apply one operation, and return data. What is the right fix?

options.text: Collapse the nineteen into one transform_data tool whose transform_type enum selects the operation.
options.rationale: Tools that are variations on one job and share a shape consolidate into a single parameterised tool.

options.text: Give a dedicated transformation agent all nineteen tools so every agent keeps to one role.
options.rationale: Splitting by role here just relocates a nineteen-tool selection problem one level down.

options.text: Move the transformation tools to a second MCP server so the client presents two smaller sets.
options.rationale: Server boundaries are invisible to the model, which still receives one flat list.

options.text: Rewrite all nineteen descriptions with inputs, examples, and boundaries against one another.
options.rationale: Description quality cannot rescue selection once decision complexity is the binding constraint.

cards.explanation: Nineteen near-identical transformations share a shape, so they collapse into one parameterised tool and every operation stays reachable as an enum value.

cards.prompt: Two agents both misroute. One is choosing among five tools, the other among twenty-two. What does the lesson say about the remedies?

options.text: Both are description problems, because tool selection always reduces to how clearly the tools are described.
options.rationale: The same symptom has two different diseases, and only one of them is an ambiguity problem.

options.text: The five-tool case is a description problem; the twenty-two-tool case is complexity and needs fewer tools.
options.rationale: Count the tools before choosing a remedy: wording fixes ambiguity, not overload.

options.text: Both are overload problems, since misrouting only ever appears once a toolkit has passed four or five tools.
options.rationale: A five-tool agent that cannot tell two lookalike tools apart has an ambiguity problem, not overload.

options.text: The five-tool case needs forced tool choice, and the twenty-two-tool case needs much richer descriptions.
options.rationale: This reverses both remedies and forces a tool where clearer wording was the fix.

cards.explanation: Same symptom, different disease: ambiguity among a handful of tools is fixed by descriptions, while a twenty-two-tool toolkit has to shrink.

cards.prompt: Does collapsing nineteen transformations into one parameterised tool weaken least privilege?

options.text: Yes, because a single tool that accepts an enum can reach operations the agent could not previously reach.
options.rationale: Every one of those operations was already reachable as its own tool; nothing new is granted.

options.text: Yes, because least privilege requires one tool for each distinct operation an agent is permitted to perform.
options.rationale: Least privilege constrains what can be reached, not how many tool definitions express it.

options.text: No, the agent gains no new capability: consolidation shrinks the choice, constraining shrinks the reach.
options.rationale: The two moves do different jobs and can both be right in the same system.

options.text: No, because least privilege governs MCP server boundaries rather than individual tool definitions.
options.rationale: Least privilege applies directly to tool design, as the fetch_url and load_document example shows.

cards.explanation: Every one of those operations was reachable before the merge, so no privilege is added. Shrinking the menu and shrinking a tool's reach are separate moves.

cards.prompt: Which description matches tool_choice set to auto?

options.text: The model has to call a tool, and the caller names in advance which tool that will be.
options.rationale: That is forced selection, which pins the call to one named tool.

options.text: The model has to call a tool but is free to pick which one it calls.
options.rationale: That is the 'any' setting, which guarantees a tool call without naming the tool.

options.text: The model is prevented from calling tools and must answer in text.
options.rationale: None of the three settings blocks tool use in this way.

options.text: The model decides for itself whether to call a tool or reply in text.
options.rationale: This is the default, used where the model needs room to answer conversationally.

cards.explanation: 'auto' is the default: the model chooses between calling a tool and returning text.

cards.prompt: An extraction pipeline holds separate schemas for invoices, receipts and contracts, and the document type is unknown when the call is made. Which setting guarantees structured output?

options.text: tool_choice 'any', which compels a tool call while leaving the schema choice to the model.
options.rationale: It guarantees structured output from one of the schemas instead of a conversational reply.

options.text: tool_choice 'auto', which lets the model answer in prose whenever no schema quite fits.
options.rationale: Under 'auto' the model may return text, which is exactly the failure to avoid here.

options.text: Forced selection of the invoice tool, with the model correcting the type inside its arguments.
options.rationale: Forcing the wrong schema produces structured output in the wrong shape.

options.text: Three sequential requests, one per schema, keeping whichever result happens to parse.
options.rationale: This triples cost and still does not guarantee the model calls a tool on any given request.

cards.explanation: 'any' forces a tool call while letting the model select among the schemas, which is what an extraction pipeline with an unknown document type needs.

cards.prompt: Metadata extraction has to run before any enrichment tool. How do you guarantee the ordering?

options.text: State the ordering in the system prompt and rely on the model to follow the stated sequence.
options.rationale: A prompt instruction is guidance, not a guarantee; the model can still skip or reorder.

options.text: Set tool_choice to the tool type naming extract_metadata on the first request.
options.rationale: Forced selection makes the mandatory first step unskippable, after which later turns can use 'auto'.

options.text: Set tool_choice to 'any', which makes the model call whichever tool is listed first.
options.rationale: 'any' guarantees a call but not which tool, and list order does not decide it.

options.text: Withhold the enrichment tools until extraction returns, then add them back mid-turn.
options.rationale: Tools are declared per request; juggling the toolkit is neither the documented nor the simplest mechanism.

cards.explanation: Forced selection, tool_choice with type tool and the tool's name, is the mechanism for enforcing a mandatory first step.

cards.prompt: A synthesis agent bounces every fact check back to the coordinator, adding two or three hops and around 40% latency, and 85% of those checks are simple single-source lookups. What is the best fix?

options.text: Strip fact checking out of the synthesis stage so the workflow no longer pays for verification hops.
options.rationale: Removing the check trades latency for unverified output, which is not a fix at all.

options.text: Let the coordinator serve verification requests concurrently so the queue behind them clears faster.
options.rationale: Concurrency does nothing about the extra hops each individual request still has to make.

options.text: Hand the synthesis agent a narrow verification tool it calls itself for single-source checks, escalating the rest.
options.rationale: The common case is settled locally while genuinely complex verifications still use the full pipeline.

options.text: Keep a verification cache on the coordinator so a check already answered once comes back immediately.
options.rationale: A cache helps only on repeats; a first-time simple lookup still pays for the whole round trip.

cards.explanation: A scoped cross-role tool handles the high-frequency simple case directly, leaving the coordinator round trip for the complex minority.

cards.prompt: In the lesson's multi-agent research system, what does the coordinator's own toolset look like?

options.text: Every tool in the system, so it can take over any step a subagent leaves unfinished.
options.rationale: That recreates the overload problem in the one agent that most needs clear decisions.

options.text: The union of the search and analysis toolsets, minus the synthesis tools.
options.rationale: The coordinator holds no domain tools at all, let alone most of them.

options.text: Only search tools, on the grounds that coordination is mostly evidence gathering.
options.rationale: Search belongs to the web search agent; the coordinator does not gather evidence itself.

options.text: Workflow tools: spawning subagents, reviewing their output, and requesting revisions.
options.rationale: The coordinator runs the workflow and holds no domain-specific tools of its own.

cards.explanation: The coordinator carries only workflow tools such as subagent spawning, output review and revision requests, and no domain-specific capability.

cards.prompt: An agent's toolkit covers genuinely distinct jobs, querying, transforming and exporting, and there are far too many tools in total. Which remedy does the lesson's table give?

options.text: Split the tools across agents by role, giving each roughly four or five.
options.rationale: Distinct jobs split cleanly by role, which is the table's prescription for this row.

options.text: Collapse them into a single parameterised tool whose enum selects the job.
options.rationale: Consolidation is for variations on one job that share a shape, not for genuinely different jobs.

options.text: Expand every description with inputs, examples and explicit boundaries.
options.rationale: Descriptions cure ambiguity in a small toolkit, not a toolkit that is simply too large.

options.text: Register each job's tools on its own MCP server so the sets are presented separately.
options.rationale: The client flattens every server's tools into one list, so the agent's choice is unchanged.

cards.explanation: Tools that do different jobs split by role, with roughly four or five per agent; consolidation is reserved for variations on a single job.

cards.prompt: A team needs a shared Claude Code MCP server definition without committing personal credentials. Which setup fits?

options.text: Place the server URL only in a prose instruction file.
options.rationale: Instructions do not register the server connection.

options.text: Require every developer to copy credentials from the shared README.
options.rationale: Publishing credentials is not a private authentication mechanism.

options.text: Version a project .mcp.json and obtain credentials through an appropriate private mechanism.
options.rationale: Share the connection definition while keeping personal secrets out of source control.

options.text: Commit one developer's complete personal Claude configuration.
options.rationale: That can expose private settings and credentials unrelated to the project.

cards.explanation: Share the connection definition while keeping personal secrets out of source control.

cards.prompt: What distinguishes a typical local stdio MCP connection from a remote HTTP one?

options.text: The local entry launches a process; the remote entry specifies the supported network transport and endpoint.
options.rationale: Transport configuration must match how the server communicates.

options.text: Both require placing access tokens inside CLAUDE.md.
options.rationale: Instruction files are not an appropriate secret configuration mechanism.

options.text: A local process is identified only by a public HTTPS URL.
options.rationale: That describes a network endpoint rather than launching stdio.

options.text: The remote entry is configured as a local executable regardless of server type.
options.rationale: Using the wrong transport prevents the intended connection.

cards.explanation: Transport configuration must match how the server communicates.

cards.prompt: A shared MCP definition exists, but a teammate cannot access the service. What else may be required?

options.text: Assuming a committed definition bypasses server-side policy.
options.rationale: The server still controls access to its resources.

options.text: Workspace trust, connection approval and that teammate's authentication or service permissions.
options.rationale: Sharing connection metadata does not share or grant every user's access.

options.text: Copying another teammate's private tokens into version control.
options.rationale: That is not a proper access setup.

options.text: Running a memory-inspection command to authorize the server.
options.rationale: Memory inspection is not service authorization.

cards.explanation: Sharing connection metadata does not share or grant every user's access.

cards.prompt: A project MCP definition needs a token on each developer's machine. Which arrangement fits?

options.text: Encode the token with Base64 and commit it.
options.rationale: Encoding does not make a credential secret.

options.text: Write the token into generated answer explanations.
options.rationale: Output text is not an appropriate credential store.

options.text: Reference privately supplied credentials through supported configuration.
options.rationale: Share the definition while provisioning secrets separately.

options.text: Commit a long-lived token as a convenience default.
options.rationale: Source control would distribute the credential.

cards.explanation: Share the definition while provisioning secrets separately.

cards.prompt: An engineering team is standing up issue-tracker access for their Claude Code setup, and one developer volunteers to write the server from scratch. Where should they start?

options.text: Skip MCP and call the Jira REST API from shell commands, avoiding server configuration entirely.
options.rationale: This abandons the integration layer the question is about and gives up tool discovery and scoping.

options.text: Evaluate the maintained community Jira servers first, and build only if team workflows need more.
options.rationale: Jira is a standard integration with maintained community servers, so those are assessed before any custom build.

options.text: Build the custom server so the tool surface matches exactly the endpoints this team uses.
options.rationale: Custom work is justified only when community servers cannot meet specific team requirements.

options.text: Add Jira to each developer's user-level configuration so everyone connects independently.
options.rationale: This is a scoping answer to a build-versus-use question, and it also fragments a team-wide server.

cards.explanation: For standard integrations the pragmatic answer is always to evaluate community servers first and build custom only when they cannot meet team-specific needs.

cards.prompt: Which situation justifies building a custom MCP server rather than adopting a community one?

options.text: The community server is maintained by volunteers instead of by the vendor.
options.rationale: Maintenance model alone is not the criterion; community servers are the default for standard integrations.

options.text: The team would prefer a different naming convention for the exposed tools.
options.rationale: Cosmetic preferences do not justify the development and maintenance burden of a custom build.

options.text: The integration targets a proprietary internal system for which no community server exists.
options.rationale: Proprietary systems, team-specific workflows and custom business logic in the tool layer are the stated justifications.

options.text: The community server exposes more tools than the team expects to actually use.
options.rationale: An oversized tool surface is handled by scoping what the agent receives, not by rewriting the server.

cards.explanation: Custom servers are justified by team-specific workflows, custom business logic, or proprietary systems with no community equivalent.

cards.prompt: A .mcp.json entry supplies a url but omits the type field. What does Claude Code do with it?

options.text: It infers HTTP from the presence of a url and connects to the remote endpoint as normal.
options.rationale: No such inference happens; the missing type is treated as a configuration error.

options.text: It connects anyway but withholds the server's tools until a type is added later.
options.rationale: The server is not connected at all, so there are no withheld tools.

options.text: It rejects the entire file, so none of the project's configured servers load.
options.rationale: Only the malformed entry is skipped; the rest of the configuration still loads.

options.text: It reads the entry as a stdio server, skips it, and tells you to add the type.
options.rationale: A url with no type is a configuration error, and the entry is skipped with that message.

cards.explanation: Without a type field the entry is treated as a local launcher, so the server never connects and you are told to declare its transport.

cards.prompt: How do tools from configured MCP servers become available to an agent?

options.text: Every reachable server's tools are discovered at connection time and usable at once.
options.rationale: There is no manual activation step; project-level and user-level servers alike appear as soon as they connect.

options.text: Each server has to be activated within the session before its tools enter the toolkit.
options.rationale: No activation step exists in the model the lesson describes.

options.text: Project-level servers load automatically while user-level ones load on first use.
options.rationale: Both scopes are discovered the same way; the difference between them is sharing, not loading.

options.text: Tools appear only after the model requests them by name through a listing call.
options.rationale: Tool listing is a protocol detail handled by the client, not something the model triggers per tool.

cards.explanation: All tools from all configured and reachable servers, project-level and user-level, are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously.

cards.prompt: What does ${WORKSPACE_ROOT:-.} do when it appears in a .mcp.json argument?

options.text: It expands only when WORKSPACE_ROOT is unset, substituting the current directory in that case.
options.rationale: The logic is the other way round: the variable wins when it is set.

options.text: It expands to WORKSPACE_ROOT when that variable is set, and falls back to the current directory otherwise.
options.rationale: This is the default-value form of expansion, useful for machine-specific paths with a sensible fallback.

options.text: It expands to both values, passing the variable and the directory as two separate arguments.
options.rationale: Expansion produces one value, not a pair of arguments.

options.text: It requires WORKSPACE_ROOT to be set and checks that it resolves to the current directory.
options.rationale: The form exists precisely so an unset variable is tolerated.

cards.explanation: ${VAR:-default} expands to the variable when set and to the default when it is not, which suits machine-specific paths.

cards.prompt: A developer clones the repository but never sets the token that .mcp.json references, and there is no default form on it. What happens?

options.text: Claude Code refuses to start until every referenced variable has a value.
options.rationale: Startup is not blocked by an unset variable.

options.text: The literal text of the variable reference is sent to the server as the credential.
options.rationale: The reference is not passed through verbatim as a credential value.

options.text: Claude Code warns and carries on loading, so the missing token fails quietly.
options.rationale: The rest of the configuration still loads, which is why a missing token cannot be relied on to fail loudly.

options.text: Every other server in the file is skipped alongside the one that needed the token.
options.rationale: The remaining configuration continues to load; only that server is affected.

cards.explanation: An unset variable with no default does not halt configuration loading: Claude Code warns and continues, so the failure is quiet.

cards.prompt: What problem do MCP resources solve for an agent working against a database server?

options.text: They let the agent write to the tables without holding a separate write tool in its toolkit.
options.rationale: Resources expose content for reading; acting on data is what tools are for.

options.text: They compress large query results so that considerably more rows fit inside the context window.
options.rationale: Resources are catalogues of available content, not a compression mechanism.

options.text: They authenticate the agent against the database before its very first tool call is issued.
options.rationale: Authentication is handled by the server's configuration, not by resources.

options.text: They present the schema up front, sparing the agent a round of exploratory listing calls.
options.rationale: Without a schema resource the agent burns tool calls on list_tables and describe_table just to orient itself.

cards.explanation: Resources expose content catalogues such as a database schema up front, so the agent does not spend tool calls discovering what data exists.

cards.prompt: How does the MCP specification describe control over resources?

options.text: They are application-controlled: the server lists them and the client decides when to attach one to context.
options.rationale: The host surfaces a resource, for example through an @server:resource mention, so the agent sees it only then.

options.text: They are model-controlled: the model pulls in any listed resource whenever it judges it useful.
options.rationale: Model-controlled is the description of tools, not resources.
