options.rationale: This is the plan-then-execute hybrid the lesson says the exam tests.

options.text: Direct execution first, moving to plan mode if the edits stop being mechanical.
options.rationale: Waiting for complexity to appear is the trap; here it is stated in the task.

cards.explanation: Library migrations are the lesson's example of the hybrid pattern: plan the migration strategy, then execute it file by file. It is plan then direct, not plan or direct.

cards.prompt: The task is stated up front as restructuring a monolith into microservices. What does the lesson call out as the wrong move?

options.text: Beginning with direct execution and reaching for a plan once the work turns messy.
options.rationale: The complexity is already in the requirements, so planning should come first.

options.text: Choosing plan mode before reading any of the existing service boundaries.
options.rationale: Reading the existing structure is part of what plan mode is for.

options.text: Evaluating more than one decomposition before committing to a strategy.
options.rationale: Weighing multiple approaches is a reason to plan, not an error.

options.text: Using a subagent to gather the dependency map before the plan is written.
options.rationale: That is the recommended way to keep discovery output out of the main context.

cards.explanation: When the requirements already state that the work is complex, plan mode is the upfront choice; waiting for surprises before switching is the trap.

cards.prompt: What should you observe while Claude Code works through a task in plan mode?

options.text: Files are edited, but the changes are staged rather than written to the working tree.
options.rationale: Plan mode does not produce staged edits; it produces an approach.

options.text: Each proposed edit is applied and then reverted so that its effect can be measured.
options.rationale: No apply-and-revert cycle happens during planning.

options.text: Only test files are touched, leaving production sources unchanged until approval.
options.rationale: The distinction is not between test and production files; nothing is modified.

options.text: No files are modified at all; the codebase is read and an approach is proposed.
options.rationale: Plan mode enables safe exploration and design without changing files.

cards.explanation: Plan mode reads the codebase, analyses dependencies and proposes an approach without modifying any files.

cards.prompt: Three items are queued: splitting a shared library into two packages, correcting an off-by-one error with a clear stack trace, and moving forty files from one HTTP client to another. Which assignment follows the lesson's framework?

options.text: Plan mode for all three, since every item ends in code changes.
options.rationale: The well-scoped fix with a known cause gains nothing from planning.

options.text: Plan mode for the split and the client move, direct execution for the off-by-one fix.
options.rationale: Architectural restructuring and a many-file migration plan first, while a clear single-function fix goes direct.

options.text: Direct execution for all three, given a detailed enough opening prompt.
options.rationale: Multi-file architectural work risks costly rework without a strategy.

options.text: Plan mode for the split only, direct execution for the other two items.
options.rationale: A forty-file migration needs a consistent strategy, so it plans before it executes.

cards.explanation: Architectural restructuring and a multi-file migration both call for plan mode, while a single-function fix with a clear stack trace is the textbook direct execution case.

cards.prompt: An integration can be built two ways, each carrying different infrastructure requirements. What does that fact alone tell you about the mode?

options.text: Direct execution fits, because both approaches are already understood in outline.
options.rationale: Understanding the options is not the same as having chosen between them.

options.text: Either mode fits, because the choice depends only on how many files are touched.
options.rationale: Multiple valid approaches is its own criterion, independent of file count.

options.text: Plan mode fits, because competing approaches need evaluating before you commit.
options.rationale: Multiple valid approaches is one of the lesson's plan-mode criteria.

options.text: Direct execution fits, because implementing one approach reveals which is better.
options.rationale: Building first and comparing afterwards is the costly rework the lesson wants to avoid.

cards.explanation: Multiple valid approaches with different downstream requirements is one of the lesson's stated triggers for plan mode.

cards.prompt: Which of these does the lesson's decision framework send to direct execution?

options.text: Updating a configuration value whose location and new setting are both known.
options.rationale: Known fix, known location, known approach is the direct execution case.

options.text: Reorganising a module system so that imports flow in a single direction.
options.rationale: Restructuring a module system is listed under plan mode.

options.text: Mapping data flows through the codebase before any change has been chosen.
options.rationale: Codebase exploration is a plan mode trigger, ideally with the Explore subagent.

options.text: Deciding where a new service boundary should fall between two teams.
options.rationale: Service boundaries are architectural decisions, which the framework sends to plan mode.

cards.explanation: A configuration value update has a known location, a known change and no design decision, which is the framework's direct execution profile.

cards.prompt: A requested transformation repeatedly handles one edge case incorrectly. What feedback is most actionable?

options.text: Give a minimal failing input, actual output, expected output and relevant constraint.
options.rationale: A concrete counterexample makes the required correction testable.

options.text: Repeat that the result should be better.
options.rationale: That does not identify the failed behavior.

options.text: Ask for a longer explanation of the unchanged implementation.
options.rationale: More explanation does not supply the missing acceptance case.

options.text: Remove the edge case from the examples.
options.rationale: Removing the evidence conceals the defect.

cards.explanation: A concrete counterexample makes the required correction testable.

cards.prompt: A correction fixes one example but breaks a previously valid case. What should the next iteration include?

options.text: Removal of the earlier expected result.
options.rationale: Deleting a requirement hides the regression.

options.text: A larger prompt with no concrete examples.
options.rationale: More text does not necessarily preserve the missing case.

options.text: Both examples as explicit acceptance cases.
options.rationale: Refinement must preserve known-good behavior while fixing the defect.

options.text: Only the latest failing case, forgetting earlier requirements.
options.rationale: That encourages oscillating regressions.

cards.explanation: Refinement must preserve known-good behavior while fixing the defect.

cards.prompt: Generated code fails a meaningful assertion. What is the right refinement target?

options.text: Delete the assertion because the model wrote the code.
options.rationale: Authorship does not establish correctness.

options.text: Add a skip for every generated-code failure.
options.rationale: Skipping removes the evidence rather than repairing behavior.

options.text: Rename the test so it is no longer discovered.
options.rationale: That disguises an unresolved failure.

options.text: The implementation or a demonstrated mismatch in the test's intended contract.
options.rationale: The failure needs diagnosis; a valid assertion should not be weakened just to pass.

cards.explanation: The failure needs diagnosis; a valid assertion should not be weakened just to pass.

cards.prompt: A small bug fix keeps accumulating unrelated formatting and architecture changes. What feedback helps?

options.text: Restate the affected behavior and constrain the patch to the necessary scope.
options.rationale: A focused diff makes cause, effect and verification easier to assess.

options.text: Request a complete rewrite without identifying the bug.
options.rationale: That further expands uncertainty.

options.text: Judge quality only by the number of changed lines.
options.rationale: Diff size alone is not correctness.

options.text: Accept unrelated changes because they look modern.
options.rationale: Appearance does not establish relevance to the task.

cards.explanation: A focused diff makes cause, effect and verification easier to assess.

cards.prompt: A data migration is complex, with many edge cases around nulls, empty inputs and boundary values. Which technique does the lesson call most effective for that situation?

options.text: Rewriting the request in more precise technical prose before trying again.
options.rationale: More prose still leaves the work to interpretation, which is the failure mode the lesson names.

options.text: Asking Claude to interview you about the migration's requirements first.
options.rationale: The interview pattern is for domains you do not know well, not for pinning down edge cases you can already state.

options.text: Writing the tests first and iterating by sharing the failures.
options.rationale: Test-driven iteration is the lesson's pick for complex transformations.

options.text: Supplying one worked example and asking for the remaining cases by analogy.
options.rationale: A single example is thinner than the lesson's own guidance and does not cover the edge cases.

cards.explanation: Test-driven iteration is the lesson's most effective technique for complex transformations, because a failure message stating expected versus actual leaves no room for interpretation.

cards.prompt: You need a caching layer for an API but have never designed one. Which opening does the lesson recommend?

options.text: Ask Claude to pose questions about requirements and constraints before implementing.
options.rationale: The interview pattern surfaces considerations you would otherwise miss.

options.text: Give two input and output examples of the cache API you expect back.
options.rationale: Examples pin a transformation you already know; here you do not yet know what to ask for.

options.text: Write failing tests for the cache and share them before any implementation exists.
options.rationale: You cannot write meaningful tests for requirements you have not identified yet.

options.text: Describe the cache in as much technical detail as you can manage up front.
options.rationale: Detail you supply cannot cover the invalidation and consistency questions you do not know to ask.

cards.explanation: In an unfamiliar domain the interview pattern has Claude ask about invalidation, TTL, consistency and failure modes, surfacing considerations you would not have raised.

cards.prompt: What separates the interview pattern from the concrete-examples technique?

options.text: The interview pattern suits long transformations, while examples suit short simple ones.
options.rationale: Length of the transformation is not what distinguishes them.

options.text: The interview pattern is for batched feedback, while examples are for sequential feedback.
options.rationale: Batching and sequencing are a separate axis about interdependent versus independent issues.

options.text: The interview pattern applies to generated tests, while examples apply to generated code.
options.rationale: Neither technique is tied to a particular kind of artefact.

options.text: The interview pattern surfaces requirements you would miss; examples pin a transformation you know.
options.rationale: They address different problems, which the lesson flags as a common confusion.

cards.explanation: The interview pattern is for unfamiliar domains where you might overlook requirements; concrete examples are for when you know the exact transformation but the model keeps interpreting it differently.

cards.prompt: The same prose instruction produces a differently structured result on each run. The lesson warns against one instinctive response. Which one?

options.text: Reaching for more precise prose, which still leaves the request open to interpretation.
options.rationale: The lesson says the answer to inconsistent interpretation is examples first, not better prose.

options.text: Providing two before-and-after pairs that fix the transformation exactly.
options.rationale: This is the recommended first move, not the mistake.

options.text: Testing the result on a fresh case to confirm the pattern generalised.
options.rationale: Verifying generalisation is a step in the recommended process.

options.text: Adding one further example that demonstrates a specific edge case.
options.rationale: Adding an edge case example is the recommended follow-up when the standard case works.

cards.explanation: Refining prose still depends on interpretation; concrete input and output examples remove the ambiguity, so examples come first.

cards.prompt: Changing the error response shape also forces a change to the log format and to the client SDK type definitions. How should that feedback reach Claude?

options.text: As three separate turns, so each change can be reviewed before the next begins.
options.rationale: Sequencing interdependent fixes lets each one conflict with the others.

options.text: As one message listing all three, so the model sees the interacting constraints together.
options.rationale: The lesson batches feedback when fixes interact.

options.text: As one message naming only the response shape, letting the other two follow from it.
options.rationale: Leaving constraints unstated invites a fix that satisfies one and breaks the rest.

options.text: As three separate turns in reverse order, beginning with the SDK type definitions.
options.rationale: Ordering does not fix the underlying problem of splitting interdependent constraints.

cards.explanation: When fixes interact, all of the feedback belongs in a single message so the model can produce one coherent change across the interacting constraints.

cards.prompt: Two unrelated complaints remain: the function names are not camelCase, and the indentation uses four spaces instead of two. What does the lesson advise?

options.text: Combine them, since fewer turns always yield a more coherent overall result.
options.rationale: Fewer turns is not the goal; batching independent issues can confuse which feedback applies where.

options.text: Drop the smaller one, since style issues rarely justify another iteration.
options.rationale: The lesson does not advise dropping feedback; it advises sequencing it.

options.text: Fix them one at a time, since batching independent issues can confuse the model.
options.rationale: Independent issues are handled sequentially.

options.text: Restate both inside the original prompt and regenerate the whole file from scratch.
options.rationale: Regenerating discards working output and is not the lesson's refinement path.

cards.explanation: Independent issues are corrected sequentially, because batching feedback that does not interact can confuse the model about which correction applies to which part of the code.

cards.prompt: How many examples does the lesson consider enough, and what comes immediately after supplying them?

options.text: Two or three well-chosen ones, then a test on a new case to confirm it generalised.
options.rationale: The lesson says two or three set the pattern, and the next step is verifying generalisation.

options.text: One canonical example, then a prose summary restating the rule it demonstrates.
options.rationale: Falling back to prose reintroduces the interpretation problem examples were meant to remove.

options.text: As many examples as there are cases, since the model applies only patterns it has seen.
options.rationale: The lesson explicitly says you do not need to hand it every possible case.

options.text: Ten or more, then a ranking exercise so the model learns which cases matter most.
options.rationale: Piling on examples is not the technique; a few well-chosen ones suffice.

cards.explanation: Two or three well-chosen examples set the pattern, and the next step is trying a new case to confirm the model generalised it correctly.

cards.prompt: When you define expected behaviour through tests before iterating, which set of cases does the lesson name?

options.text: Randomly generated inputs, so that the transformation cannot simply be memorised.
options.rationale: Random inputs are not part of the described technique.

options.text: Happy path only, because failures on edge cases muddy the refinement signal.
options.rationale: Edge cases are exactly where the lesson expects the informative failures.

options.text: Regression cases drawn from the previous session's transcript of failures.
options.rationale: The lesson defines cases from expected behaviour, not from an earlier transcript.

options.text: Happy path, edge cases such as nulls and empty inputs, and performance requirements.
options.rationale: These are the three categories the lesson lists for test-driven iteration.

cards.explanation: Test-driven iteration defines expected behaviour through the happy path, edge cases such as nulls, empty inputs and boundaries, and performance requirements where they apply.

cards.prompt: A CI job must send a prompt to Claude Code and collect its output without an interactive conversation. Which invocation mode fits?

options.text: A prompt instruction saying the terminal has no keyboard.
options.rationale: Prompt text does not choose the CLI's execution mode.

options.text: Print mode using claude -p, with credentials and permissions configured for the job.
options.rationale: Print mode supports programmatic invocation; it does not bypass authentication or permission policy.

options.text: An interactive session that waits for a developer to type the prompt.
options.rationale: That requires the interaction the job is meant to avoid.

options.text: Resume mode alone, without specifying how the job supplies input or receives output.
options.rationale: Session selection does not replace programmatic invocation.

cards.explanation: Print mode supports programmatic invocation; it does not bypass authentication or permission policy.

cards.prompt: A CI step must parse Claude Code's result. What should it request and handle explicitly?

options.text: The absence of comments as proof the process executed successfully.
options.rationale: No findings and no successful execution are different outcomes.

options.text: A supported structured output format, with separate error and incomplete-result handling.
options.rationale: Automation needs a parseable contract and failure semantics.

options.text: Only prose formatted differently on each run.
options.rationale: Unstable prose is a fragile machine interface.

options.text: Any stdout as proof the review passed.
options.rationale: Output can describe failure or partial work.

cards.explanation: Automation needs a parseable contract and failure semantics.

cards.prompt: A CI review is authorized to inspect code but not modify it. How should that be implemented?

options.text: Allow writes and delete the audit trail afterward.
options.rationale: That conceals effects rather than preventing them.

options.text: Give deployment credentials to simplify repository reads.
options.rationale: That adds unnecessary privilege.

options.text: Use permissions or an execution environment that enforces read-only access.
options.rationale: The boundary belongs in executable policy, not only review instructions.

options.text: Rely only on the phrase 'please do not edit'.
options.rationale: A request is not an enforced capability limit.

cards.explanation: The boundary belongs in executable policy, not only review instructions.

cards.prompt: A review reruns after a new commit. How should it use earlier findings?

options.text: Repost every old comment without inspecting the changes.
options.rationale: That can resurrect fixed issues.

options.text: Suppress every previously seen location forever.
options.rationale: A later change may introduce a new defect there.

options.text: Assume the newest commit resolves all previous findings.
options.rationale: A commit's existence is not proof of repair.

options.text: Re-check them against the new diff and report new or still-relevant issues with stable references.
options.rationale: Historical findings are context to verify, not conclusions to repeat blindly.

cards.explanation: Historical findings are context to verify, not conclusions to repeat blindly.

cards.prompt: A colleague proposes fixing a Claude Code job that hangs in CI by exporting CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true before the command. How should you respond?

options.text: It works, but only if the runner also redirects stdin from /dev/null.
options.rationale: Redirecting stdin does not properly address interactive mode, and the variable still does not exist.

options.text: It works, though --batch is the documented flag for the same purpose.
options.rationale: Neither the variable nor that flag exists in Claude Code.

options.text: No such variable exists; print mode through the -p flag is the documented fix.
options.rationale: -p (also --print) is the supported way to run non-interactively.

options.text: It must be exported before the checkout step in order to take effect.
options.rationale: Export ordering is irrelevant to a variable Claude Code never reads.

cards.explanation: CLAUDE_HEADLESS and --batch do not exist, and stdin redirection does not address interactive mode. The documented fix is the -p flag.

cards.prompt: A CI job runs claude -p with both --output-format json and --json-schema. Where does the schema-validated data end up?

options.text: At the top level of the JSON object, replacing the envelope that would otherwise wrap it.
options.rationale: The envelope is still there; the validated data sits inside it.

options.text: In the envelope's structured_output field, which the job reads with jq .structured_output.
options.rationale: The lesson is explicit that it is not read from the top level.

options.text: In a sidecar file named after the schema, written beside the working directory.
options.rationale: No sidecar file is produced.

options.text: Inside the result text as fenced JSON, which the job extracts by string matching.
options.rationale: Schema validation exists precisely so the job does not have to scrape prose.

cards.explanation: Schema-conforming data lands in the JSON envelope's structured_output field, extracted with jq .structured_output rather than from the top level.

cards.prompt: What does --output-format json wrap around a print-mode run?

options.text: A stream of newline-delimited events, one for each tool call the run performs.
options.rationale: That shape belongs to stream-json, not to the json envelope.

options.text: A diff of every file the run touched, for the pipeline to apply or reject.
options.rationale: The run does not emit a patch as its output format.

options.text: A schema definition the job can publish so downstream steps agree on the shape.
options.rationale: The schema is something you supply with --json-schema, not something the envelope emits.

options.text: An envelope carrying the result text, the session ID, and cost and usage metadata.
options.rationale: This is what the lesson lists as the envelope's contents.

cards.explanation: The json output format wraps the run in an envelope holding the result text, the session ID and cost and usage metadata instead of human-readable text.

cards.prompt: A pipeline generates an authentication middleware and then asks the same session to review it. What does the lesson recommend instead?

options.text: Keep the one session but word the review request differently on the second turn.
options.rationale: The reasoning context that biases the review is still present regardless of wording.

options.text: Keep the one session and raise the turn cap so the review has room to work.
options.rationale: More turns do not remove the prior justification the session is carrying.

options.text: Run the review in the same session after compacting the generation history first.
options.rationale: Compaction shortens the history rather than giving the review a genuinely independent view.

options.text: Run the review as a separate invocation that shares no session context.
options.rationale: An independent reviewer evaluates the code on its own merits.

cards.explanation: Session context isolation means a second, independent claude -p invocation reviews the code with no access to the generation session's reasoning.

cards.prompt: Why does the lesson call same-session self-review a measurably weaker check?

options.text: The session has already spent most of its turn budget producing the code.
options.rationale: The effect is about retained reasoning, not about how many turns remain.

options.text: The session retains the reasoning that justified its choices, so it questions them less.
options.rationale: Prior justification biases the review against reopening settled decisions.

options.text: The session's tools are downgraded to read-only once it has written code.
options.rationale: No such downgrade happens after a write.

options.text: The session drops its memory files after the first file has been written.
options.rationale: Memory files are not discarded partway through a session.

cards.explanation: A session that generated code still holds the tradeoffs it weighed and the alternatives it rejected, so it is less likely to question decisions it already justified.

cards.prompt: An automated review reruns on every push with no memory of earlier runs. Which findings keep reappearing in its comments?

options.text: The ones the developer fixed, since the reviewer cannot see which commit fixed them.
options.rationale: A genuine fix drops out on its own, because the changed code no longer triggers the finding.

options.text: The ones raised by the generation session rather than by the review session.
options.rationale: Which session raised a finding does not determine whether it reappears.

options.text: The ones the schema marked low severity, which get re-ranked on each run.
options.rationale: Severity ranking is not what makes findings recur.

options.text: The ones the developer read, weighed and decided to leave exactly as they are.
options.rationale: Unchanged code keeps producing the same finding, and a context-free rescan cannot tell that apart from a new issue.

cards.explanation: Fixed issues disappear because the code changed, so the findings that recur are the ones the developer consciously declined to act on, and a review without prior context re-flags them every push.

cards.prompt: What reason does the lesson give for carrying prior findings into each subsequent review run?

options.text: Reruns cost roughly double once a pull request passes twenty commits.
options.rationale: Cost is not the argument the lesson makes here.

options.text: Repeated comments erode developer trust until people stop reading them.
options.rationale: Incremental context preserves the signal-to-noise ratio of the review.

options.text: Findings expire from the API after a day and cannot be fetched again later.
options.rationale: Findings are stored by the pipeline; nothing expires them.

options.text: Review platforms reject a second comment posted at the same file and line.
options.rationale: No such platform restriction is described.

cards.explanation: If the same comments appear on every push regardless of what was fixed, developers stop reading them, so incremental review context protects the signal.

cards.prompt: CI-invoked test generation keeps producing generic boilerplate that ignores the project's factories and fixtures. What does the lesson prescribe?

options.text: Raise the turn cap so the run has time to discover the factories for itself.
options.rationale: The problem is missing project context, which more turns do not supply.

options.text: Move the job onto the Batch API so a longer run can explore the repository.
options.rationale: Batch changes latency and cost, not the project knowledge available to the run.

options.text: Replace the system prompt with one describing the testing framework in use.
options.rationale: Replacing the prompt discards the defaults and still omits the project's own standards.

options.text: Document the testing standards, fixtures and review criteria in CLAUDE.md, which CI also reads.
options.rationale: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md in CI exactly as it does interactively.

cards.explanation: Claude Code reads project CLAUDE.md files in CI just as in interactive use, so testing standards, fixture paths and review criteria documented there turn boilerplate into tests that follow team patterns.

cards.prompt: A CI run should stay a coding assistant while also following three extra house rules. Which flag fits?

options.text: --append-system-prompt, which keeps the default prompt and adds your rules to it.
options.rationale: Appending preserves the default tool guidance, safety instructions and conventions.

options.text: --system-prompt, which supplies the house rules as the entire prompt for the run.
options.rationale: That drops the default prompt, so everything the task still needs must be resupplied.

options.text: --system-prompt-file, which swaps in a file containing just the house rules.
options.rationale: This also replaces the default prompt rather than adding to it.

options.text: --output-format json, which attaches the rules to the response envelope.
options.rationale: The output format shapes results; it carries no instructions.

cards.explanation: Appending keeps Claude Code's default prompt, including its tool guidance and safety instructions, so you supply only what differs.

cards.prompt: When does the lesson say replacing the entire system prompt is the right call?

options.text: Whenever the run is non-interactive, since the default prompt assumes a human is present.
options.rationale: Print mode alone is no reason to discard the default prompt.

options.text: Whenever the prompt text is long enough to justify keeping it in a version-controlled file.
options.rationale: File versus inline is about the flag variant, not about replace versus append.

options.text: When the agent's identity and permission model differ from Claude Code's own.
options.rationale: For example a non-coding agent in a pipeline no human watches.

options.text: When the job needs the default tool guidance but a different set of coding conventions.
options.rationale: Needing the defaults is precisely the case for appending instead.

cards.explanation: Replace when the identity or permission model differs from Claude Code's, such as a non-coding agent in an unattended pipeline; replacing drops the default prompt, so you own everything the task still needs.

cards.prompt: Which flag caps how many agentic turns a print-mode run takes before it exits?

options.text: --permission-mode
options.rationale: This sets the starting permission mode for the session.

options.text: --max-turns
options.rationale: It caps the number of agentic turns and then exits.

options.text: --input-format
options.rationale: This selects the input shape for print mode.

options.text: --bare
options.rationale: This skips auto-discovery of project configuration.

cards.explanation: --max-turns caps the number of agentic turns a run may take, after which it exits.

cards.prompt: Which value is a documented setting for --permission-mode?

options.text: readonly
options.rationale: Read-only behaviour comes from tool and permission rules, not from a mode of this name.

options.text: headless
options.rationale: Non-interactive execution is the -p flag, not a permission mode.

options.text: acceptEdits
options.rationale: It appears alongside default, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions and manual.

options.text: strict
options.rationale: No such mode is listed.

cards.explanation: The documented modes are default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions and manual, the last being an alias for default from v2.1.200.

cards.prompt: What does a bare tool name listed in --disallowedTools do, according to the lesson?

options.text: It asks for confirmation the first time that tool is called during the run.
options.rationale: Deny rules do not degrade into a prompt.

options.text: It removes the tool from context entirely rather than merely denying its calls.
options.rationale: The lesson states this explicitly for a bare tool name.

options.text: It downgrades the tool so it runs but cannot write outside the working directory.
options.rationale: No scoping-down behaviour is described for deny rules.

options.text: It applies only to subagents, leaving the main loop's tool set unchanged.
options.rationale: The rule applies to the run, not just to subagents.

cards.explanation: In --disallowedTools a bare tool name removes the tool from context entirely, while --allowedTools names the tools that may run without a permission prompt.

cards.prompt: A run needs to read and edit a sibling repository checked out next to the project. What does --add-dir give it?

options.text: File access to that directory, without configuration discovery inside it.
options.rationale: The lesson notes it grants file access, not configuration discovery.

options.text: File access plus that directory's CLAUDE.md and skills as loaded configuration.
options.rationale: Configuration in the added directory is not discovered by this flag.

options.text: Read access only, since edits stay confined to the launch directory.
options.rationale: The flag adds a directory Claude may read and edit.

options.text: A second session scoped to that directory, resumable by its own identifier.
options.rationale: No additional session is created.

cards.explanation: --add-dir adds a directory Claude may read and edit; it grants file access and does not pull that directory's configuration into the session.

cards.prompt: Which description of the session flags matches the lesson?

options.text: -c resumes a session by name, while -r resumes the most recent one in this directory.
options.rationale: The two are the other way round.

options.text: -c starts a fresh session in print mode, while -r replays the previous run's transcript.
options.rationale: Neither flag starts a fresh session or replays a transcript.

options.text: -c resumes the most recent conversation in the current directory, while -r resumes a specific session.
options.rationale: --continue takes no identifier, and --resume takes an id or a name.

options.text: -c and -r are aliases that differ only in whether the session identifier is quoted.
options.rationale: They are distinct flags with distinct behaviour.

cards.explanation: -c (--continue) resumes the most recent conversation in the current directory, while -r (--resume) takes a session id or name.

cards.prompt: A scripted call should start quickly and load no project configuration at all. Which flag does the lesson name, and what does it skip?

options.text: --bare, which skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md.
options.rationale: It leaves Claude with only the Bash and file read and edit tools.

options.text: --bare, which skips MCP servers and plugins while memory files still load normally.
options.rationale: Auto memory and CLAUDE.md are skipped as well.

options.text: --tools, which restricts the built-in tool set and therefore skips discovery too.
options.rationale: That flag restricts available built-in tools and does not affect configuration discovery.

options.text: --max-turns, which shortens a run by skipping its discovery phase entirely.
options.rationale: The turn cap limits agentic turns; it does not change what configuration loads.

cards.explanation: --bare is minimal mode: it skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, leaving only Bash and file read and edit tools.

cards.prompt: What trade-off does the lesson attach to the Message Batches API?

options.text: Half the cost, with processing up to twenty-four hours and no latency guarantee.
options.rationale: The saving comes with no latency SLA.

options.text: Half the cost, with a guaranteed one-hour turnaround for every queued request.
options.rationale: There is no guaranteed turnaround.

options.text: The same cost, with higher rate limits and priority scheduling for long jobs.
options.rationale: The defining benefit is the cost saving, not priority scheduling.

options.text: Half the cost, but only for runs that produce schema-validated structured output.
options.rationale: The saving is not conditional on the output format.

cards.explanation: The Message Batches API offers 50% cost savings with processing times up to 24 hours and no guaranteed latency.

cards.prompt: Which workload does the lesson keep on the real-time API rather than moving it to batch?

options.text: An overnight technical debt report that someone reads the following morning.
options.rationale: Not time-sensitive, so it is a batch candidate.

options.text: A weekly code audit scheduled to run outside working hours.
options.rationale: Scheduled and latency-tolerant, so batch suits it.

options.text: A nightly test generation run reviewed by developers the next day.
options.rationale: Runs overnight and is reviewed later, so batch suits it.

options.text: A pre-merge check that blocks the merge until it reports back.
options.rationale: Developers are waiting on it, so it needs the synchronous API.

cards.prompt: A CI test-generation job keeps proposing tests that the suite already contains. What does the lesson suggest?

options.text: Lower the turn cap so that fewer tests are proposed on each invocation.
options.rationale: Fewer suggestions does not make the remaining ones aware of existing coverage.

options.text: Include the existing test files in context so the run identifies coverage gaps.
options.rationale: Without them Claude cannot tell which scenarios are already covered.

options.text: Ask for prose recommendations instead of generated test code.
options.rationale: Changing the output shape does not address the duplication.

options.text: Move the job to the Batch API so a slower pass can compare more files.
options.rationale: Batch affects latency and cost, not what the run can see.

cards.explanation: Including existing test files in context lets Claude Code identify coverage gaps instead of duplicating scenarios the suite already has.

cards.prompt: A pipeline should expose only Bash, Edit and Read to the run, with every other built-in tool unavailable. Which flag expresses that?

options.text: --allowedTools naming those three, which is what removes every other tool from the run.
options.rationale: That flag names tools that run without a permission prompt; it does not limit availability.

options.text: --tools naming those three, which restricts which built-in tools are available at all.
options.rationale: This is the flag that narrows the available built-in tool set.

options.text: --model with a restricted alias, which limits the tool set the session exposes.
options.rationale: That flag sets the session model and has nothing to do with tools.

options.text: --permission-mode dontAsk, which narrows the session down to the three named tools.
options.rationale: A permission mode governs prompting behaviour, not which tools exist.

cards.explanation: --tools restricts which built-in tools are available at all, while --allowedTools only pre-approves tools so they run without a prompt.

cards.prompt: A classifier labels similar tickets inconsistently. Which instruction best defines a testable decision boundary?

options.text: Ask it to use the most impressive-sounding label.
options.rationale: Presentation quality is unrelated to the intended classification rule.

options.text: Tell it to choose whichever label appears first.
options.rationale: List order is not a valid classification criterion.

options.text: Specify the label conditions, exclusions and treatment of ambiguous cases.
options.rationale: Explicit criteria let outputs be compared against a known policy.

options.text: Ask for careful decisions without defining the labels.
options.rationale: Carefulness does not define category membership.

cards.explanation: Explicit criteria let outputs be compared against a known policy.

cards.prompt: An instruction says 'report important problems' but never defines important. What is missing?

options.text: Operational inclusion and exclusion criteria.
options.rationale: A testable boundary needs more than an evaluative adjective.

options.text: A longer greeting before the request.
options.rationale: A greeting does not define the policy.

options.text: A different name for the model.
options.rationale: Model naming does not resolve the ambiguity.

options.text: A requirement to make every report longer.
options.rationale: Length is not a severity definition.

cards.explanation: A testable boundary needs more than an evaluative adjective.

cards.prompt: A document being classified contains text telling the model to change its labels. How should the application treat that text?

options.text: As authorization to run any requested tool.
options.rationale: Data content does not grant tool permission.

options.text: As task data, while enforcing the trusted classification contract.
options.rationale: Embedded source text does not gain authority over the application task.

options.text: As a replacement for the application's instructions.
options.rationale: That promotes untrusted data into control.

options.text: As automatic proof that every label is invalid.
options.rationale: Hostile text does not determine all classification outcomes.

cards.explanation: Embedded source text does not gain authority over the application task.

cards.prompt: A review prompt needs actionable findings. Which output contract helps?

options.text: Require one finding per file regardless of evidence.
options.rationale: A quota can force unsupported findings.

options.text: Require only praise so the report is concise.
options.rationale: That cannot satisfy a defect-review task.

options.text: Require the location, violated criterion and supporting evidence for each finding.
options.rationale: Those fields let a reviewer inspect and reproduce the claim.

options.text: Require only a numeric confidence value.
options.rationale: Confidence alone does not explain the issue.

cards.explanation: Those fields let a reviewer inspect and reproduce the claim.

cards.prompt: A code review system prompt currently reads 'be conservative and use your best judgement.' Which replacement gives the model an actionable decision boundary?

options.text: Report bugs and security vulnerabilities, and skip style preferences and local patterns.
options.rationale: This names concrete categories to report and to skip, which is the explicit categorical criteria the lesson prescribes.

options.text: Report any issue you are more than eighty percent certain is a genuine defect.
options.rationale: A confidence threshold is not a criterion; self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and gives no definition of a valid finding.

options.text: Report issues that an experienced engineer would consider genuinely important.
options.rationale: This is another evaluative adjective with no operational boundary, exactly the class of instruction the lesson rejects.

options.text: Report issues in priority order and keep the finding count under ten per file.
options.rationale: A volume cap limits output without ever defining what qualifies as a finding.

cards.explanation: Explicit categorical criteria state what to report and what to skip, which is the lesson's replacement for vague instructions such as 'be conservative'.

cards.prompt: Your review bot's documentation-mismatch findings are wrong about 40 percent of the time, while its security findings run at high accuracy. Developers now ignore the security findings too. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Security findings degrade in accuracy when documentation findings share the same prompt.
options.rationale: The security category's accuracy is unchanged; what changed is whether developers read it.

options.text: Reviewers only ever read the category that appears first in a generated report.
options.rationale: The lesson attributes the behaviour to lost trust, not to report ordering.

options.text: Trust is not category-specific, so one noisy category degrades confidence in the whole output.
options.rationale: The lesson states that high false positive rates in one category destroy trust in all categories, because trust bleeds across the output.

options.text: Precision only matters as an average across categories rather than per category.
options.rationale: The opposite holds: a single bad category drags down a system whose average precision looks acceptable.

cards.explanation: High false positive rates in one category destroy developer trust in every category, because trust is not category-specific.

cards.prompt: That same pipeline emits documentation-mismatch findings that are wrong roughly 40 percent of the time, and developers have stopped reading all categories. Which response restores trust fastest?

options.text: Raise the temperature, run the review repeatedly, and keep findings that appear in every run.
options.rationale: Sampling variation is not the cause, and repeated runs do not supply the missing criteria.

options.text: Switch off the documentation-mismatch category while you rewrite its criteria with concrete code examples.
options.rationale: Disabling the high false positive category restores trust in the categories that already work, and the criteria are reworked before it returns.

options.text: Append an instruction telling the model to report only high-confidence documentation issues.
options.rationale: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so this does not reduce false positives.

options.text: Add a second model pass that silently discards documentation findings it cannot confirm.
options.rationale: An extra pass adds cost without defining what a valid documentation finding is, and the noisy category keeps running.

cards.explanation: Temporarily disabling the high false positive category restores system-wide trust immediately while its criteria are rebuilt with concrete code examples.

cards.prompt: Your prompt defines severity in prose, such as 'Critical: issues that could cause system failures or data loss.' Classifications still vary between runs. What does the lesson prescribe?

options.text: Add a numeric score range beside each label so the model can calculate severity.
options.rationale: A numeric range still leaves the model to decide which issues land in it.

options.text: Ask the model to justify its severity choice in prose before it assigns a label.
options.rationale: Justification does not remove the ambiguity in the definition being applied.

options.text: Cut the number of severity levels to two so there is less room for interpretation.
options.rationale: Fewer levels do not fix the underlying problem, which is that prose definitions must be interpreted.

options.text: Replace the prose definitions with actual code snippets that exemplify each severity level.
options.rationale: Concrete code examples remove the interpretation step and produce consistent classification across invocations.

cards.explanation: Severity calibration needs concrete code examples for each level, because prose definitions force the model to interpret what a phrase like 'system failures' covers.

cards.prompt: Why does adding 'only report high-confidence findings' fail to reduce false positives?

options.text: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so the model is often certain about wrong findings.
options.rationale: The lesson states the model is frequently sure about wrong findings and hesitant about right ones, so the filter removes the wrong items.

options.text: Confidence values cannot be returned in a structured field alongside each finding.
options.rationale: Findings can carry confidence fields; the problem is the quality of the value, not whether it can be emitted.

options.text: Confidence filtering discards the highest severity findings before developers see them.
options.rationale: Severity and confidence are independent, and the failure is not severity-specific.

options.text: Confidence values change the sampling temperature and make the output less deterministic.
options.rationale: Asking for confidence does not alter sampling parameters.

cards.explanation: Large language model self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so filtering on it removes good findings and keeps bad ones.

cards.prompt: Where do confidence scores legitimately earn their place in a review pipeline?

options.text: As the primary filter deciding which findings the model produces in the first place.
options.rationale: The lesson explicitly rejects confidence as the mechanism that defines a valid finding.

options.text: As a replacement for categorical criteria once precision reaches an acceptable level.
options.rationale: Criteria are never replaced by confidence; they remain the first step.

options.text: As a routing signal that sends uncertain findings to human review once criteria exist.
options.rationale: The lesson allows confidence for routing low-certainty findings to human review, but only after explicit criteria are defined.

options.text: As a substitute for severity levels, since both express how serious a finding is.
options.rationale: Confidence expresses certainty, not impact, so it cannot stand in for severity.

cards.explanation: Confidence scores are useful for routing uncertain findings to human review, but only after explicit criteria define what counts as a finding.

cards.prompt: Precision on one review category is poor. What order of work does the lesson require?

options.text: Tune a confidence threshold first, then write criteria for whatever still slips through.
options.rationale: This inverts the hierarchy; a threshold applied to undefined findings has nothing reliable to filter.

options.text: Write explicit criteria first, and only then layer confidence-based routing on top.
options.rationale: The lesson states the hierarchy plainly: explicit criteria first, confidence-based routing second.

options.text: Introduce routing and criteria simultaneously so their effects can be compared directly.
options.rationale: The lesson does not treat these as competing options to A/B test; criteria are a prerequisite.

options.text: Skip criteria altogether if the routing threshold already keeps finding volume low.
options.rationale: Low volume is not precision, and skipping the first step is the error the lesson warns against.

cards.explanation: The hierarchy is explicit criteria first, confidence-based routing second, and the first step is never skipped.

cards.prompt: The lesson's example review prompt allows comments to be flagged under exactly one condition. Which is it?

options.text: When a comment is missing from a public function that has no documentation.
options.rationale: Absent documentation is not the trigger the example prompt defines.

options.text: When a comment uses terminology that differs from the local naming conventions.
options.rationale: Local patterns and style are explicitly in the skip list.

options.text: When a comment has not been updated since the file was last modified.
options.rationale: Staleness by timestamp is not a behavioural contradiction and is not the stated trigger.

options.text: When the behaviour a comment claims contradicts what the code actually does.
options.rationale: The example prompt flags comments only where claimed behaviour contradicts actual code behaviour.

cards.explanation: The example prompt permits a comment finding only when the claimed behaviour contradicts the code's actual behaviour.

cards.prompt: In the lesson's build exercise, what false positive rate triggers temporarily disabling a review category?

options.text: Above 25 percent for that category.
options.rationale: The exercise sets the threshold at 25 percent and asks for a documented re-enablement plan.

options.text: Above 50 percent for that category.
options.rationale: This is looser than the exercise specifies and leaves badly performing categories running.

options.text: Any category producing fewer findings than the security category.
options.rationale: Finding volume is unrelated to the precision threshold in the exercise.

options.text: Any category whose findings developers dismiss more than once a week.
options.rationale: Dismissal frequency is not the metric the exercise defines for this decision.

cards.explanation: The build exercise disables any category whose false positive rate exceeds 25 percent until its criteria are refined.

cards.prompt: You have switched off a noisy review category while you rework it. What does the lesson say this decision represents?

options.text: The category is permanently retired because its precision cannot be recovered.
options.rationale: The lesson is explicit that the category is not being abandoned, only paused.

options.text: System-wide trust is being prioritised over category completeness while criteria are rebuilt.
options.rationale: The lesson frames the trade-off exactly this way, with the category switched back on once precision improves.

options.text: The remaining categories must also be paused so the comparison stays fair.
options.rationale: Pausing working categories would destroy the trust the manoeuvre is meant to protect.

options.text: The findings should still be generated but hidden from the report as a control group.
options.rationale: The lesson calls for disabling the category, not for shadow reporting.

cards.explanation: Disabling the category trades category completeness for system-wide trust, and it is re-enabled once its precision improves.

cards.prompt: Instructions describe an output convention, but valid edge cases are formatted inconsistently. Which addition can demonstrate the convention?

options.text: Several copies of the same easy example.
options.rationale: Repeated easy cases do not demonstrate the troublesome boundary.

options.text: Only examples whose outputs violate the intended convention.
options.rationale: Unexplained wrong outputs teach the wrong pattern.

options.text: Examples of unrelated tasks with a similar word count.
options.rationale: Length similarity does not show the required mapping.

options.text: A small set of varied input/output examples, including the edge cases.
options.rationale: Examples show how the rule applies; their effect still needs evaluation.

cards.explanation: Examples show how the rule applies; their effect still needs evaluation.

cards.prompt: Few-shot examples cover only easy cases from the dominant class. What is missing?

options.text: More copies of the same dominant example.
options.rationale: Duplication does not add missing coverage.

options.text: A rule that minority classes never occur.
options.rationale: That changes the task instead of teaching it.

options.text: Examples with their correct labels removed.
options.rationale: The intended mapping becomes unclear.

options.text: Representative boundary and minority cases.
options.rationale: Examples should demonstrate the distinctions the task actually requires.

cards.explanation: Examples should demonstrate the distinctions the task actually requires.

cards.prompt: Several examples demonstrate a mandatory access rule. What still enforces the rule?

options.text: Application authorization or permission checks.
options.rationale: Examples can shape behavior but are not an execution boundary.

options.text: The count of examples alone.
options.rationale: No example count proves enforcement.

options.text: The order of the answer choices.
options.rationale: Presentation order does not authorize actions.

options.text: A promise that the model understood every example.
options.rationale: Understanding claims are not control mechanisms.

cards.explanation: Examples can shape behavior but are not an execution boundary.

cards.prompt: New examples improve the cases used to write the prompt. What should be checked next?

options.text: Nothing; fitting examples proves production readiness.
options.rationale: Unseen inputs may still fail.

options.text: Performance on held-out cases and relevant failure slices.
options.rationale: Development examples alone can overstate generalization.

options.text: Only whether the prompt is longer.
options.rationale: Length is not an evaluation result.

options.text: Whether it repeats the examples verbatim.
options.rationale: Memorization does not establish transfer.

cards.explanation: Development examples alone can overstate generalization.

cards.prompt: How many targeted few-shot examples does the lesson recommend, and on what grounds?

options.text: One, because a single clear demonstration avoids biasing the model toward it.
options.rationale: One example does not establish a pattern for the model to follow.

options.text: Two to four, because fewer fails to establish a pattern and more wastes tokens.
options.rationale: The lesson sets this range exactly, noting that examples beyond four cost tokens without proportional benefit.

options.text: Five to ten, because covering every document type matters more than token cost.
options.rationale: This exceeds the recommended range and buys little additional benefit.

options.text: As many as the context window allows, because accuracy rises with example count.
options.rationale: Accuracy does not scale with example count; targeting the failing cases matters more than volume.

cards.explanation: The lesson prescribes two to four targeted examples: fewer than two establishes no pattern, and more than four wastes tokens.

cards.prompt: Your few-shot examples are plain input and output pairs, and the model still mishandles ambiguous cases it has not seen. What is missing from the examples?

options.text: A reasoning section in each example explaining why that choice beat the alternatives.
options.rationale: Reasoning teaches the decision principle, so the model generalises to novel patterns instead of matching surface features.

options.text: A larger number of near-identical examples covering the same decision.
options.rationale: Repeating similar cases reinforces pattern matching rather than teaching the principle.

options.text: An explicit statement that the examples are authoritative and must be followed.
options.rationale: Asserting authority does not tell the model how to decide an unseen case.

options.text: A confidence score attached to each example output so they can be weighted.
options.rationale: Weighting examples by confidence is not part of the technique and does not convey reasoning.

cards.explanation: Examples must show the reasoning behind each decision, which teaches the model the general principle rather than a literal pattern to match.

cards.prompt: Which symptom is one of the three stated triggers for reaching for few-shot examples?

options.text: The model returns malformed JSON that the parser cannot read.
options.rationale: Malformed JSON is mapped to tool use with a JSON schema, not to few-shot examples.

options.text: Responses stop early and truncate before the final field is written.
options.rationale: Truncation is a token budget problem, not one of the three triggers.

options.text: Extraction returns empty fields for information the document actually contains.
options.rationale: This is the third stated trigger: the data exists but sits in an unexpected structure, so examples of that structure resolve it.

options.text: The model calls an external tool that is not available in the environment.
options.rationale: Tool availability is unrelated to the triggers the lesson lists.

cards.explanation: Empty or null fields for information that is present in the document is one of the three triggers for few-shot examples.

cards.prompt: A thorough prompt already specifies the output format, yet structure varies between runs, sometimes a table and sometimes prose. What should you try first?

options.text: Expand the format section of the instructions with more precise wording.
options.rationale: If detailed instructions already exist and output is still inconsistent, more instructions do not fix it.

options.text: Lower the temperature so the model's formatting choices become deterministic.
options.rationale: Temperature is not the technique the lesson prescribes for formatting consistency.

options.text: Ask the model to restate the required format before it produces the answer.
options.rationale: Restating an instruction is still an instruction and does not demonstrate the target format.

options.text: Add two to four examples that display the exact format you want.
options.rationale: Few-shot examples are the lesson's first-choice technique for consistency when instructions alone have failed.

cards.explanation: When detailed instructions already exist and output is still inconsistent, few-shot examples showing the exact format are the correct next step.

cards.prompt: Your pipeline occasionally receives JSON that fails to parse. Which technique does the lesson's decision table map to this problem?

options.text: Define the extraction as a tool and constrain it with a JSON schema.
options.rationale: The table maps malformed JSON output to tool use with JSON schemas, which removes syntax errors.

options.text: Add few-shot examples that show correctly formatted JSON documents.
options.rationale: Few-shot examples address consistency and structural variety, not JSON syntax guarantees.

options.text: Run a validation-retry loop that feeds the parse error back to the model.
options.rationale: Retries are mapped to semantic failures such as sums that do not match, not to syntax.

options.text: Mark the optional properties in the schema as nullable rather than required.
options.rationale: Nullable fields address fabrication of missing values, not malformed output.

cards.explanation: The lesson maps malformed JSON to tool use with JSON schemas, which eliminates syntax errors entirely.

cards.prompt: The model invents plausible values for fields the source document never mentions. Which technique does the lesson map to this failure?

options.text: More few-shot examples showing documents that omit some information.
options.rationale: The lesson states explicitly that fabrication of missing data does not improve with examples.

options.text: Optional or nullable schema fields so that absence can be reported honestly.
options.rationale: Fabricated values for missing fields map to optional and nullable schema fields in the decision table.

options.text: A stricter instruction forbidding the model from guessing any value at all.
options.rationale: An instruction does not relieve the pressure a required field places on the model.

options.text: A second review pass that deletes any value it is unable to confirm.
options.rationale: This hides the symptom after the fact instead of removing the cause in the schema.

cards.explanation: Fabricated values for missing fields are a schema problem: optional or nullable fields let the model return nothing honestly.

cards.prompt: Extracted line items do not add up to the stated total. Which technique does the lesson map to this failure?

options.text: Few-shot examples demonstrating arithmetic over extracted line items.
options.rationale: Examples address structure and consistency, not verification of computed values.

options.text: A tool schema that declares the total as a field computed from the items.
options.rationale: A schema constrains shape and cannot enforce cross-field arithmetic.

options.text: A validation-retry loop that feeds the discrepancy back to the model.
options.rationale: The decision table maps an extraction sum that does not match the total to a validation-retry loop.

options.text: An enum field recording whether the model judged the total trustworthy.
options.rationale: A self-reported flag is not an independent check of the arithmetic.

cards.explanation: A sum that does not match the stated total is a semantic error, which the lesson routes to a validation-retry loop.

cards.prompt: An agent routes requests to the wrong tool. What does the lesson's table say to try first, and what after that?

options.text: Few-shot routing examples first, then stricter tool schemas if the problem persists.
options.rationale: This reverses the order; descriptions come before examples for tool selection.

options.text: A forced tool choice first, then few-shot examples if flexibility is later needed.
options.rationale: Forcing a tool removes selection entirely rather than improving it.

options.text: A validation-retry loop first, then better tool descriptions if the problem persists.
options.rationale: Retry loops address extraction semantics, not routing decisions.

options.text: Better tool descriptions first, then few-shot examples if the problem persists.
options.rationale: The table lists wrong tool selection as better tool descriptions first, then few-shot.

cards.explanation: For wrong tool selection the lesson prescribes improving tool descriptions first, and only then adding few-shot examples.

cards.prompt: A reviewer model labels variable shadowing 'critical' in one file and 'minor' in another. Why is a confidence threshold the wrong fix?

options.text: Thresholds are poorly calibrated and leave the inconsistent judgement itself untouched.
options.rationale: The lesson warns that thresholds do not address the root cause; examples showing the correct judgement do.

options.text: Thresholds can be applied to extraction tasks only, never to review tasks.
options.rationale: Thresholds can be applied anywhere; the objection is that they do not work, not that they are unavailable.

options.text: Thresholds force the model to return text instead of structured findings.
options.rationale: Asking for a confidence value has no effect on whether output is structured.

options.text: Thresholds increase the number of findings overall, which worsens the variance.
options.rationale: A threshold filters findings; the problem is that the surviving judgements are still inconsistent.

cards.explanation: Confidence thresholds are poorly calibrated and never address the root cause; examples demonstrating the correct judgement on ambiguous cases do.

cards.prompt: Why do examples drawn from several document structures reduce fabrication during extraction?

options.text: They shorten the prompt, leaving more of the context window for the source document.
options.rationale: Examples lengthen the prompt; the benefit is not a context saving.

options.text: They raise the model's self-reported confidence on unfamiliar page layouts.
options.rationale: Self-reported confidence is not the mechanism, and it is poorly calibrated in any case.

options.text: They teach the model to handle structural variety instead of inventing missing values.
options.rationale: Showing extraction from tables, narrative text and mixed formats teaches the model to cope with variety rather than fabricate.

options.text: They make the model skip any section whose structure it does not recognise.
options.rationale: Skipping content would produce empty fields, which is the failure the examples are meant to remove.

cards.explanation: Examples covering varied document structures teach the model to handle structural variety, which cuts both empty fields and invented values.

cards.prompt: In a code review prompt, what second job do well-chosen few-shot examples perform?

options.text: They cap how many findings the model may report, keeping reviews short.
options.rationale: Examples shape judgement rather than impose a volume limit.

options.text: They remove the need for severity levels by ranking the examples by importance.
options.rationale: Examples calibrate severity levels; they do not replace them.

options.text: They let the model skip files resembling an example it has already processed.
options.rationale: Nothing in the technique licenses skipping files.

options.text: They show which patterns to ignore as well as which to flag, cutting false positives.
options.rationale: Examples that separate acceptable patterns from genuine defects reduce false positives while preserving real detections.

cards.explanation: Few-shot examples in review prompts demonstrate both what to flag and what to ignore, which reduces false positives.

cards.prompt: A supported Claude API integration needs schema-constrained output. What else must the application still check?

options.text: Domain correctness, source support and unsuccessful or incomplete responses.
options.rationale: A valid structure does not establish factual correctness or successful completion.

options.text: Nothing, because schema conformance proves every field is true.
options.rationale: Types and shape do not prove the values are factual.

options.text: Only whether the answer contains a confident phrase.
options.rationale: Confidence wording is not validation.

options.text: Only the number of fields, ignoring their values.
options.rationale: Field count does not establish meaning or correctness.

cards.explanation: A valid structure does not establish factual correctness or successful completion.

cards.prompt: A document omits an optional field, but the schema requires a fabricated string to fill it. What should change?

options.text: Copy the value from an unrelated document.
options.rationale: That mixes records without evidence.

options.text: Treat the field name itself as its value.
options.rationale: That satisfies neither the intended meaning nor the evidence requirement.

options.text: Allow an explicit missing value where the domain contract permits it.
options.rationale: The schema should represent absence rather than pressure the model to invent data.

options.text: Insert a plausible value to keep the type valid.
options.rationale: Plausibility is not source support.

cards.explanation: The schema should represent absence rather than pressure the model to invent data.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between forcing a tool choice and constraining its argument schema?

options.text: Forcing a tool automatically validates every business fact.
options.rationale: Choosing an operation does not prove its inputs are true.

options.text: A schema decides whether external side effects are authorized.
options.rationale: Authorization is a separate application concern.

options.text: Both settings are just output styling preferences.
options.rationale: They affect structured interaction, not merely appearance.

options.text: Selection controls which call is requested; schema controls constrain its structure.
options.rationale: These are separate controls, and application validation still matters.

cards.explanation: These are separate controls, and application validation still matters.

cards.prompt: An output-constrained request ends with refusal or truncation. What should the caller do?

options.text: Handle that outcome explicitly before consuming a complete result.
options.rationale: A requested format does not eliminate unsuccessful response paths.

options.text: Assume a complete business result must exist.
options.rationale: The completion status contradicts that assumption.

options.text: Fill missing fields with arbitrary defaults and claim success.
options.rationale: Defaults can conceal unavailable output.

options.text: Parse only the first valid-looking fragment as the final answer.
options.rationale: A fragment may omit required content or meaning.

cards.explanation: A requested format does not eliminate unsuccessful response paths.

cards.prompt: Which statement matches the reliability hierarchy the exam guide expects for structured output?

options.text: Prompt-based JSON ranks higher because it avoids the token cost of tool definitions.
options.rationale: Token cost does not enter the hierarchy, and prompt-based output ranks below tool use.

options.text: Tool use with a JSON schema eliminates the syntax errors that prompt-based output still produces.
options.rationale: The hierarchy places tool use with JSON schemas above prompt-based JSON precisely because it removes syntax errors.

options.text: The two approaches are equivalent once the prompt contains a formatted example.
options.rationale: An example improves the odds but gives no structural guarantee.

options.text: Prompt-based JSON is safer because the model can explain any fields it leaves empty.
options.rationale: Commentary alongside JSON makes parsing harder rather than safer.

cards.explanation: The guide's hierarchy is tool use with JSON schemas above prompt-based JSON, because the schema removes syntax errors that prompting cannot.

cards.prompt: Incoming documents may be invoices, receipts or contracts, you have one extraction tool per type, and the type is unknown at request time. Which tool_choice setting fits?

options.text: auto, so the model can answer in text when the document type is unclear.
options.rationale: auto permits a text-only reply, so structured output is not guaranteed.

options.text: A specific named tool such as extract_invoice, so one schema always applies.
options.rationale: Forcing one schema misclassifies every document that is not of that type.

options.text: any, so a tool call is guaranteed while the model selects the matching schema.
options.rationale: any guarantees a tool call and still lets the model choose among the extraction tools, which is the case the lesson describes.

options.text: none, so the model classifies the document before any tool is invoked.
options.rationale: none blocks tool calls entirely and produces no structured output.

cards.explanation: tool_choice 'any' guarantees a tool call while leaving the choice of extraction schema to the model, which suits an unknown document type.

cards.prompt: Metadata extraction must run before any enrichment step, with no discretion left to the model. Which setting enforces that?

options.text: tool_choice set to auto, with the metadata tool listed first in the tools array.
options.rationale: Ordering does not oblige the model to call anything, and auto allows a text reply.

options.text: tool_choice set to any, with only extraction tools defined for the request.
options.rationale: any guarantees a call but not which tool is called.

options.text: tool_choice set to none until the enrichment stage begins.
options.rationale: none prevents tool calls, so the mandatory step never runs.

options.text: tool_choice set to the specific named metadata tool for that request.
options.rationale: Naming the tool forces exactly that call, which is how the lesson enforces a mandatory first step.

cards.explanation: Setting tool_choice to a specific named tool forces that exact call, which is how a mandatory first step such as metadata extraction is guaranteed.

cards.prompt: You forced a specific tool call on the first request of a multi-step flow. What must the following request do?

options.text: Switch back to auto or omit tool_choice, or the model is obliged to call the same tool again.
options.rationale: tool_choice applies per request, so leaving the forced setting in place loops on the same tool.

options.text: Repeat the same forced tool_choice, because the setting persists across the conversation.
options.rationale: The parameter is per request, not per conversation, so nothing persists.

options.text: Remove the tool definition entirely, because a forced tool cannot be redefined later.
options.rationale: Tools may be redefined freely; removing them is unnecessary.

options.text: Set tool_choice to none, because a conversation permits only a single tool call.
options.rationale: There is no such per-conversation limit, and none would block legitimate later calls.

cards.explanation: tool_choice applies per request, so the follow-up request must relax it to auto or omit it, otherwise the forced tool is called again and the flow loops.

cards.prompt: Your extraction runs through a tool constrained by a strict JSON schema. Which failure can still reach production?

options.text: A trailing comma that stops the JSON parser from reading the response.
options.rationale: Trailing commas are a syntax error, which the schema-constrained tool call eliminates.

options.text: A missing closing bracket somewhere in a nested object.
options.rationale: Unbalanced brackets are a syntax error and cannot survive schema-constrained output.

options.text: An unquoted key appearing in the returned object.
options.rationale: Unquoted keys are a syntax error removed by the same mechanism.

options.text: Line items that do not add up to the stated total on the document.
options.rationale: Sum discrepancies are semantic errors, which schemas do not prevent and which need separate validation.

cards.explanation: Tool use with a JSON schema removes syntax errors only; semantic errors such as sums that do not reconcile still require validation logic.

cards.prompt: A classification field must cope with documents whose type is genuinely ambiguous. What does the lesson recommend?

options.text: Leave the field null whenever the classification cannot be decided confidently.
options.rationale: Null signals absence of data rather than a positive judgement that the evidence is ambiguous.

options.text: Add an explicit 'unclear' member to the enum for genuinely ambiguous cases.
options.rationale: An 'unclear' enum value stops the model forcing a classification when the evidence does not support one.

options.text: Drop the enum and accept free text so any classification can be recorded.
options.rationale: Free text abandons the constraint and makes downstream handling unreliable.

options.text: Default to the most frequent category and attach a low confidence score.
options.rationale: Defaulting invents a classification, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.

cards.explanation: An explicit 'unclear' enum value lets the model report genuine ambiguity instead of forcing a classification.

cards.prompt: How does the lesson keep a categorisation schema extensible for cases the predefined categories do not cover?

options.text: An 'other' enum value paired with a freeform detail string field.
options.rationale: This is the lesson's extensible categorisation pattern: a catch-all value plus a place to describe the actual case.

options.text: Permission for the model to invent new enum values when none of them fit.
options.rationale: Unconstrained values defeat the purpose of an enum and break downstream consumers.

options.text: A separate extraction tool for every category that might appear in future.
options.rationale: Proliferating tools does not address unforeseen categories within a single field.

options.text: An optional category field that returns null whenever the case is unknown.
options.rationale: Null loses the information about what the document actually was.

cards.explanation: An 'other' enum value combined with a freeform detail string captures edge cases without breaking the constrained field.
