options.text: Because the coordinator will retry the query indefinitely once it sees no results returned.
options.rationale: It will not retry at all, and that absence of recovery is the actual problem.

options.text: Because the coordinator reads it as a genuine empty answer, so no recovery is ever attempted at all.
options.rationale: Silent suppression is invisible: the output looks complete while an entire area is missing.

options.text: Because empty result lists cannot be merged into the final synthesis output.
options.rationale: They merge without difficulty, which is precisely why the gap goes undetected.

options.text: Because the status field is reserved for the coordinator to set rather than the subagent.
options.rationale: No such protocol rule exists; subagents report their own status.

cards.explanation: Silent suppression makes the coordinator treat a failure as a genuine empty answer, so it never retries or tries alternatives and the output carries undetectable gaps.

cards.prompt: An order lookup service is down and the tool wrapper returns no records as a successful result. What does the customer experience?

options.text: A timeout message suggesting that they try their request again a little later.
options.rationale: The failure was hidden, so no such message is ever produced.

options.text: A request for additional identifiers so the agent can narrow its search.
options.rationale: The agent has no reason to ask, because it believes the lookup succeeded.

options.text: An escalation to a human reviewer, because the tool reported that it had failed.
options.rationale: Nothing was reported as a failure, so no escalation trigger fires.

options.text: An agent confidently telling them there are no orders on their account.
options.rationale: Suppressing the outage behind a successful empty result makes the agent assert a false fact.

cards.explanation: Silent suppression in a support context turns an outage into a confident false statement that the customer has no orders.

cards.prompt: One of five research subagents times out and the pipeline's top-level handler aborts the entire run. What is wrong with this design?

options.text: It discards four completed results and leaves no path to partial recovery.
options.rationale: Workflow termination is a disproportionate response that wastes work the other subagents finished.

options.text: It hides the failure from the coordinator in the same way a success status would.
options.rationale: The failure is fully visible here; it is the response to it that is wrong.

options.text: It breaks the requirement that transient failures be retried at the coordinator level.
options.rationale: Local retry for transient failures belongs in the subagent, not the coordinator.

options.text: It prevents the coordinator from categorising the failure as transient or permanent.
options.rationale: Categorisation remains possible; the run simply ends before recovery can happen.

cards.explanation: Workflow termination throws away the results other subagents completed and offers no recovery path, which is disproportionate to a single failure.

cards.prompt: A database query executes normally and matches no records. What should the subagent report?

options.text: An error with failure type transient and the retry flag set to true.
options.rationale: Nothing failed, so classifying it as an error invites a pointless retry.

options.text: A partial failure carrying an empty array of partial results.
options.rationale: The operation completed in full, so partial failure misdescribes it.

options.text: Success with an empty results array and the retry flag set to false.
options.rationale: A query that ran and matched nothing is a valid empty result, and that emptiness is the answer.

options.text: Success with the retry flag set to true, so the coordinator can confirm the result.
options.rationale: A confirming retry will return the same nothing and waste resources.

cards.explanation: A valid empty result means the query executed and found no matches, so it is reported as a success that needs no retry.

cards.prompt: A coordinator reruns every query that comes back with no rows, on the assumption that emptiness signals a problem. What is the consequence?

options.text: Access failures get caught sooner, at the cost of some additional latency.
options.rationale: Access failures are a separate case that is already reported as an error.

options.text: Time and quota are spent on queries that will keep returning nothing.
options.rationale: A valid empty result is the answer, so retrying it can never change the outcome.

options.text: Partial results from earlier subagents are overwritten on each successive rerun.
options.rationale: Rerunning a query does not overwrite another agent's collected output.

options.text: The coordinator loses its ability to tell the four failure types apart.
options.rationale: The type information remains present in each structured report.

cards.explanation: Retrying a valid empty result burns time and resources on a query that will always return nothing.

cards.prompt: After three backoff attempts fail, a subagent returns the single status 'search unavailable'. What does the coordinator lose?

options.text: Nothing significant, because the coordinator only needs to know whether to retry.
options.rationale: It also has to choose among alternatives and decide what to do with partial results.

options.text: Its ability to run retries of its own, which the subagent has already consumed.
options.rationale: Local retries do not forbid a further coordinator-level attempt.

options.text: The failure type, which can no longer be determined once retries are exhausted.
options.rationale: The type is perfectly knowable; the generic message simply omits it.

options.text: The attempted query, any partial results and the alternative approaches worth trying.
options.rationale: A generic status strips exactly the context that informed recovery depends on.

cards.explanation: A generic status hides the attempted query, the partial results and the suggested alternatives, preventing any informed recovery decision.

cards.prompt: One subagent could not reach the journals covering geothermal energy. How should the synthesis report handle that topic?

options.text: Note that the geothermal section is limited because journal access was unavailable during research.
options.rationale: Coverage annotations tell the consumer which areas are well supported and which have known gaps.

options.text: Omit the geothermal section entirely, since no sources were retrieved for it.
options.rationale: A silent omission reads as irrelevance rather than as a known limitation.

options.text: Fill the section from the model's background knowledge and mark it as provisional.
options.rationale: This substitutes unsourced content for what should be a documented gap.

options.text: Mark the whole report unreliable until the missing journals can be reached.
options.rationale: That is disproportionate when only one section is affected.

cards.explanation: Coverage annotations state which topics are well supported and which are limited, so a gap is not mistaken for an irrelevant topic.

cards.prompt: Where should retry logic for timeouts and rate limits live in a coordinator-and-subagent system?

options.text: In the coordinator, so one consistent retry policy governs every subagent uniformly.
options.rationale: This forces the coordinator to model every transient failure mode of every subagent.

options.text: In each subagent, which escalates only the failures it cannot resolve locally.
options.rationale: Local recovery for transient failures keeps coordinator logic simple and propagates only persistent problems.

options.text: In neither, since transient failures should be reported immediately for a human decision.
options.rationale: Transient failures are exactly the class that local recovery is meant to absorb.

options.text: In the synthesis step, so that retries happen once all subagent results are in.
options.rationale: By synthesis time the opportunity to recover the missing data has passed.

cards.explanation: Subagents implement local retry and fallback for transient failures and propagate only what they cannot resolve, which reduces coordinator complexity.

cards.prompt: After lengthy exploration, an agent describes generic patterns instead of the code it inspected. What is the most useful context repair?

options.text: Replace the findings with a generic architecture tutorial.
options.rationale: That removes the repository-specific evidence.

options.text: Append the entire repository to every subsequent prompt.
options.rationale: Indiscriminate context can add noise and cost.

options.text: Treat fluent explanations as proof that earlier findings remain accurate.
options.rationale: Fluency does not establish source fidelity.

options.text: Maintain compact findings linked to paths, symbols and revisions, then re-read evidence as needed.
options.rationale: Concrete references support verification without carrying every raw tool output.

cards.explanation: Concrete references support verification without carrying every raw tool output.

cards.prompt: You need the call path for one endpoint in a large repository. What is a focused approach?

options.text: Read every file before identifying the endpoint.
options.rationale: That adds large unrelated context without a dependency plan.

options.text: Infer the path from a generic framework tutorial.
options.rationale: Framework patterns do not prove this repository's implementation.

options.text: Change unrelated modules to see what breaks.
options.rationale: Discovery should not require speculative mutation.

options.text: Locate the entry point, trace relevant symbols and inspect their actual dependencies.
options.rationale: Targeted exploration builds evidence for the requested path.

cards.explanation: Targeted exploration builds evidence for the requested path.

cards.prompt: A persistent exploration note points to code that changed. What should you do?

options.text: Revalidate the affected claims against the current files.
options.rationale: Stored notes retain findings, not a guarantee of continuing accuracy.

options.text: Treat the note as immune to source changes.
options.rationale: Persistence does not prevent staleness.

options.text: Trust the note whenever it has more detail than the code.
options.rationale: Length is not a source-of-truth rule.

options.text: Delete all tests to make the note match.
options.rationale: Changing evidence to fit a claim is not verification.

cards.explanation: Stored notes retain findings, not a guarantee of continuing accuracy.

cards.prompt: A delegated code search produces many raw reads. What should the parent ideally receive?

options.text: A claim that unseen modules behave identically.
options.rationale: Inspection of one area does not establish another.

options.text: A focused answer with file or symbol references and unresolved uncertainties.
options.rationale: The parent needs usable findings and a way to inspect their support.

options.text: Every raw read with no answer to the task.
options.rationale: Volume does not supply a clear conclusion.

options.text: A generic architecture claim without source references.
options.rationale: The finding would be difficult to verify.

cards.explanation: The parent needs usable findings and a way to inspect their support.

cards.prompt: An exploration agent begins describing generic patterns instead of the classes it read, and a teammate suggests switching to a model with a larger context window. How should you respond?

options.text: Agree, since the specific findings were evicted once the window filled up.
options.rationale: Nothing was evicted; the earlier findings are still present in the context.

options.text: Agree, but only if the session is also restarted so the window begins empty.
options.rationale: Restarting without saving state discards every finding accumulated so far.

options.text: Disagree, because a larger window still fills with verbose output and the detail is still lost.
options.rationale: Context degradation is an attention problem, not a capacity problem, so more room does not fix it.

options.text: Disagree, because context degradation only affects sessions that delegate to subagents.
options.rationale: It affects any extended exploration session, delegated or not.

cards.explanation: Context degradation is not about running out of tokens, so enlarging the context window leaves the underlying attention problem untouched.

cards.prompt: What causes an agent's specific discoveries to fade during a long codebase exploration session?

options.text: The model discards older messages from the session once it has answered the question that raised them.
options.rationale: The model does not drop earlier turns; they remain in the request.

options.text: Directory listings and file contents are retained in a lower-fidelity form than ordinary prose turns are.
options.rationale: No such distinction exists between kinds of content in the context.

options.text: Each tool call resets the model's working memory to only the details of the step currently in progress.
options.rationale: Prior context is still supplied on every call; nothing is reset.

options.text: Verbose output accumulates each step, pushing earlier precise findings back and shifting attention to recent material.
options.rationale: Accumulating discovery output buries the earlier specifics and draws attention to the newest content.

cards.explanation: Every exploration step adds verbose output that pushes earlier precise discoveries further back, so the model's attention drifts to recent material.

cards.prompt: When should an exploration agent start writing key findings to a scratchpad file?

options.text: From the start of the session, as a deliberate strategy rather than a rescue move.
options.rationale: Scratchpads are meant to be maintained from the outset of any extended exploration.

options.text: Once the model first refers to a typical pattern instead of a real class name.
options.rationale: By that point the specific details are already hard to recover.

options.text: Only once the session begins to approach its context limit.
options.rationale: Degradation is not tied to the limit, so waiting for it misses the problem.

options.text: After the exploration finishes, as a record for whoever picks it up next.
options.rationale: That misses the purpose of protecting the current session's findings.

cards.explanation: Scratchpad files should be maintained from the start of an extended exploration session, not adopted after degradation has already appeared.

cards.prompt: Which scratchpad entry best serves an agent that will face follow-up questions about a refund flow?

options.text: A note that the service follows a conventional layered design built around repositories.
options.rationale: Generic description is exactly the degraded output the scratchpad exists to prevent.

options.text: Named classes with their file paths, the dependency chain between them, and the concrete gaps found.
options.rationale: Specific symbols, paths and chains are what later questions actually need.

options.text: The full text of every source file the agent opened during its exploration.
options.rationale: Copying raw content simply moves the verbosity problem into a file.

options.text: A list of the search queries the agent ran, recorded without their outcomes.
options.rationale: Queries without findings cannot answer a later question about the flow.

cards.explanation: A useful scratchpad records specific class names, file paths, dependency chains and concrete findings rather than generic descriptions or raw dumps.

cards.prompt: A reviewer says delegating exploration to subagents is worthwhile only when the investigations can run at the same time. What is the better justification?

options.text: Subagents are allocated larger context windows than the coordinating agent is.
options.rationale: Window size is not what delegation changes.

options.text: Subagents can open files that the coordinating agent is not permitted to read.
options.rationale: Permissions are not the reason the lesson recommends delegation.

options.text: Each subagent explores in its own context, keeping verbose output out of the coordinator's.
options.rationale: Context isolation is the primary benefit; parallelism is the more obvious but lesser one.

options.text: Subagents keep their context between sessions, so findings persist automatically.
options.rationale: Persistence comes from scratchpad files and state manifests, not from subagents.

cards.explanation: The primary benefit of subagent delegation here is context isolation: verbose exploration stays in the subagent and only a structured summary returns.

cards.prompt: Phase one mapped the architecture of a service. What keeps phase two subagents from rediscovering the same structure?

options.text: Injecting a phase one findings summary into each phase two subagent's initial prompt.
options.rationale: Summary injection gives the later agents the earlier findings up front and avoids the cold start.

options.text: Giving phase two subagents read access to the full phase one conversation transcript.
options.rationale: That reintroduces the verbose output that delegation was meant to keep out.

options.text: Running phase two with the same subagents that carried out phase one.
options.rationale: Each invocation still begins without the earlier context.

options.text: Telling phase two subagents to skip any file that phase one has already opened.
options.rationale: A skip list is not the architectural understanding phase two needs.

cards.explanation: Summarising phase one findings and injecting them into phase two prompts prevents the cold start that causes duplicated exploration.

cards.prompt: How should the /compact command be used during a long Claude Code exploration session?

options.text: Only after the session reports that its context has been exhausted.
options.rationale: The lesson calls for proactive use rather than last-resort use.

options.text: Proactively during the session, to protect context quality rather than only capacity.
options.rationale: Compacting early keeps verbose discovery output from crowding out earlier findings.

options.text: Before any exploration begins, in order to clear project instructions from context.
options.rationale: That is not what the command is for.

options.text: Instead of scratchpad files, since compaction already preserves the specific findings.
options.rationale: Compaction summarises the conversation; scratchpads are what hold the specifics.

cards.explanation: /compact should be used proactively during extended sessions because it protects context quality, not merely free space.

cards.prompt: What belongs in the state manifest an exploration agent writes for crash recovery?

options.text: The raw contents of every file read, so that nothing needs rereading on resume.
options.rationale: That recreates the verbose context the manifest is meant to avoid.

options.text: Only a session identifier and a timestamp, with the findings rebuilt on resume.
options.rationale: Rebuilding the findings is exactly the loss the manifest prevents.

options.text: The coordinator's prompt template together with the model settings in use.
options.rationale: Configuration is not a record of exploration progress.

options.text: Explored paths, key findings, the current phase and the next steps.
options.rationale: This captures what was done, what was learned and where the session had reached.

cards.explanation: The manifest records explored paths, key findings, the current phase and the next steps, so a resumed session continues instead of restarting.

cards.prompt: An agent's context has degraded and the developer plans to restart the session immediately. What is missing from that plan?

options.text: Persisting findings to a scratchpad or manifest first, then injecting them into the new session.
options.rationale: Restarting without saving state throws away everything the session learned.

options.text: Raising the context limit before the replacement session is started.
options.rationale: The limit was never the constraint; degradation is an attention problem.

options.text: Disabling subagents in the new session so that its context stays simpler.
options.rationale: Subagents reduce context pressure rather than adding to it.

options.text: Repeating the same exploration steps so the new session matches the old one.
options.rationale: Repeating the work is the cost that saving state is supposed to avoid.

cards.explanation: Findings must be written to a scratchpad or state manifest and injected into the fresh session, otherwise the restart discards all accumulated knowledge.

cards.prompt: A coordinator resumes an interrupted exploration and loads the saved manifest. What should happen next?

options.text: The agent re-reads every path listed as explored in order to confirm the manifest.
options.rationale: That repeats the very work the manifest was written to save.

options.text: The coordinator starts a fresh manifest and treats the saved one as history.
options.rationale: The point of the manifest is to continue from the recorded state.

options.text: The manifest is injected into the agent's prompt so it continues from the recorded next steps.
options.rationale: Injecting the saved state lets the agent pick up where it left off without repeating exploration.

options.text: The coordinator asks the user to restate the original exploration objective.
options.rationale: The objective and the next steps are already captured in the manifest.

cards.explanation: On resume the coordinator loads the manifest and injects it into the agent's prompt so exploration continues from the recorded next steps.

cards.prompt: Overall extraction accuracy is high, but scanned forms often fail. What should guide the review policy?

options.text: Measure performance by document slice and calibrate review decisions against labeled cases.
options.rationale: Aggregate accuracy can conceal weak subgroups; observed errors should inform review allocation.

options.text: Use overall accuracy to exempt every document type from review.
options.rationale: A strong aggregate does not establish quality on the failing slice.

options.text: Use only the model's self-reported confidence without checking it.
options.rationale: Uncalibrated confidence is not demonstrated reliability.

options.text: Review only the document type that already performs best.
options.rationale: That can neglect the known failure concentration.

cards.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can conceal weak subgroups; observed errors should inform review allocation.

cards.prompt: Only low-confidence outputs receive human review. What blind spot remains?

options.text: All low-confidence outputs must actually be correct.
options.rationale: Review selection does not establish their outcome.

options.text: The number of reviewers determines every model prediction.
options.rationale: Review staffing does not control the model's original correctness.

options.text: Confident errors in the automatically accepted population.
options.rationale: Sampling accepted outputs can reveal mistakes confidence failed to flag.

options.text: There can be no blind spot above the threshold.
options.rationale: An unverified threshold does not guarantee accuracy.

cards.explanation: Sampling accepted outputs can reveal mistakes confidence failed to flag.

cards.prompt: Among outputs assigned confidence 0.9, about 60% are correct on representative labeled cases. What does this suggest?

options.text: The system is perfectly calibrated because the score is high.
options.rationale: Calibration compares scores with outcomes.

options.text: Every individual output is exactly 60% correct.
options.rationale: A group frequency is not a per-output fractional truth score.

options.text: The labels can be ignored because the model supplied a number.
options.rationale: Calibration requires comparison against trustworthy outcomes.

options.text: The confidence is overestimated for that evaluated population.
options.rationale: The score exceeds its observed correctness frequency.

cards.explanation: The score exceeds its observed correctness frequency.

cards.prompt: A new document format enters production after review thresholds were calibrated. What should happen?

options.text: Evaluate the new slice and adjust review routing using evidence.
options.rationale: Old calibration may not transfer to a changed input distribution.

options.text: Assume the previous aggregate covers the new format.
options.rationale: The new slice may behave differently.

options.text: Automatically exempt the format from review.
options.rationale: There is no supporting quality evidence yet.

options.text: Choose a threshold based only on filename length.
options.rationale: That has no established relationship to error risk.

cards.explanation: Old calibration may not transfer to a changed input distribution.

cards.prompt: An extraction system reports 97% aggregate date accuracy while international documents sit near 45%. How can both figures be true?

options.text: The aggregate is computed from the best-performing document type only.
options.rationale: The aggregate covers all types, which is why it is misleading rather than wrong.

options.text: Standard invoices dominate the volume, so the volume-weighted average hides the weak segments.
options.rationale: A dominant high-accuracy type pulls the average up and conceals segments that fail badly.

options.text: Rare document types are excluded from the aggregate until enough samples accumulate.
options.rationale: The weak types are included in the figure and still masked by volume.

options.text: The aggregate measures whether a field was populated rather than whether it was correct.
options.rationale: It is an accuracy figure over the same fields, not a completeness measure.

cards.explanation: The aggregate is volume-weighted, so a dominant high-accuracy document type conceals segments with unacceptable error rates.

cards.prompt: What must be validated before any part of an extraction pipeline is automated?

options.text: The aggregate accuracy measured across all documents processed last quarter.
options.rationale: Aggregate figures are exactly what hide the risky segments.

options.text: The average of the per-field confidence scores that the model reports.
options.rationale: Raw confidence scores are uncalibrated and cannot stand in for measured accuracy.

options.text: The throughput each reviewer sustains at the current review volume.
options.rationale: Reviewer capacity is a staffing question, not an accuracy validation.

options.text: Accuracy broken down by document type and by field segment.
options.rationale: Per-type and per-field validation is the rule the lesson states before any automation.

cards.explanation: Automation decisions require accuracy validated by document type and by field segment, never aggregate metrics alone.

cards.prompt: You are designing ongoing verification sampling for an extraction system. What defines the strata you sample from?

options.text: Document type, confidence band and field type.
options.rationale: These are the strata the lesson names for representative sampling.

options.text: The calendar week in which each document arrived for processing.
options.rationale: Arrival time does not track where errors actually concentrate.

options.text: The reviewer who happens to be available to check the item.
options.rationale: Staffing does not define a stratum of the data.

options.text: The order in which the extractions were written to the database.
options.rationale: Insertion order carries no signal about accuracy.

cards.explanation: Stratified sampling draws a representative sample from each stratum: document type, confidence band and field type.

cards.prompt: Beyond confirming that each segment still meets its validated accuracy, what does stratified sampling provide?

options.text: A replacement for the labelled validation set used during calibration.
options.rationale: Calibration still requires ground truth labels; sampling does not replace them.

options.text: A way to reduce how many documents need to be extracted at all.
options.rationale: Sampling verifies output; it does not reduce the input volume.

options.text: Detection of novel error patterns that were absent from the original validation set.
options.rationale: Sampling automated high-confidence output is the only way new failure modes surface.

options.text: Proof that reviewer capacity is spread evenly across all document types.
options.rationale: Even distribution of reviewers is the anti-pattern, not a goal to demonstrate.

cards.explanation: Stratified sampling both measures ongoing accuracy per segment and detects novel failure modes that the original validation set never contained.

cards.prompt: A model reports 0.90 confidence on a date field and 0.90 on an amount field. What can you conclude?

options.text: The two fields are equally likely to be correct, since the reported scores match.
options.rationale: Identical scores can correspond to quite different observed accuracy.

options.text: Nothing yet, because the same score maps to different real accuracy per field and document type.
options.rationale: Raw confidence is relative rather than absolute and means nothing until calibrated.

options.text: Both fields are correct roughly 90% of the time, which is what the score states.
options.rationale: Raw scores are not probabilities of correctness.

options.text: The amount field is the more trustworthy of the two, since numeric fields are easier to read.
options.rationale: In the lesson's data amount fields calibrate worse than dates, not better.

cards.explanation: Raw confidence is relative, so 0.90 on dates and 0.90 on amounts can correspond to very different actual accuracy rates.

cards.prompt: What is required to turn raw confidence scores into thresholds you can route on?

options.text: A larger sample of production extractions with no ground truth attached to them.
options.rationale: Without labels there is nothing to compare the reported scores against.

options.text: Instructions telling the model to report its confidence more conservatively.
options.rationale: Rewording the prompt does not calibrate the resulting number.

options.text: A second model that scores the first model's outputs for agreement with it.
options.rationale: Agreement between models is not the same as measured accuracy.

options.text: A labelled validation set used to compare reported confidence against actual accuracy.
options.rationale: Ground truth data is what produces the calibration curve that thresholds rest on.

cards.explanation: Calibration compares reported confidence against known-correct extractions from a labelled validation set to build a calibration curve.

cards.prompt: Once thresholds have been calibrated, how should extracted fields be routed?

options.text: Above threshold to automation with stratified sampling, below to review, ambiguous zone to prioritised review.
options.rationale: This is the three-way routing that calibrated thresholds are meant to drive.

options.text: Above threshold to automation with no further checking at all, and every other field to review.
options.rationale: Automated output still needs stratified sampling to catch novel errors.

options.text: All fields to human review regardless of score, with the thresholds used only for reporting.
options.rationale: That abandons the routing the calibration work exists to enable.

options.text: Above threshold to prioritised human review, below threshold to automation, ambiguous zone to sampling.
options.rationale: This inverts the routing and automates exactly the fields that need judgement.

cards.explanation: Calibrated thresholds send high-confidence fields to automation with stratified sampling, low-confidence fields to human review, and the ambiguous band to prioritised review.

cards.prompt: A review team currently checks a fixed percentage of every extraction type. What should change?

options.text: Nothing, because uniform coverage is the fairest way to use a limited team.
options.rationale: Even distribution is the anti-pattern the lesson names.

options.text: Review should be split evenly by reviewer rather than evenly by document type.
options.rationale: That is still an even spread and still wastes capacity on easy items.

options.text: Capacity should concentrate on the highest-uncertainty items where judgement adds most value.
options.rationale: Prioritising uncertain items is how limited reviewer capacity is best spent.

options.text: Review should follow arrival order so that no document waits longer than another.
options.rationale: Chronological service ignores uncertainty entirely.

cards.explanation: Spreading reviewers evenly wastes effort on items the model already handles well, so capacity should go to the most uncertain items first.

cards.prompt: How should the pending human review queue behave as new extractions keep arriving?

options.text: It should stay fixed once built, so reviewers can finish the batch they started.
options.rationale: A static order ignores newly arrived items that are more uncertain.

options.text: It should reorder so each reviewer next receives the highest-uncertainty item remaining.
options.rationale: Prioritisation has to be dynamic rather than static as the queue changes.

options.text: It should serve items in arrival order so that waiting times stay predictable.
options.rationale: Chronological ordering is explicitly rejected by the lesson.

options.text: It should alternate between high- and low-confidence items so both get sampled.
options.rationale: Sampling of automated output is a separate mechanism from the review queue.

cards.explanation: Prioritisation must be dynamic: the queue reorders by uncertainty so the next item served is always the most uncertain one remaining.

cards.prompt: Which ordering matches the validation-before-automation sequence the lesson prescribes?

options.text: Reduce review on strong segments, then calibrate confidence, then measure per-segment accuracy, then sample.
options.rationale: Reducing review first is exactly the trap; it precedes any evidence.

options.text: Calibrate confidence, reduce human review, then measure per-segment accuracy, then add stratified sampling.
options.rationale: Per-segment measurement has to come before any reduction in review.

options.text: Add stratified sampling, reduce human review, then measure per-segment accuracy, then calibrate confidence.
options.rationale: Calibration cannot come last, since thresholds depend on it.

options.text: Measure per-segment accuracy, calibrate confidence, set thresholds, add stratified sampling, then reduce review.
options.rationale: Each step guards a specific failure mode, and reducing review comes last on validated segments only.

cards.explanation: The sequence measures per-segment accuracy, calibrates confidence, sets thresholds, adds stratified sampling, and only then reduces human review.

cards.prompt: Two sources report different values for the same metric in different months. How should a synthesis preserve accuracy?

options.text: Present both values as simultaneous facts without qualification.
options.rationale: That hides the temporal distinction needed to interpret them.

options.text: Retain each value's date, definition and source before deciding whether they conflict.
options.rationale: Different time periods or definitions can explain an apparent contradiction.

options.text: Average the values and discard their dates.
options.rationale: Averaging can create a claim supported by neither source.

options.text: Select the longer source without considering measurement periods.
options.rationale: Length does not establish comparability or truth.

cards.explanation: Different time periods or definitions can explain an apparent contradiction.

cards.prompt: Two credible sources disagree on the same definition and period. What should the report preserve?

options.text: A certainty statement with no source discussion.
options.rationale: That hides the unresolved evidence.

options.text: Both attributed claims and the unresolved disagreement.
options.rationale: Do not silently manufacture a consensus the evidence does not support.

options.text: Their arithmetic average labeled as a quoted source fact.
options.rationale: The average may appear in neither source.

options.text: Only the claim with the more polished prose.
options.rationale: Style does not resolve a factual conflict.

cards.explanation: Do not silently manufacture a consensus the evidence does not support.

cards.prompt: A citation points to a real document. Does that prove it supports the attached claim?

options.text: Yes; adding two more unrelated links completes verification.
options.rationale: Link count does not establish support.

options.text: No; citations can never help verification.
options.rationale: Relevant source references are useful when checked.

options.text: No; the relevant passage must support the claim's actual meaning.
options.rationale: Existence and entailment are different checks.

options.text: Yes; a valid URL makes every attached statement grounded.
options.rationale: The page may say something else.

cards.explanation: Existence and entailment are different checks.

cards.prompt: A summary contains a factual claim whose original source mapping was lost. What should happen before treating it as verified?

options.text: Assign the nearest-looking source title without reading it.
options.rationale: Similarity is not evidence of support.

options.text: Treat the summary's confidence as the missing citation.
options.rationale: Confidence does not locate a source.

options.text: Copy the claim into another summary to make it authoritative.
options.rationale: Repetition does not create provenance.

options.text: Recover supporting evidence or mark the claim unsupported.
options.rationale: The attribution chain must be restored rather than guessed.

cards.explanation: The attribution chain must be restored rather than guessed.

cards.prompt: Which set of fields makes up the structured claim-source mapping that each finding must carry?

options.text: Claim, source URL, document name, relevant excerpt and publication date.
options.rationale: These five fields are what let a reader trace and verify the assertion.

options.text: Claim, author, word count, retrieval time and reported confidence score.
options.rationale: None of these let a reader check that the source supports the claim.

options.text: Claim, summary, subagent name, token cost and assigned topic label.
options.rationale: This is pipeline metadata rather than provenance.

options.text: Claim, source URL, reading level, sentiment and total citation count.
options.rationale: This mixes one provenance field with attributes irrelevant to verification.

cards.explanation: A finding's provenance record is the claim plus source URL, document name, the supporting excerpt and the publication date.

cards.prompt: In a research, analysis, synthesis and report pipeline, where is attribution most often lost?

options.text: At collection, because subagents rarely record the source URL of a finding.
options.rationale: The structured claim-source format is applied at the collection step.

options.text: At the analysis step, because assessments replace the original findings.
options.rationale: Analysis adds its assessment while preserving the original mappings.

options.text: At synthesis, where findings are combined and paraphrased without carrying mappings forward.
options.rationale: Combining and paraphrasing is where source mappings silently disappear.

options.text: At report generation, because inline citations cannot represent multiple sources.
options.rationale: Inline citations handle multiple sources without difficulty.

cards.explanation: Synthesis is the most common failure point, because combining and paraphrasing drops source mappings unless the prompt requires them to survive.

cards.prompt: How do you stop a synthesis agent from producing vague claims such as 'investment has grown significantly'?

options.text: Limit the synthesis agent's output length so that it has no room to generalise.
options.rationale: Brevity does not force the agent to attribute anything.

options.text: Require in its prompt that every claim in its output trace to a specific source.
options.rationale: An explicit instruction to preserve claim-source mappings is what keeps attribution alive through synthesis.

options.text: Have the synthesis agent quote whole source documents rather than summarising them.
options.rationale: That abandons synthesis instead of making it attributable.

options.text: Run the synthesis twice and keep whichever output happens to name more sources.
options.rationale: A selection heuristic is not a structural guarantee of traceability.

cards.explanation: The synthesis agent's prompt must explicitly require that every claim it produces remains traceable to a specific source.

cards.prompt: Two subagent outputs about the same metric arrive without publication dates. What risk does that create for the synthesis agent?

options.text: It will merge the two values into a single figure that cannot later be separated.
options.rationale: The risk described is misinterpretation, not irreversible merging.

options.text: It will refuse to include either of the two values in the final report.
options.rationale: It may well include them, but with the wrong interpretation attached.

options.text: It will treat the newer of the two sources as authoritative by default.
options.rationale: Without dates it has no way to tell which source is newer.

options.text: It may read a genuine trend as a contradiction and flag or suppress consistent findings.
options.rationale: Temporal context is what distinguishes an accelerating trend from a data conflict.

cards.explanation: Without publication or collection dates, an accelerating trend looks like a contradiction, and the synthesis may wrongly flag or suppress valid findings.

cards.prompt: A report section compares investment totals and growth rates across three consecutive years. What presentation fits?

options.text: A table, so that values and trends can be compared row by row.
options.rationale: Financial data is most readable in tabular form, where comparisons are direct.

options.text: Flowing prose, so that each figure gains surrounding narrative context.
options.rationale: Prose makes numeric comparison harder and obscures patterns.

options.text: A bulleted list, matching the format used for technical findings elsewhere.
options.rationale: Lists suit technical detail rather than numeric comparison across periods.

options.text: A single sentence summarising the overall direction of the change.
options.rationale: This discards the very values the section exists to present.

cards.explanation: Financial data belongs in tables, where values and trends across periods are easiest to compare.

cards.prompt: A synthesis covers market figures, recent regulatory developments and an API's configuration options. How should it be rendered?

options.text: As tables throughout, so every section of the report shares one consistent structure.
options.rationale: Forcing all content into a single format degrades readability.

options.text: As flowing prose throughout, since one narrative voice reads best across a report.
options.rationale: Numbers and configuration options are hard to compare when buried in prose.

options.text: Figures as a table, developments as prose, and configuration options as a structured list.
options.rationale: Rendering should follow content type rather than flatten everything into one form.

options.text: As structured lists throughout, so that no single section dominates the report layout.
options.rationale: Uniform formatting is precisely what the lesson warns against.

cards.explanation: Content-appropriate rendering means financial data as tables, news and events as prose, and technical findings as structured lists.

cards.prompt: One finding is backed by three independent sources and another rests on a single report. How should the output present them?

options.text: Identically throughout the report, so that the reader is not steered toward either of the two findings.
options.rationale: Equal presentation hides a real difference in evidentiary support.

options.text: In sections that separate well-established findings from contested ones, keeping each source's characterisation.
options.rationale: Reports should distinguish the two and preserve the original methodological context.

options.text: By dropping the single-source finding from the report until a second source can corroborate it.
options.rationale: This discards information instead of qualifying it.

options.text: By merging all four sources into one combined confidence figure presented to the reader.
options.rationale: A single number erases the source characterisations and methodological context.

cards.explanation: Reports should include explicit sections distinguishing well-established findings from contested ones and preserve each source's own characterisation.

cards.prompt: A document analysis agent finds two different annual revenue figures for the same company. What should it do?

options.text: Stop the analysis and return an error describing the inconsistency it encountered.
options.rationale: The analysis should be completed rather than abandoned at the conflict.

options.text: Select the audited figure, on the grounds that audited statements outrank filings.
options.rationale: Resolving the conflict is not the analysis agent's decision to make.

options.text: Report the average of the two figures with both sources listed beneath it.
options.rationale: Averaging manufactures a value that neither source actually states.

options.text: Finish the analysis with both values annotated as a detected conflict.
options.rationale: Completing the work with the conflict intact leaves resolution to the coordinator or consumer.

cards.explanation: The analysis agent completes its work with the conflict included and explicitly annotated, since resolution belongs to the coordinator or the consumer.

cards.prompt: What should a recorded field-level conflict contain besides the competing values themselves?

options.text: A conflict flag, the source and context for each value, and a possible explanation for the difference.
options.rationale: This is the structure that lets a coordinator judge whether the values truly disagree.

options.text: A ranking of the two sources ordered by the reputation of each publisher.
options.rationale: Ranking edges toward resolving the conflict, which is not the analysis agent's role.

options.text: The analysing agent's confidence that one of the two values is the correct one.
options.rationale: A confidence score is not source context and does not explain the difference.

options.text: A note instructing downstream agents to adopt the more recently published value.
options.rationale: That imposes the arbitrary selection the lesson explicitly rejects.

cards.explanation: A conflict record marks the conflict, attaches a source and context to each value, and offers a possible explanation such as audited versus preliminary figures.

cards.prompt: Once a conflict has been annotated and passed upward, who decides what happens to it?

options.text: The subagent that first retrieved the lower value, since it holds the most context.
options.rationale: Retrieval order confers no authority over the resolution.

options.text: The report generator, which picks whichever value fits the surrounding narrative best.
options.rationale: Fitting the narrative is exactly the arbitrary selection the lesson forbids.

options.text: The coordinator or the consumer, who may present both, investigate further or escalate.
options.rationale: Resolution is deliberately left to the level that can weigh the options.

options.text: Nobody, because an annotated conflict is already the final form of the finding.
options.rationale: Annotation preserves the choice for someone else; it does not remove the choice.

cards.explanation: Resolution belongs to the coordinator or the consumer, who can present both values, investigate further or escalate to a human analyst.

cards.prompt: Two credible reports give different growth rates for the same market, each drawn from a different year of data. The synthesis agent currently keeps whichever report is newer. What should it do instead?

options.text: Average the two rates and attach a footnote recording the variance between them.
options.rationale: An average is a figure neither source states, and it conceals both of the reported values.

options.text: Present both rates with their source attribution and the publication date behind each.
options.rationale: Annotating both values with attribution and dates preserves the full picture and lets the consumer decide.

options.text: Hold the finding back and escalate to a human analyst before either rate is included.
options.rationale: The synthesis should complete with both values annotated; escalation is not a precondition for reporting them.

options.text: Keep the newer rate in the body and record the older one in an appendix instead.
options.rationale: This is still arbitrary selection, and it presents false certainty in the part readers actually read.

cards.explanation: Arbitrarily selecting one value destroys information, so both rates are annotated with their source attribution and publication dates and the consumer decides.

cards.prompt: What must structured subagent output always carry so that differing figures can be interpreted correctly?

options.text: The number of sources the subagent consulted before settling on the figure.
options.rationale: A source count says nothing about when the figure was measured or published.

options.text: A note ranking each source by how authoritative its publisher appears to be.
options.rationale: Publisher ranking invites exactly the arbitrary selection the lesson forbids.

options.text: The subagent's own verdict on whether the figures genuinely conflict at all.
options.rationale: That judgement belongs downstream, and it cannot be made without the dates in the first place.

options.text: The publication or data collection date attached to every reported figure.
options.rationale: Dates are what let a synthesis agent tell a real trend from a genuine contradiction.

cards.explanation: Publication and data collection dates must be required in all structured outputs, because they are what make correct temporal interpretation possible.

cards.prompt: A research subagent returns its findings as flowing prose, and the synthesis agent is instructed to preserve attribution. Why does attribution still fail?

options.text: The mappings were never created, so attribution was already lost before synthesis began.
options.rationale: Subagents must emit the structured claim-source format from the start or there is nothing left to preserve.

options.text: Prose inputs push the synthesis agent past the context budget it has available.
options.rationale: The failure here is missing provenance, not context pressure.

options.text: The synthesis agent can only merge mappings drawn from more than one subagent.
options.rationale: No such constraint exists; a single subagent's mappings merge without difficulty.

options.text: Preservation instructions bind only the report step, never the synthesis step.
options.rationale: The synthesis prompt is precisely where preservation has to be required.

cards.explanation: Subagents must output the structured format from the start; if they return unstructured prose, attribution is gone before synthesis has a chance to preserve it.

cards.prompt: What must the final report contain for every claim it makes to count as traceable?

options.text: A statement of how confident the pipeline is in the claim as a whole.
options.rationale: A confidence statement is not provenance and cannot be checked by a reader.

options.text: The name of the subagent that originally contributed the underlying finding.
options.rationale: This identifies a pipeline step rather than a source anyone can verify.

options.text: A count of how many sources were reviewed across the whole research phase.
options.rationale: A total for the phase says nothing about any individual claim.

options.text: Inline citations, or a structured reference section tying each claim to its source.
options.rationale: Traceability requires that each claim resolve to a specific source in the output itself.

cards.explanation: The final output must make every claim traceable through inline citations or a structured reference section that ties each claim to its source.

cards.prompt: How does a conflict handler decide that two findings need annotating as a conflict?

options.text: It compares the wording of the two findings and flags any that read differently.
options.rationale: Paraphrase differences are not value conflicts and would flag agreeing findings.

options.text: It finds claims that overlap on the same measure but report different values.
options.rationale: Detecting overlapping claims with differing values is what triggers annotation.

options.text: It flags any two findings that were retrieved from different source documents.
options.rationale: Two documents that agree are not in conflict, so this flags far too much.

options.text: It flags findings whose publication dates fall more than a year apart.
options.rationale: A gap between dates often explains a difference rather than creating a conflict.

cards.explanation: Conflict handling detects overlapping claims that report different values for the same measure, then preserves both with full attribution and a possible explanation.
